author: Tullie Murrell
content: To fully grasp this shift, it's helpful to see it as the third major era of machine learning: ML 0.0: Pre-Deep Learning. This was the era of hand-crafted features, logistic regression, SVMs, and gradient boosting. Systems were powerful but brittle, requiring expert domain knowledge for every new problem. ML 1.0: Deep Learning & Task-Specific Models. With the rise of deep learning, we saw CNNs for vision, RNNs for sequences, and matrix factorization for recommendations. Each team trained bespoke models for narrow tasks. This led to huge progress, but organizationally, models fragmented into silos. ML 2.0: Foundation Models & Scaling Laws. This is the current era, driven by the realization that scaling data, compute, and parameters yields smooth, predictable gains. Instead of bespoke models, organizations unify around large, general-purpose models—with embeddings as the universal interface. Most of the hype has focused on ML 2.0 in language

content: Sparse attention reduces complexity of attention from O(n²) to near O(n log n). Sliding-window sampling during training ensures coverage of long user histories. name: Scaling Laws Beyond LLMs: The Future of Search and Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? There are several main reasons: Better results for end-users and businesses: Bigger, more general-purpose models consistently outperform fragmented task-specific models. More accurate recommendations, better fraud detection, smarter personalization. This means better experiences for end-users and better outcomes for the business. Unification and organizational leverage: Maintaining a zoo of domain-specific models is expensive and brittle. A single foundation model reduces operational overhead and allows teams to focus on high-value improvements instead of plumbing. The predictability of scaling laws: The final piece of the puzzle is the reliable return on investment. Meta's research confirmed that recommendation quality follows predictable power-law curves. This is the proof that investing in more data and larger models isn't a gamble; it's a measurable engineering roadmap. This is the essence of ML 2.0: models scale, embeddings unify, and organizations consolidate around shared infrastructure.

content: . At Netflix, the same embedding can drive: Retrieval : approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search over embeddings to generate candidate recommendations. Ranking : use embeddings as input features to a downstream ranker optimized for engagement. Search : match user queries to content in the same vector space, reducing the gap between lexical and semantic search. At Stripe, embeddings serve as a universal representation of “trust signals.” A merchant risk model and a fraud model are different tasks, but they both consume the same embedding vector—because the embedding already encodes patterns of suspicious behavior

RecSys : system proactively suggests items a user may want. But under the hood, both boil down to matching in embedding space

name: Scaling Laws Beyond LLMs: The Future of Search and Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In search: encode the query and documents into the same space; compute similarity. In recsys: encode the user state (sequence of interactions) and items into the same space; compute similarity. As embeddings become the unifying medium, the boundary between the two dissolves

From models to representations : Embeddings become the core interface — reusable, composable, extensible. From narrow optimization to scaling roadmaps : Just as NLP teams track scaling curves, recommendation and search teams will plan capacity around predictable scaling laws. name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A major shift is underway in recommender systems, moving from traditional Two-Tower and DLRM models to a new paradigm that treats user behavior as a language

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This approach models a user's sequence of interactions, such as clicks and purchases, allowing Transformer-based models to predict the next action with a more nuanced understanding of intent

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . While this evolution offers powerful capabilities for capturing dynamic user preferences, it also introduces significant new engineering challenges in managing inference costs, adapting feature stores for sequential data, and solving for new user cold-starts

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For the last decade, the architecture of state-of-the-art recommender systems has been a story of two models: the Two-Tower for efficient retrieval and the Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) for powerful, feature-based ranking

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This paradigm was stable, effective, and scaled to billions of users

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Now, that era is giving way to a new one

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Sparked by a wave of research, including Meta's influential "Generative Recommenders" paper, the industry is rapidly shifting towards a new paradigm: treating user behavior as a language

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This isn't just an incremental improvement; it's a fundamental change in how we represent user intent and build our systems

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This post is a deep dive into this new world

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We will deconstruct the modeling techniques that make this possible, and then map out the new set of engineering challenges that teams face when taking these powerful models to production.

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The core idea is to move away from summarizing a user's history in a fixed-size feature vector and instead to model the raw, ordered sequence of their recent interactions
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The New Paradigm: Modeling Behavior As Language"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A user's history, like [viewed_item_A, clicked_item_B, purchased_item_B, ...] , is treated like a sentence
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The New Paradigm: Modeling Behavior As Language"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The model, typically a Transformer, learns the "grammar" and "vocabulary" of that user's behavior to predict the next "word"—the next item they are most likely to interact with
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The New Paradigm: Modeling Behavior As Language"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This approach, building on a history of research from N-Grams to SASRec and BERT4Rec , moves the burden of intelligence from the feature pipeline to the model architecture itself.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The New Paradigm: Modeling Behavior As Language"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: While we often simplify the input sequence to a list of item IDs, a production system typically uses a much richer representation for each step
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Anatomy of a Token: It's More Than Just an Item ID"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A single "token" or time-step in the sequence is often a concatenation of multiple embeddings
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Anatomy of a Token: It's More Than Just an Item ID"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For a given interaction, this might include: The Item's Semantic ID embedding. An Action Type embedding (e.g., view, click, add_to_cart, purchase). A Time Delta embedding (representing the time elapsed since the previous action, often bucketized). A Dwell Time embedding (representing how long the user spent on the item). This multi-modal representation allows the Transformer's attention mechanism to learn far more nuanced patterns, like "the user quickly clicks through several items (low_dwell_time) before making a considered purchase (high_dwell_time) on an item they've seen before."
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Anatomy of a Token: It's More Than Just an Item ID"}

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A major challenge is that the "vocabulary" of items is not static

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A standard Transformer with a fixed vocabulary can't handle this

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where the Semantic ID comes in, a technique detailed in Google's "Better Generalization with Semantic IDs." The process is a two-stage masterpiece: Offline Compression: A Residual-Quantized Variational Autoencoder (RQ-VAE) is trained to compress rich, high-dimensional content embeddings into a short, hierarchical sequence of discrete codes (e.g., [1024, 45, 1888, 9]). This sequence is the Semantic ID. Online Adaptation: In the ranking model, instead of learning one embedding per item, you learn embeddings for smaller, shared "subwords" of the Semantic ID, often using a SentencePiece Model (SPM) . This provides the best of both worlds: the generalization of content embeddings (solving the item cold-start problem) and the memorization capacity of discrete IDs.

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The user's history is not the only signal

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The model still needs to understand the real-time context

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A common advanced architecture is a dual-stream model

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . One stream (a Transformer) processes the sequence of user interactions, while a second stream (an MLP) processes request-time features

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But representing actions within the sequence is computationally expensive

name: Modeling Behavior As Language: The Next Era of Recommendations
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A production ranking system requires a robust MLOps backbone to function as a reliable, ever-improving "model factory."

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The first step in automating our system is to move beyond running train.py on a laptop or a single VM

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A production training process is a multi-step pipeline that needs to be executed reliably and repeatedly

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A typical ranking model training pipeline might include: Data Extraction: Pulling the latest training data from the Offline Feature Store. Data Validation: Checking for data quality issues, unexpected shifts in distribution, etc. Model Training: Running the actual training job, often on specialized hardware. Model Evaluation: Calculating offline metrics (like NDCG) on a hold-out test set. Model Validation: Comparing the new model's metrics against the currently deployed model. Model Registration: If the new model is better, publishing it to a central Model Registry. Executing these steps manually is slow and error-prone

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We need a workflow orchestrator to manage this pipeline

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Technology Choices: Apache Airflow: The classic, battle-tested choice. It's great for complex, schedule-based batch jobs but can be heavy for ML-specific workflows. Kubeflow Pipelines: A Kubernetes-native solution. It's excellent if your entire stack is built on Kubernetes, as it allows you to define each step of your pipeline as a container. Metaflow: An open-source tool from Netflix that is highly focused on the data scientist's user experience. It makes it easy to write Python-native workflows that can scale from a laptop to the cloud. The choice of orchestrator depends on your team's existing infrastructure and expertise, but the principle is the same: codify your training process into a repeatable, automated pipeline.

It provides a source of truth for your serving systems and allows you to easily roll back to a previous version if a deployment goes wrong. Technology Choices: MLflow: The most popular open-source choice. It provides a clean UI for tracking experiments and includes a robust Model Registry. Weights & Biases (W&B): A commercial platform that offers a highly polished, collaboration-focused experience for experiment tracking. Using these tools is non-negotiable for any serious ML team

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We need to monitor its performance to ensure it's behaving as expected and actually improving the product

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This requires a multi-layered monitoring strategy: System Monitoring: This is standard infrastructure monitoring. Are the pods healthy? What are the latency (P99), error rates, and CPU/GPU utilization? (Tools: Prometheus, Grafana). Data Monitoring: Is the data our live model is receiving consistent with the data it was trained on? This is prediction drift detection. If the distribution of input features changes, the model's performance will degrade. Model and Business Monitoring: Is the new model actually better? This is where we track the online A/B test metrics. We monitor not just the model's predictions (e.g., average CTR) but, more importantly, the downstream business metrics (e.g., user engagement, conversion rates).

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The most brilliant model in the world is useless without a reliable, scalable, and maintainable system to power it

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The architecture we've outlined—a decoupled microservice serving layer, a specialized data layer with feature and vector stores, and an automated MLOps pipeline—is a powerful and proven blueprint

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It's a system designed not just to serve a single model, but to function as a continuously learning "model factory," a platform for rapid experimentation and reliable iteration

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 3: The MLOps Backbone - From Training to Deployment
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Building this infrastructure is a significant undertaking, but it's the foundation upon which all modern, world-class ranking systems are built.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Welcome back to our series on the infrastructure of modern ranking systems

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In Part 1, we designed the online serving layer: a set of decoupled, scalable microservices orchestrated by Kubernetes to handle real-time requests

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We built the engine of our ranking system

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But an engine is useless without fuel

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The highest-performing engine in the world will sputter and fail if it's fed low-quality data, or if the fuel can't be delivered fast enough

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In a ranking system, that fuel is data, and the delivery systems are a set of highly specialized data stores

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Standard databases like Postgres or MySQL are not designed for the unique demands of high-throughput, low-latency machine learning inference

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A production ranking system relies on a specialized data layer

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In this post, we'll deconstruct the two most critical components of this layer: the Feature Store and the Vector Database .

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The scoring models we discussed in our "Anatomy" series rely on a rich set of features to make their predictions

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The engineering challenge is that these features are needed in two very different contexts: Offline Training: We need access to massive, historical datasets of all features to train our models. This requires high-throughput access to terabytes of data. Online Inference: We need to fetch the exact same features for a given user and a set of candidates in real-time, with a latency budget of a few milliseconds. This dual requirement creates the most insidious problem in production ML: online/offline skew

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If the way you compute a feature for training (e.g., a daily batch job in Spark) is even slightly different from how you compute it for serving (e.g., a real-time lookup in a Python service), your model's performance will degrade silently and catastrophically

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A Feature Store is a centralized platform designed to solve this exact problem.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The core architectural pattern of a feature store is a dual-database design that provides two interfaces to the same underlying feature data: The Offline Store: A high-throughput data store (e.g., a data warehouse like BigQuery or a data lake like S3 with Delta Lake). This is the source of truth for historical feature data used in model training. The Online Store: A low-latency, key-value data store (e.g., Redis, DynamoDB). This store holds the most recent feature values for every user and item, optimized for fast lookups at inference time. A feature store provides an abstraction layer that ensures that the same feature generation logic populates both stores, eliminating skew by design.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The DIY Approach (e.g., using Redis and Airflow): Pros: Maximum control, leverages existing infrastructure, and can be cheaper to start. Cons: This is a trap for many teams. You are now responsible for building and maintaining the complex data pipelines that keep the online and offline stores consistent. This includes handling backfills, point-in-time correctness for training data, and monitoring for data quality issues. This "hidden" engineering cost is massive. Managed Feature Store Platforms (Tecton, Chalk, or open-source Feast): Pros: They solve the online/offline skew problem as their primary value proposition. They provide a declarative framework for defining features, and the platform handles the underlying data engineering (dual writes, backfills, etc.). This drastically accelerates ML development. Cons: Higher direct cost (for commercial platforms), potential for vendor lock-in, and it introduces a new, complex piece of infrastructure that the team must learn and manage. Decision Framework: If your team is small, your feature set is simple, and you have strong data engineering discipline, a well-managed Redis cluster and a robust set of Airflow DAGs might suffice

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If you have multiple teams building models, a complex and rapidly evolving feature set, and a high reliability requirement, a managed platform will almost certainly pay for itself in engineering hours saved and production incidents avoided.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The second critical component of our data layer is the Vector Database

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Its purpose is to solve a single, difficult problem: finding the most similar vectors to a given query vector from a corpus of millions or billions, in milliseconds

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is known as Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A vector database is crucial for both semantic search (finding documents that are semantically similar to a query) and embedding-based recommendations (finding items similar to a user's interest vector).

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The vector database space is evolving rapidly

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The options can be broken down into a few categories: Libraries (FAISS, ScaNN): Pros: These are the engines of vector search, created by Meta and Google respectively. They are open-source and offer unparalleled performance and control. You can tune every aspect of the index (quantization, number of probes, etc.) to meet your exact latency/recall trade-off. Cons: It's just a library. You have to build the entire car around the engine: the serving API, the infrastructure for building and periodically swapping massive indexes, and the logic for scaling it. Managed Vector Databases (Pinecone, Weaviate, etc.): Pros: A fully managed, turn-key solution. They provide a simple API, handle scaling and index management automatically, and often include crucial features like metadata filtering. This dramatically reduces time-to-market. Cons: Can be expensive at scale, performance can sometimes be a "black box" where you have less control over the underlying index parameters, and you are dependent on the vendor's roadmap. The New Wave (LanceDB, In-process DBs): Pros: A new, serverless paradigm. They often use a zero-copy data format (like Apache Arrow) and run in-process with your application, avoiding network hops. This can be much cheaper and simpler for analytics and certain serving workloads. Cons: This is a newer approach. While maturing quickly, it may not have all the production-hardening or the same ecosystem maturity as the managed services for all use cases.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: One of the most important practical considerations when choosing a vector database is how it handles metadata filtering

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 2: The Data Layer - Fueling the Models with Feature and Vector Stores
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Imagine you want to find "semantically similar articles" but only from the "tech" category and published in the "last 7 days." Post-filtering: The system first performs the ANN search over the entire vector index to get the top 1000 candidates, and then filters those 1000 results by your metadata criteria. This is inefficient, as much of the search work is wasted on items that will be filtered out. Pre-filtering (or filtered search): The system uses the metadata filters to constrain the search space before or during the ANN search. This is vastly more efficient but is a much harder engineering problem for the database to solve. Support for efficient pre-filtering is a key differentiator between vector database solutions and should be a top consideration in any evaluation.

roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Whether it's returning the top 10 blue links for a search query or populating a personalized "For You" feed, modern ranking systems face the same core challenge: sift through a massive corpus, execute a multi-stage ranking pipeline, and return a perfectly ranked list in under 200 milliseconds at the 99th percentile

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is not a modeling problem; it's an infrastructure and systems design problem

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A monolithic service that tries to do everything—fetch candidates, hydrate features, and run models—will inevitably fail

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It creates coupled scaling concerns: the part of your code that calls a vector database has very different performance characteristics from the part that runs a Transformer model on a GPU

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . To solve this, we must adopt a decoupled, purpose-built microservice architecture.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A robust ranking system is an ensemble of specialized services, each optimized for a specific part of the pipeline and capable of scaling independently

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Let's break down the role of each component: Ranking Gateway Service: This is the public-facing entry point and the orchestrator of the entire process. It takes the initial request (e.g., a search query or a user ID for recommendations), enforces timeouts, and manages the fan-out/fan-in logic of calling the downstream services in the correct sequence. Candidate Generation Services: Instead of one service, it's best practice to have multiple, specialized services for each retrieval strategy (e.g., a vector-retrieval-service that talks to the vector DB, a keyword-retrieval-service using Elasticsearch). This allows you to scale your most expensive retrieval methods independently. Feature Hydration Service: A critical but often overlooked service. Its sole job is to take a list of candidate IDs and enrich them with the feature data needed for the scoring model. It acts as a performance-caching and abstraction layer in front of your feature store, batching lookups and simplifying the interface for the Gateway. Model Inference Service: This is a highly optimized service dedicated to running the scoring/ranking models. It's responsible for managing hardware accelerators (like GPUs), handling model versioning, and running inference on batched inputs for maximum throughput.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: This microservice architecture maps cleanly onto Kubernetes, but effective scaling requires choosing the right strategy for the right service

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Each service becomes a Kubernetes Deployment exposed via a Service

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The real nuance lies in the autoscaling policies.

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA): The standard autoscaler in Kubernetes. It scales pods based on observed metrics like CPU and Memory utilization . Pros: Simple, built-in, and effective for purely compute-bound workloads. Cons: It's a lagging indicator . It scales up only after the existing pods are already under high load, which can lead to latency spikes during sudden traffic increases. Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling (KEDA): A more powerful, open-source alternative that scales based on external metrics. For serving systems, the most important metric is requests per second (RPS) or a related metric from a message queue. Pros: It's a leading indicator . It scales proactively based on incoming demand, allowing for much more responsive and stable performance under variable load. Cons: Requires installing and managing the KEDA operator. Here's a decision framework for our ranking system:

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Running this entire pipeline on a single type of machine is incredibly inefficient

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Each service has a different performance profile and requires different hardware to operate optimally
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Hardware Question: Matching Compute to the Workload"}

name: The Infrastructure of Modern Ranking Systems, Part 1: The Serving Layer - Real-time Ranking at Scale
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Candidate Generation & Feature Hydration: These services are typically CPU-bound . Their work involves network calls, data serialization/deserialization, and simple business logic. Heavy-duty, standard CPU-based nodes are the most cost-effective choice. Feature Store (The Dependency): While not a service we build, the online feature store it relies on is Memory-bound . Its performance is dictated by how much of the feature data can be kept in RAM for low-latency access. This service should run on high-memory instances. Model Inference: This is where specialized hardware provides a massive return on investment. For complex ranking models like Transformers or large DLRMs, running batched inference on GPUs can provide a 10-100x throughput increase over CPUs. This is often the key to meeting a strict latency budget. Deploying these models using a dedicated inference server like NVIDIA's Triton Inference Server or TorchServe is best practice, as they handle batching, model versioning, and hardware optimization automatically.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Welcome to the final post in our series on the anatomy of modern recommender systems

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Over the last four parts, we've deconstructed the online request path, following a user's request from the initial billions of items all the way to a final, ranked page.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: In Part 1 , we established the multi-stage architecture. In Part 2 , we covered the Retrieval Stage , where we generated a high-recall candidate set. In Part 3 , we dove into the Scoring Stage , where we assigned precise, pointwise scores to each candidate. In Part 4 , we explored the Ordering Stage , where we applied listwise logic like diversity and exploration to construct a final page. A recommender system that only serves results is a static, unintelligent system
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Data and Evaluation Engine"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The true power of a modern recommender lies in its ability to learn from its own outputs
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Data and Evaluation Engine"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It is a data product , a living system that is constantly being shaped by the interactions of its users
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Data and Evaluation Engine"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In this final post, we will "zoom out" from the online request path and look at the infrastructure that powers this learning: the feedback loop and the evaluation engine
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Data and Evaluation Engine"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is the circulatory and nervous system of the recommender, responsible for processing user feedback and measuring whether our changes are actually making the product better.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Data and Evaluation Engine"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The feedback loop is the data pipeline that turns user interactions into training signals for the next generation of our models
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Engine of Improvement"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It is a continuous, cyclical process that connects the online serving system to the offline training world
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Engine of Improvement"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Let's break down the key components of this loop: Event Logging: Every meaningful user interaction—impressions, clicks, watches, purchases, likes, shares—is logged as a structured event. These logs are the raw material of learning. A typical log for a clicked item might contain ( user_id , item_id , timestamp , request_id , model_version ). Streaming & Batch Pipelines: These raw events are published to a real-time message queue like Apache Kafka. From there, the data flows down two parallel paths: Streaming Path: A stream processor like Flink or Spark Streaming consumes events in real-time to compute fresh, short-term features (e.g., "number of clicks by this user in the last 5 minutes"). These features are written to the low-latency Online Feature Store . Batch Path: Events are archived in bulk to a data lake or warehouse (e.g., S3, BigQuery). This creates a historical record of all interactions. Training Data Generation: On a periodic basis (e.g., daily), a batch job runs on the data lake to generate the training datasets for our models. This job joins the raw interaction logs with feature data to create the labeled examples our models need (e.g., "at this time, for this user with these features, we showed this item with these features, and they clicked"). Model Retraining: The machine learning training pipeline consumes this new data to train updated versions of all our models—from the Two-Tower retrieval models to the pointwise scorers. Deployment: The newly trained models are validated and then deployed back to the production serving environment, completing the loop. The cadence of this loop determines how quickly the system can adapt
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Engine of Improvement"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Some systems retrain daily, while others have moved towards near-real-time learning, where models are updated intra-day.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Feedback Loop: The Engine of Improvement"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A recommender system has a huge number of moving parts

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . How do we know if a new model, a change to the ordering logic, or a new feature is actually improving the user experience

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? We need a rigorous evaluation framework

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Like the data pipeline, this framework has two parts: offline and online.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Before deploying a new model, we need to have some confidence that it's better than the current one

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Offline evaluation provides this sanity check by testing the model on a historical, held-out dataset

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Key offline metrics for ranking include: Precision@K: What fraction of the top K recommended items were actually relevant? Simple and interpretable. Recall@K: Of all the relevant items in the test set, what fraction did we find in our top K recommendations? Crucial for the Retrieval stage. Mean Average Precision (MAP): A measure that rewards putting relevant items higher up in the list. Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG): The workhorse of ranking evaluation. It's similar to MAP but more sophisticated, as it can handle graded relevance (e.g., a "purchase" is more relevant than a "click") and applies a logarithmic discount to the relevance of items further down the list. It's critical to create your offline test set by splitting your data by time

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, you might train on data from Monday to Saturday and test on data from Sunday

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This simulates the real-world scenario where you are predicting future interactions based on past data

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, offline evaluation has a fundamental limitation: the offline/online gap

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A model that performs better on a static, historical dataset will not always perform better with live users

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is because the offline data is biased by what the previous version of the system chose to show

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Your new model might be great at recommending items that the old system never surfaced, an improvement that offline metrics would never be able to measure.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Because of the offline/online gap, the only way to truly know if a change is an improvement is to test it on live traffic

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A/B testing is the gold standard for online evaluation

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The process is simple in concept: Split Users: Randomly segment users into groups. Assign Treatments: The "control" group sees the existing, production version of the recommender. The "treatment" group sees the new version with your proposed change (e.g., the new scoring model). Measure and Compare: Collect data on the key business metrics for both groups over a period of time (e.g., one to two weeks) and check for a statistically significant difference. The choice of metrics here is crucial

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We move beyond model-centric metrics like NDCG and look at the high-level business KPIs that the recommender is intended to drive: Engagement Metrics: Click-through rate, session length, number of interactions per user. Business Metrics: Conversion rates, gross merchandise value (GMV), subscription rates. Long-Term Health Metrics: User retention, diversity of consumed content, un-follow or "show less of this" rates. A successful change is one that moves these key business metrics in a positive direction

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Only after a successful A/B test is a new model or feature promoted to serve 100% of traffic, becoming the new "control" for the next experiment.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: We've now journeyed through the entire anatomy of a modern recommender system

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We've seen that it's not a single model, but a complex, multi-stage architecture of cascading approximations

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It's an ensemble of retrievers to cast a wide net, a set of precise scoring models to find the signal in the noise, and a final ordering stage to apply the nuanced logic of product design

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Most importantly, it's a living system, powered by a continuous feedback loop of user interactions and governed by a rigorous evaluation framework

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Building one is a journey through the trade-offs between relevance, latency, and cost, and between the art of feature engineering and the science of model architecture

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This blueprint is not static

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . As new modeling techniques emerge and user expectations evolve, so too will the architecture

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 5
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But the fundamental principles—of multi-stage ranking, of the online/offline split, and of data-driven iteration—will remain the bedrock of how we connect people with the content and products that matter to them.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Welcome back to our series on the anatomy of modern recommender systems

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . So far, we've deconstructed the core machine learning pipeline.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: In Part 1 , we established the multi-stage architecture. In Part 2 , we covered the Retrieval Stage, where we generated a high-recall candidate set. In Part 3 , we dove into the Scoring Stage, where we assigned precise, pointwise scores to each of those candidates. At the end of the last stage, we were left with a list of roughly a thousand candidate items, each with one or more independent scores (e.g., p(click), expected_watch_time )
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A naive approach would be to simply sort this list by our primary score and call it a day
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is a common mistake that separates a basic recommender from a production-grade system
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A simple sorted list is not a product
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It often leads to a monotonous, unengaging, and commercially suboptimal user experience
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Ordering Stage is the final, crucial mile
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Its job is to take the raw, scored candidates and apply listwise logic to construct the final page or feed
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where machine learning predictions meet product design, business rules, and a holistic view of the user experience
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The thinking shifts from "how good is this one item?" (pointwise) to "how good is this set of items together?" (listwise).
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Ordering Stage: From Scores to a Final Page"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: If you sort a list of YouTube video recommendations purely by predicted click-through rate, you will likely get ten videos from the same creator on the same topic
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Problem with a Simple Sort: Homogeneity and Filter Bubbles"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If you sort an e-commerce catalog purely by p(purchase) , you might see ten nearly identical-looking black t-shirts
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Problem with a Simple Sort: Homogeneity and Filter Bubbles"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is because the scoring model, working pointwise, correctly identifies that if a user is likely to engage with one of these items, they are probably likely to engage with all of them
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Problem with a Simple Sort: Homogeneity and Filter Bubbles"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But showing a user ten of the same thing is a terrible experience
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Problem with a Simple Sort: Homogeneity and Filter Bubbles"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is the homogeneity problem , and it's the first thing the Ordering Stage must solve.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Problem with a Simple Sort: Homogeneity and Filter Bubbles"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The most common and effective algorithm for solving this is Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR)

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The intuition is simple: we want to build our final ranked list greedily, one item at a time

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . At each step, we select the item that offers the best trade-off between its individual relevance and its novelty compared to the items we've already selected

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . MMR is defined by the following formula for selecting the next item i from the set of unselected candidates C: MMR(i) = λ * Score(i) - (1 - λ) * max_{j ∈ S} Similarity(i, j) Let's break this down: Score(i) : The original relevance score from our scoring model. Similarity(i, j) : A measure of similarity between candidate item i and an already selected item j. This is often the cosine similarity of their item embeddings. S: The set of items already selected for our final list. λ (lambda): A tuning parameter between 0 and 1 that controls the trade-off. If λ = 1, the formula ignores similarity, and we're back to a simple sort by score. If λ = 0, the formula ignores relevance and picks the most dissimilar items, which is not what we want. A typical value is around λ = 0.7, which prioritizes relevance but applies a penalty for redundancy. Here is a simple, clear Python implementation of the MMR algorithm: mmr_rerank.py 📋 Copy 1 import numpy as np 2 from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity 3 4 def maximal_marginal_relevance( 5 candidate_embeddings: np.ndarray, 6 candidate_scores: np.ndarray, 7 selected_indices: list, 8 lambda_param: float = 0.7, 9 top_k: int = 10 10 ) -> list: 11 """ 12 Performs Maximal Marginal Relevance to re-rank a list of candidates

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 13 Args: 14 candidate_embeddings (np.ndarray): Embeddings for all candidate items

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 15 candidate_scores (np.ndarray): Original relevance scores for all candidates

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 16 selected_indices (list): The list of indices already selected (can start empty)

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 17 lambda_param (float): The trade-off parameter between relevance and diversity

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 18 top_k (int): The number of items to select for the final list

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 19 Returns: 20 list: A list of indices representing the re-ranked items

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 21 """ 22 num_candidates = len (candidate_scores) 23 remaining_indices = list ( set ( range (num_candidates)) - set (selected_indices)) 24 25 while len (selected_indices) < top_k and remaining_indices: 26 mmr_scores = {} 27 28 for i in remaining_indices: 29 relevance_score = candidate_scores[i] 30 31 if not selected_indices: 32 diversity_penalty = 0 33 else : 34 selected_embeddings = candidate_embeddings[selected_indices] 35 candidate_embedding = candidate_embeddings[i].reshape( 1 , - 1 ) 36 similarity_with_selected = cosine_similarity(candidate_embedding, selected_embeddings) 37 diversity_penalty = np.max(similarity_with_selected) 38 39 mmr_scores[i] = lambda_param * relevance_score - (1 - lambda_param) * diversity_penalty 40 41 best_candidate_index = max (mmr_scores, key=mmr_scores.get) 42 selected_indices.append(best_candidate_index) 43 remaining_indices.remove(best_candidate_index) 44 45 return selected_indices

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The models and algorithms we've discussed so far are masters of exploitation
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Explore-Exploit Trade-off: Surfacing New and Uncertain Items"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . They are designed to exploit known user preferences and item characteristics to predict the most likely positive outcomes
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Explore-Exploit Trade-off: Surfacing New and Uncertain Items"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If a user has clicked on 10 sci-fi movie recommendations, the model will confidently predict they will click on an 11th
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Explore-Exploit Trade-off: Surfacing New and Uncertain Items"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If left unchecked, this pure exploitation leads to two severe problems: User Monotony: The user gets stuck in a "filter bubble," only ever seeing recommendations similar to what they've engaged with in the past. We never discover if their interests have evolved or if they might enjoy a different genre. Item Starvation & Feedback Loops: New items, which have no interaction data, will receive very low scores from the scoring model. They will never be surfaced, never gather interactions, and therefore will always have low scores. The system creates a self-fulfilling prophecy where only popular items stay popular. This is a classic feedback loop . The Ordering Stage is where we must explicitly break this loop by injecting exploration
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Explore-Exploit Trade-off: Surfacing New and Uncertain Items"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We need to intelligently surface items that the model is uncertain about, giving them a chance to be seen and gather data
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Explore-Exploit Trade-off: Surfacing New and Uncertain Items"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here are a few common, practical strategies for managing the explore-exploit trade-off.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Explore-Exploit Trade-off: Surfacing New and Uncertain Items"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The simplest method is to apply a heuristic "boost" to the scores of new or under-exposed items

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Age-Based Boosting: A common formula is to add a bonus to an item's score that decays with its age or the number of impressions it has received. final_score = model_score + w_boost * exp(-decay_rate * item_age_in_hours) This gives new items a temporary lift, allowing them to compete with established items

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The w_boost and decay_rate are hyperparameters that are tuned to control how aggressively the system explores

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Cold-Start Slots: A variation on this is to use the "slotting" technique we'll discuss later to reserve specific slots in the ranking for new items (e.g., "always show one item from the 'New Arrivals' retriever in the top 10").

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A more principled approach is to use a probabilistic method that naturally balances exploration and exploitation

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Thompson Sampling is a powerful and elegant algorithm for this

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The intuition is to treat the predicted score not as a single point estimate, but as a probability distribution

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, instead of our model predicting that p(click) = 0.05 , we can model this prediction as a Beta distribution, which is defined by two parameters: alpha (successes, e.g., clicks) and beta (failures, e.g., non-clicks)

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The ranking process at request time then becomes: For each candidate item, we have its historical alpha (total clicks) and beta ( total impressions - clicks ). Instead of using the average score (`alpha / (alpha + beta)`), we draw a random sample from each item's Beta distribution: sampled_score = Beta.sample(alpha + 1, beta + 1) . We then rank all candidates based on these sampled_score values. This has a beautiful emergent property: For well-known items (high alpha , high beta ): The Beta distribution is very narrow and peaked around its true mean. The sampled score will be very close to the historical CTR, so we exploit . For new or uncertain items (low alpha , low beta ): The Beta distribution is very wide and flat. The sampled score could be anywhere from very low to very high. This gives uncertain items a "chance to be lucky" and get ranked highly, allowing them to explore . As an uncertain item gets more impressions, its distribution narrows, and the system will naturally either exploit it (if it's good) or ignore it (if it's bad).

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Another popular method is Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Instead of sampling, UCB calculates an optimistic "potential score" for each item and ranks by that

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The formula is typically of the form: UCB_score = mean_score + exploration_bonus exploration_bonus = C * sqrt(log(total_impressions) / (item_impressions + epsilon)) Let's break this down: mean_score : The historical, observed score for the item (the "exploit" term). exploration_bonus : This is the "explore" term. It is highest for items that have been seen very few times (item_impressions is low) relative to the total number of requests. The constant C controls how much we value exploration. UCB effectively says, "Let's rank by the upper end of the confidence interval for each item's true score." Like Thompson Sampling, this gives a natural boost to new and uncertain items

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Injecting one of these exploration strategies into the ordering stage is non-negotiable for building a healthy, adaptive recommender system

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It's the primary mechanism we have to gather new training data, discover new user interests, and prevent our models from getting stuck in the past.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: As we discussed in Part 1, a production system generates candidates from multiple sources (the "ensemble of retrievers")
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Blending and Interleaving: Weaving the DAG Back Together"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Scoring Stage then produces scored lists for each source
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Blending and Interleaving: Weaving the DAG Back Together"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This leaves us with a new problem: the scores are not comparable
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Blending and Interleaving: Weaving the DAG Back Together"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A p(click)=0.8 from a mature organic model is not the same as a score from a cold-start model or a bid_price from an ad server
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Blending and Interleaving: Weaving the DAG Back Together"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Ordering Stage is responsible for merging these disparate lists into a single, coherent ranking
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Blending and Interleaving: Weaving the DAG Back Together"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Common strategies include: Heuristic Normalization: A simple but brittle approach is to try and normalize all scores to a common scale (e.g., 0-1) and then sort. This often fails because the score distributions from different models can vary wildly. Dedicated Blending Model: A more sophisticated approach is to train a second-level model that takes the scores from all the first-level models as features and learns the optimal way to combine them. This is powerful but adds complexity. Slotting and Templating: This is the most common and robust pattern in production. The final page is treated as a template with pre-defined slots. Business logic determines how to fill these slots. For example: Slot 1: Pinned promotional banner. Slots 2, 3, 5: Top organic results. Slot 4: Top ad result. Slot 6: Top result from a "New and Trending" retriever to ensure freshness.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Blending and Interleaving: Weaving the DAG Back Together"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The final step in the Ordering Stage is to apply a layer of hard-coded business rules and assemble the final page
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Final Polish: Applying Business Logic and Page Construction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where the recommender system truly becomes a product
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Final Polish: Applying Business Logic and Page Construction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These rules are often non-negotiable and override any model's prediction: Pinning: Forcing a specific item (like a major movie release or a site-wide announcement) to the top position. Content Pacing: Enforcing rules like "don't show more than two videos from the same creator in the first ten results." Deduplication: Ensuring an item doesn't appear in multiple carousels on the same page. Page Assembly: For complex UIs like the Netflix homepage, the Ordering Stage is responsible for assembling the entire page. It doesn't just produce one list; it produces many lists, one for each carousel ("Trending Now," "Because You Watched...", etc.), and delivers them as a single, structured response.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Final Polish: Applying Business Logic and Page Construction"}
