name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The Ordering Stage is the crucial final translator between raw model predictions and a polished user experience

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It takes a list of independently scored items and applies listwise logic—enforcing diversity, blending multiple sources, and applying business rules—to construct a final ranking that is coherent, engaging, and aligned with product goals

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We have now followed a single request from the initial billions of items all the way to a final, ordered list

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But how does the system learn and improve

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? How do we know if our changes are actually making the product better

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 4
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? In our final post, we'll close the loop and explore the Feedback and Evaluation Engine that powers the entire system's learning cycle.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Welcome back to our series on the anatomy of modern recommender systems

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In Part 1, we introduced the multi-stage architecture as a blueprint for balancing relevance, latency, and cost

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In Part 2, we explored the Retrieval Stage, where we used an ensemble of strategies to generate a high-recall candidate set of about a thousand items.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: That Retrieval Stage was about casting a wide net to ensure we didn't miss potential gems
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Scoring Stage: The Art of Pointwise Prediction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Scoring Stage is where we get out the jeweler's loupe
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Scoring Stage: The Art of Pointwise Prediction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Its job is to apply a much more powerful, computationally expensive model to this smaller set of candidates to calculate precise, multi-objective scores for each one
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Scoring Stage: The Art of Pointwise Prediction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where we shift our focus from recall to precision
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Scoring Stage: The Art of Pointwise Prediction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This stage is a higher-fidelity approximation of our "perfect scorer" function
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Scoring Stage: The Art of Pointwise Prediction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We can afford to use richer features and more complex models because we are only dealing with a thousand items, not billions.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Scoring Stage: The Art of Pointwise Prediction"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The fundamental task of the scoring stage is pointwise prediction

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For each candidate item, we want to answer one or more questions independently: What is the probability this user will click on this item? (p(click)) What is the probability this user will purchase this item? (p(purchase)) What is the predicted watch time for this video? (predicted_watch_time) Each (user, item, context) triplet is scored in isolation

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The model doesn't know about the other candidates in the set; its only job is to produce the best possible score for the one item it's looking at.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Machine learning models are just sophisticated pattern matchers
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Real Engine: A Deep Dive into Feature Engineering"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The quality of their predictions is fundamentally limited by the quality of the signals we provide them
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Real Engine: A Deep Dive into Feature Engineering"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In recommendation systems, this process of creating signals is called feature engineering, and it is arguably more important than the choice of model architecture itself.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Real Engine: A Deep Dive into Feature Engineering"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The features that power a scoring model can be broken down into a few key categories: Item Features: Static or slowly changing metadata about the item being scored. These are typically easy to source and serve. Examples: item_category , price , brand , textual_description , image_embedding . User & Context Features: Information about the user and the context of their request. Examples: User demographics ( country, age_group ), user's device ( device_type ), time of the request ( time_of_day , day_of_week ). Behavioral (Historical) Features: These are the most powerful and predictive features. They summarize a user's past interactions to model their current intent. Aggregated Features: Features computed over a long time window, like a user's historical click-through rate on a specific category ( user_ctr_on_electronics_30d ) or their favorite brand ( user_most_purchased_brand ). Sequence Features: A raw, ordered list of a user's most recent interactions, such as user_last_50_viewed_item_ids . These are crucial for modern sequential models. Negative Interactions: A user's history of what they've been shown but have not clicked on is a powerful negative signal that helps the model learn what the user dislikes.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Managing these features at scale is a massive engineering challenge

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where a Feature Store becomes essential

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A feature store is a centralized system that manages the entire lifecycle of features, from generation to serving

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Its key responsibility is to solve the online/offline skew problem

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It does this by providing two interfaces to the same feature data: Offline Store: A historical, high-throughput data store (e.g., a data lake or warehouse like S3, BigQuery). This is used to generate large datasets for model training. Online Store: A low-latency, real-time key-value store (e.g., Redis, DynamoDB). This is used by the online recommender system to fetch fresh features for inference in milliseconds. By using the same feature generation logic for both stores, a feature store guarantees that the data the model was trained on is consistent with the data it sees in production.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Now that we understand where our features come from, let's build a model that can consume them
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Foundational Approach: Feature-Based Models in PyTorch"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We will use PyTorch to build a simple but effective CTR prediction model that incorporates numerical, categorical, and multi-valued behavioral features
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Foundational Approach: Feature-Based Models in PyTorch"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This model demonstrates: Using nn.Embedding for single categorical features like item_category . Using nn.EmbeddingBag to efficiently process a list of recent interactions ( user_last_n_item_ids ) by averaging their embeddings. Combining all feature representations for a final prediction. simple_scoring_model.py simple_scoring_model.py 📋 Copy 1 import torch 2 import torch.nn as nn 3 import numpy as np 4 5 # --- Feature Definitions & Vocabulary --- 6 VOCAB_SIZES = { 'item_id' : 1000 , 'item_category' : 20 , 'device_type' : 5 } 7 NUM_DENSE_FEATURES = 1 # e.g., user_age_scaled 8 9 # --- Offline Training --- 10 class SimpleScoringModel(nn.Module): 11 def __init__(self, vocab_sizes, embedding_dim= 16 , last_n= 10 ): 12 """A simple but powerful feature-based model in PyTorch.""" 13 super ().__init__() 14 15 # --- Embedding Layers for Categorical Features --- 16 self.item_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_sizes[ 'item_id' ], embedding_dim) 17 self.category_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_sizes[ 'item_category' ], embedding_dim) 18 self.device_embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_sizes[ 'device_type' ], embedding_dim) 19 20 # --- EmbeddingBag for Behavioral Features --- 21 self.history_embedding_bag = nn.EmbeddingBag( 22 vocab_sizes[ 'item_id' ], 23 embedding_dim, 24 mode= 'mean' # Average the embeddings of the last N items 25 ) 26 27 # --- Final Classifier --- 28 input_dim = NUM_DENSE_FEATURES + (embedding_dim * 4 ) 29 self.classifier = nn.Sequential( 30 nn.Linear(input_dim, 64 ), 31 nn.ReLU(), 32 nn.Linear( 64 , 1 ) # Output single logit for binary classification 33 ) 34 35 def forward(self, dense_features, categorical_features, history_features): 36 """Forward pass of the model.""" 37 item_emb = self.item_embedding(categorical_features[ 'item_id' ]) 38 cat_emb = self.category_embedding(categorical_features[ 'item_category' ]) 39 dev_emb = self.device_embedding(categorical_features[ 'device_type' ]) 40 history_emb = self.history_embedding_bag(history_features) 41 42 combined_features = torch.cat([ 43 dense_features, 44 item_emb, 45 cat_emb, 46 dev_emb, 47 history_emb 48 ], dim= 1 ) 49 50 logit = self.classifier(combined_features) 51 return logit
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Foundational Approach: Feature-Based Models in PyTorch"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A recommender trained solely to optimize for clicks will inevitably learn to serve clickbait
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A modern recommender must optimize for a multi-objective value function that aligns with the long-term health of the business and user satisfaction
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A powerful and intuitive approach is to model the user's conversion funnel explicitly
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Let's say our goal is to predict the probability of a purchase
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We can decompose this using the chain rule of probability: p(Purchase) = p(Click) * p(Purchase | Click) This is an incredibly useful modeling strategy
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We train two separate models (or two heads of the same model): A CTR model (p(Click)) is trained on all impressions . A Post-Click CVR model (p(Purchase | Click)) is trained only on items that were clicked . This correctly handles the severe selection bias in the data and allows each model to learn from a cleaner distribution
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Once our model outputs these multiple predictions, the final step is to combine them into a single score that the ordering stage can use
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where machine learning meets business logic
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The final score is a composed value function
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . E-commerce: score = p(click) * p(purchase | click) * item_price Video Recommendations: score = p(click) * predicted_watch_time Social Media: score = w_like * p(like) + w_comment * p(comment) This composed score is the final output of the Scoring Stage, ready to be passed to the Ordering Stage for the last mile of ranking.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Beyond Clicks: Multi-Objective Optimization and Composed Value Models"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Once the models are trained offline, they are deployed to a serving environment

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . When a request comes in with its ~1000 candidate IDs, the online system has to assemble the feature vectors for each one and run inference, all within a few dozen milliseconds

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This process is often called feature hydration

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The online scoring path for a single candidate looks like this: Fetch Static/Pre-computed Features: Look up item metadata (e.g., category, brand) from a fast key-value store like Redis. These features are static and shared by all users. Fetch Real-time Features: This is the most latency-sensitive step. Look up fresh user features (e.g., items interacted with in the last 5 minutes) and context features (e.g., device type) from a very low-latency feature store. Assemble the Feature Vector: Combine the static, real-time, user, and context features into the exact tensor format that the trained model expects. Model Inference: Batch the 1000 assembled feature vectors and send them to the deployed scoring model (often served on a GPU or other accelerator) for prediction. The model returns a list of scores. score_candidates.py 📋 Copy 1 def score_candidates(candidate_ids, user_id, context, model, feature_store): 2 """ Hydrates features and scores a batch of candidates

content: . We've taken a large, unfiltered set of candidates and attached precise, meaningful scores to each one

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But a list of items with independent scores is still not a final product

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . How do we blend candidates from different sources

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? How do we ensure the final page is diverse and not repetitive

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 3
roles: Data Scientist Engineer ML Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? In our next post, we'll dive into the Ordering Stage , where we transform this scored list into a polished, fully-constructed user experience.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Welcome back to our series on the anatomy of modern recommender systems

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In our first post, we established the multi-stage architecture as the industry-standard blueprint for balancing relevance, latency, and cost

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We framed it as a system of cascading approximations, designed to efficiently identify the best items from a massive catalog

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Today, we're diving deep into the first and arguably most critical part of this blueprint: The Retrieval Stage.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The goal of this stage is simple in theory but complex in practice: from a corpus of millions or even billions of items, produce a slate of around 500-1000 candidates that is highly likely to contain the "perfect" items for a given user
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Retrieval Stage: Finding and Filtering Candidates"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This has to happen in tens of milliseconds
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Retrieval Stage: Finding and Filtering Candidates"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Precision isn't the primary goal here; recall is
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Retrieval Stage: Finding and Filtering Candidates"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We want to cast a wide but intelligent net, ensuring we don't prematurely discard the items that would have scored highest in our perfect, impossible oracle function.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Retrieval Stage: Finding and Filtering Candidates"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The speed of the online retrieval stage is bought with offline compute

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is a fundamental trade-off in large-scale systems

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The heavy, time-consuming work is done beforehand, producing artifacts that can be served quickly at request time

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Before a single user request is handled, the retrieval stage relies on several key offline processes: Model Training: If we're using model-based retrieval (like a Two-Tower network), the models are trained offline on historical interaction data. Embedding Generation: The trained models are then used to compute a d-dimensional embedding vector for every single item in the corpus. This can be a massive batch computation that runs daily or weekly. Indexing: These generated artifacts are then indexed for fast lookup. This is the most critical step for online performance. ANN Indexes: Item embeddings are loaded into an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index using libraries like FAISS or ScaNN. This allows us to find the "closest" item vectors to a given query vector in sub-linear time, trading a small amount of accuracy for a massive gain in speed. Inverted Indexes: Item metadata is loaded into an inverted index (like those used by Elasticsearch or Lucene) to enable fast attribute-based filtering. Preparing Heuristic Data: Simple lists, like the "top 100 most popular items of the week," are pre-calculated and stored in a key-value store (like Redis) for fast access.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: When a user request comes in, the retrieval stage executes a fast, sequential process.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The Online Request Flow: A Three-Step Process"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The most effective way to reduce latency and cost is to reduce the search space before running any expensive candidate generation logic

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Pre-filtering applies hard, binary constraints based on the request context

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A classic example is a food delivery app

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If a user is searching for a restaurant, the system can apply several pre-filters: is_open = true delivers_to = user_zip_code max_delivery_time < 45_minutes These filters are typically executed against a metadata store or an inverted index, reducing a potential pool of tens of thousands of restaurants to just a few hundred

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Only this much smaller set is then passed to the candidate generation models.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: No single retriever is perfect

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Production systems almost always use an ensemble of retrievers , running multiple candidate generation strategies in parallel and blending their results

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Each retriever has different strengths, and together they create a more robust and comprehensive candidate set

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here are the most common types: 1

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Heuristic Retrievers These are simple, rule-based sources that are cheap to implement and serve

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . They are surprisingly effective, especially for solving the cold-start problem and ensuring popular content is visible

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Most Popular: Returns the top N most popular items globally or by region. Trending: Returns items whose popularity is accelerating. Newest: Returns the most recently added items. 2

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Memorization-Based Retrievers (Collaborative Filtering) This is the classic "users who bought this also bought..." style of recommendation

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It excels at finding items with similar interaction patterns

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The most common approach is item-based collaborative filtering (I2I-CF)

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Offline, we build a co-occurrence matrix of item interactions

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Online, given a user's recent interaction history (e.g., the last item they viewed), we can look up the most similar items in this pre-computed matrix

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here’s a simplified Python implementation showing the offline calculation: item_similarity_matrix.py item_similarity_matrix.py 📋 Copy 1 import numpy as np 2 from scipy.sparse import coo_matrix 3 4 # --- Offline Calculation --- 5 def build_item_similarity_matrix(interactions, num_items): 6 """ 7 Builds a normalized item-item co-occurrence matrix

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 10 num_items (int): The total number of unique items

content: . 11 Returns: 12 scipy.sparse.coo_matrix: A sparse matrix where M[i, j] is the normalized co-occurrence of item i and item j

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Generalization-Based Retrievers (Vector Search) This is the modern workhorse of semantic retrieval

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Two-Tower model, popularized by YouTube, is the dominant architecture

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Offline: A model with two towers—one for the user/context and one for items—is trained to produce embeddings such that the dot product of a positive (user, item) pair is high. After training, the item tower is used to pre-compute and index embeddings for the entire corpus. Online: At request time, the user tower takes the user's context and generates a query vector in real-time. This query vector is then used to search the ANN index to find the top N closest item vectors. This is incredibly powerful for generalization, as it can find semantically similar items that have never been seen together in the training data. 4

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Attribute-Based Retrievers (Sparse Search) This is your classic keyword search or structured data retrieval, often powered by an engine like Elasticsearch

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It’s excellent for queries with explicit intent, like searching for "deep learning textbook" or filtering products by a specific brand.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: After generating candidates from all sources and merging them into a single list, a final, lightweight filtering step is applied

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This step handles rules that are cheap to compute in memory or require the context of the full candidate set

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Common post-filtering rules include: Removing items the user has already seen or interacted with. Applying business logic, like "don't show more than 3 items from the same category." Enforcing safety or content policies.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The output of the parallel candidate generators is a set of lists of item IDs
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Bringing It All Together: Merging and Truncating"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These are then combined into a single, deduplicated list, which is then truncated to a fixed size (e.g., 1000 candidates)
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Bringing It All Together: Merging and Truncating"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . At this stage, we don't typically try to intelligently blend or re-rank the items
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Bringing It All Together: Merging and Truncating"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The goal is simply to produce a high-quality superset of candidates for the next, more expensive stage of the system.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Bringing It All Together: Merging and Truncating"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The retrieval stage is a complete system in its own right, with a careful balance of offline preparation and online execution

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It's an ensemble of different strategies—heuristics, memorization, and generalization—all working in parallel to produce a high-recall candidate set under strict latency constraints

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It's the foundation upon which the entire relevance pipeline is built

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Now that we have our high-recall set of candidates, we can finally afford to get precise

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 2
roles: Data Scientist ML Engineer Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In the next post, we'll dive into the Scoring Stage , where we'll use powerful deep learning models like DLRMs and Transformers to assign exact relevance scores to each of these candidates.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: If you look under the hood of recommendation systems at Netflix, YouTube, or Amazon, you won't find identical models, but you will find a remarkably similar architectural blueprint

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This multi-stage ranking system is the industry's shared solution to a fundamental engineering problem: how to find the few best needles in an ever-growing haystack, and do it in milliseconds

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is the first in a series of posts where we will deconstruct this blueprint

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We'll go beyond high-level funnel diagrams and dive into the practical components, engineering trade-offs, and model architectures required to build a modern recommender system.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: This multi-stage architecture is not new
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "A Brief History of a Convergent Design"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It's a powerful design pattern that has evolved over the last decade as item corpora grew from thousands to billions, and user expectations for latency shrank to almost zero
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "A Brief History of a Convergent Design"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The core ideas have been refined and shared by engineering teams across the industry
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "A Brief History of a Convergent Design"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Much of the public understanding of this framework was shaped by a few seminal blog posts and papers that are still worth reading today: Eugene Yan's System Design for Discovery provided one of the clearest early overviews of the multi-stage funnel for a broad technical audience. NVIDIA's Recommender Systems, Not Just Recommender Models articulated the distinction between the model and the full system, emphasizing the engineering scaffolding required. The YouTube Recommendation Paper (2016) was one of the first deep dives into a production two-stage system, separating candidate generation (retrieval) from ranking. More recently, this thinking has continued to evolve
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "A Brief History of a Convergent Design"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Experts like the author of the Amatria blog , drawing on deep experience from Netflix, have pushed the community to move beyond the rigid funnel analogy
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "A Brief History of a Convergent Design"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Recsys Architectures post reframes the system as a more flexible set of interacting components, which aligns much more closely with the reality of modern production systems
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "A Brief History of a Convergent Design"}

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Our series will adopt this more nuanced, component-based view

author: Tullie Murrell

author: Tullie Murrell
content: To understand why this blueprint is ubiquitous, it’s useful to start with a thought experiment

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Imagine you had a perfect function, perfect_score(user, item, context)
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The \"Perfect Scorer\" Thought Experiment: Why This Architecture is Necessary"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This function is the oracle; it computes a multi-objective score that perfectly blends relevance, predicted user engagement, long-term user delight, business value, and alignment with platform goals
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The \"Perfect Scorer\" Thought Experiment: Why This Architecture is Necessary"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If you could run this function on every item in your catalog for every user request, your job would be done
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The \"Perfect Scorer\" Thought Experiment: Why This Architecture is Necessary"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The problem is, this function would be infinitely complex and computationally expensive

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Running it across a million-item catalog would take days

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Our P99 latency target is 200 milliseconds
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The \"Perfect Scorer\" Thought Experiment: Why This Architecture is Necessary"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The entire architecture of a modern recommender system is an exercise in approximating the output of this perfect, impossible function within our latency and cost budgets.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "The \"Perfect Scorer\" Thought Experiment: Why This Architecture is Necessary"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: This brings us to the fundamental engineering challenge: a constant balancing act between three competing forces

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You cannot maximize all three

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Pushing for maximum relevance with a huge, complex model will inevitably increase latency and cost

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Aggressively optimizing for low latency with a simple model will harm relevance

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The multi-stage architecture is a system designed to find an optimal point within this triangle, applying the right amount of computational power at the right stage.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The linear "funnel" model—Retrieval -> Filtering -> Scoring -> Ordering—is a useful teaching tool, but it's a simplification
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Production systems are rarely a simple, linear pipe
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . They are better described as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of components
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In a real system: Multiple candidate sources run in parallel. A vector search for semantic similarity might run alongside a collaborative filtering model for related items and a heuristic for "new and trending" content. Specialized rankers might operate on different candidate sets. A dedicated cold-start model might score new items, while a separate model scores ads, each using different features and objectives. Filtering logic is applied at multiple points: before retrieval to constrain the search space, and after scoring to enforce business rules. The funnel we often talk about is simply a linearization of the most common path through this more complex DAG for a single request
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Understanding this distinction is key to building and debugging real-world systems
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . As you can see, assembling, orchestrating, and maintaining this complex DAG of components is a significant, undifferentiated engineering effort
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Getting it right is the difference between a system that scales and one that collapses under its own complexity.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Production Reality: A Linearization of a DAG"}

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Building this architecture in practice reveals several common pitfalls

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Avoiding these is often more important than choosing the perfect model

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1
roles: ML Engineer Data Scientist Engineer Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The "Hero Retriever" Anti-Pattern: A common mistake is to put all effort into a single, powerful retriever, usually vector search. While essential, relying on one source creates blind spots. A v ector model is bad at discovering new, popular items (the "cold-start problem") and can easily get stuck in feedback loops. Production systems are always ensembles, blending semantic search with collaborative filtering and simple "most popular" heuristics for robustness. Treating Filtering as an Afterthought: Another trap is applying all your filters at the very end. The most expensive operation in retrieval is the candidate generation itself. By applying hard constraints before retrieval (e.g., filtering for 'in-stock' products or 'restaurants open now'), you can shrink the search space by orders of magnitude, drastically reducing cost and latency. Filtering isn't a single step; it's a continuous process. The Offline/Online Skew: The most insidious failures happen when the features available during offline training don't perfectly match the features available at online inference time. This can lead to models that perform brilliantly in notebooks but fail silently in production. We'll cover this in depth later, but the core architectural takeaway is that your feature pipelines must be designed with serving in mind from day one.

name: The Anatomy of Modern Ranking Architectures: Part 1

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This series will dedicate a post to each of the key stages: The Retrieval Stage : This first stage is a multi-step process in itself. We will cover how to efficiently query multiple candidate sources, apply pre-filtering to reduce the search space, and use post-filtering to clean the candidate set before the next stage. The Scoring Stage : Here, we'll take the ~1000 candidates from retrieval and use powerful but more expensive models to generate precise pointwise predictions. We will cover classic DLRM architectures and the modern shift toward Transformer-based sequential models. The Ordering Stage : This is the final, listwise step where we transform a list of scored items into a polished page. We will discuss blending candidates from different sources, enforcing diversity, and applying the final layer of business logic and page construction rules. The Feedback Loop : In the final post, we'll cover the data and evaluation engine that powers the entire system—how user interactions are logged and processed to train the next generation of models, and how we measure success through offline and online testing.

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Now, a new paper from YouTube and Google DeepMind, "PLUM: Adapting Pre-trained Language Models for Industrial-scale Generative Recommendations" (He, Heldt, Hong et al., arXiv:2510.07784v1) , provides a detailed look at the next generation of this technology

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We'll break down how their "SID-v2" enhances existing concepts, the three-stage process they use to adapt powerful LLMs like Gemini for this task, and the comprehensive experimental results that validate this new approach at YouTube's massive scale.

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: PLUM is a framework for adapting pre-trained LLMs to recommendation tasks

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Its core innovation is reframing recommendation as a generative retrieval task: instead of fetching candidates from an index using dot-product similarity, the model autoregressively generates the IDs of the next items a user is likely to engage with

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is accomplished through a carefully designed three-stage process.

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The foundation of this generative approach is the replacement of traditional, random hash-based item IDs with Semantic IDs (SIDs)
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Stage 1: Item Tokenization with SID-v2 (The Next Evolution of Semantic IDs)"}

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . An SID represents a single item (e.g., a YouTube video) as a sequence of discrete tokens, effectively turning the item corpus into a "language" an LLM can understand
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Stage 1: Item Tokenization with SID-v2 (The Next Evolution of Semantic IDs)"}

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Building on the foundational concept of SIDs, PLUM introduces SID-v2 , a significantly enhanced version created using a Residual-Quantized Variational AutoEncoder (RQ-VAE) with several key improvements: Fused Multi-Modal Content Representation: Instead of relying on a single content source, SID-v2 ingests and fuses multiple heterogeneous embeddings (e.g., from video, audio, and text metadata). This creates a more comprehensive semantic representation before quantization. Hierarchical Refinements in Quantization: Multi-Resolution Codebooks: The RQ-VAE uses codebooks of decreasing size at deeper levels (e.g., 2048 entries at level 1, 1024 at level 2, etc.). This creates a more compact and efficient SID space, where initial tokens are highly discriminative and later tokens refine the representation with lower-entropy residuals. Progressive Masking: During training, a random number of codebook levels are used, forcing the model to create a more robust and interpretable hierarchy. RQ-VAE with Co-occurrence Contrastive Regularization: This is a critical enhancement. To bridge the gap between content similarity and user-perceived behavioral similarity, a contrastive loss term (L_con) is added to the RQ-VAE training objective. This loss encourages items that are frequently watched together in user sessions to have similar SID representations, directly injecting a powerful collaborative signal into the item tokenization process. The overall training objective for the SID model combines reconstruction loss, quantization loss, and this new contrastive loss: L = L_recon + L_rq + L_con

Example schemas used in continued pre-training

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Effective Vocab Size: PLUM covered 95% of impressions with a 2.6x larger set of unique videos for Long-Form Video (LFV) and a staggering 13.24x larger set for Shorts. This indicates a far greater ability to recommend niche and long-tail content. CTR: PLUM achieved a +42% higher CTR for LFV and +33% for Shorts. Watch Time Metrics: While watch-time-per-view was lower for LFV, fraction-of-video-watched was significantly higher ( +32% ), suggesting better quality matches. Live A/B Test Experiments: This is the definitive test. The PLUM model's recommendations were added to the candidate pool alongside the existing production system (LEM+). Comparison of engagement: Percentage change byadding PLUM compared to LEM+ The results showed significant lifts across key engagement metrics: Panel CTR: +0.76% for LFV and a massive +4.96% for Shorts . Views: +0.80% for LFV and +0.39% for Shorts . These are substantial gains for a mature, highly-optimized system like YouTube's. The Impact of Pre-training and CPT (Ablation Study): To validate their framework, the authors conducted a 2x2 ablation study, training four 900M MoE models with different initializations and training stages. Comparison of engagement: Percentage change by adding PLUM compared to LEM+ The results unequivocally show the value of each stage: Random Init, No CPT (R1): Recall@10 of 0.19. LLM Init, No CPT (R2): Recall@10 of 0.23 (+21% lift from LLM pre-training). Random Init, With CPT (CR1): Recall@10 of 0.27 (+42% lift from CPT). LLM Init, With CPT (CR2 - Full PLUM): Recall@10 of 0.28 (+47% lift from the full framework). This clearly demonstrates that both initializing from a pre-trained LLM and performing Continued Pre-training are critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance. The CPT stage, in particular, provided the largest single improvement. 8-th Day Recall@10 and training loss vs retrieval SFT training step

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Generative Retrieval is Production-Ready: The success at YouTube's scale demonstrates that generative models can outperform highly optimized, traditional embedding-based retrieval systems on both offline and online business metrics. Semantic IDs are a Viable Successor to Embedding Tables: The SID-v2 approach, fusing multi-modal content with behavioral signals via contrastive learning, creates a powerful and scalable item representation layer. The Adapt-then-Finetune Framework is Effective: The three-stage process of (1) Item Tokenization, (2) Continued Pre-training, and (3) Task-Specific Fine-tuning is a robust method for bridging the domain gap and specializing LLMs for recommendation. Pre-training is a Force Multiplier: Both general-purpose LLM pre-training and domain-specific continued pre-training provide substantial performance lifts and improve sample efficiency. PLUM's results serve as a powerful confirmation of the architectural shift rippling through the entire personalization field

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The era dominated by memorization-focused Large Embedding Models (LEMs) is giving way to a new paradigm centered on understanding via Semantic IDs

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This trajectory suggests a future where the rigid separation between retrieval, ranking, and even user interaction layers begins to dissolve, enabling unified generative models that can retrieve candidates, rank them, and generate textual explanations for their choices

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Of course, significant engineering challenges remain for this entire paradigm, from ensuring inventory grounding to prevent hallucination, to managing the freshness of SIDs in a dynamic catalog, and controlling the inference costs of these massive models

name: YouTube gets ~5% CTR lift on Shorts by replacing embedding tables with Semantic IDs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These hurdles highlight the growing importance of platforms and infrastructure designed to abstract away this complexity, enabling teams to experiment with and deploy state-of-the-art approaches like generative retrieval without rebuilding the entire stack from scratch.

content: . More recently, I've been more nuanced with what I read

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For me, deeply personal blogs and opinions on topics I'm interested in (like AI, recommendations, research) are what's most interesting

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I try to avoid reading too much about big tech announcements since I usually hear about them at the office anyway

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I just don't have the time to dive into as many random technical topics, even though I'd still like to

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . So, the "top" feed has become a bit stale for me

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Despite my constant interest in HN, the content I want to read has changed dramatically, and the static ranking algorithms make me feel like I have to sift through noise

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I'm finding more recently that I've been digging through "new" to find things that might be interesting but aren't just the mainstream discussion

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . What I really want from HackerNews is a personalized ranking algorithm

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I want a feed with a bit of everything I enjoy, plus new topics I might not have seen before that may not make it to the top

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I also want it personalized based on context: in the morning, I typically want to read surface-level announcements; during work, I want denser content related to what I'm working on; and when I go home, I want more personal opinion pieces that I can reflect on

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Coincidentally, I'm the founder and CEO of Shaped , a company building a platform for recommendations and search

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Our bread and butter is "For You" feeds, and we've helped many companies with the exact problem I'm facing

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . So, using HackerNews's public API, I was able to take the problem into my own hands

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The site is at hn.shaped.ai , and it supports a "For You" feed that uses your "favorites" as signals for personalization

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I also added "similar stories" to make it easier to find related content

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In this post, I'm going to walk through how I built it

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It took under two days: one day for the HackerNews client and one for the feed—basically the time of a personal hackathon

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . At the end, I'll talk a bit about next steps.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: When I set out to build this, I didn't want to just demo Shaped's capabilities

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I wanted a legitimate HN experience that I'd actually use

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This meant it wasn't all about the "For You" feed; I also needed to replicate a reasonable HN experience where I could read posts and comments on mobile

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I also upvote, favorite, and comment occasionally, so those features were a must

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The only feeds I really use are "top" and "new," so I made sure they were available too.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: In the age of AI tools, building a HackerNews clone is incredibly easy

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I just went over to lovable.dev and typed in: "Can you build me a clone of HackerNews with a top and new feed?"

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It generated basically exactly what I wanted: a minimal web client that pulled from HackerNews's public APIs

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I was honestly amazed that it created such a nice design (arguably better than HN's 2000s feel) and was smart enough to find the public API

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Every couple of months, I get wowed by AI when I use it for a new use case, and this was definitely one of those times

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It really made me reflect on whether the last 15 years of obsession over coding and software engineering best practices had been worth it… Initital HackerNews client from lovable.dev I hit publish and tested it out a bit

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here's what was missing: Pagination, so I could scroll more than one page. Mobile support was lacking. The ability to log in and upvote. Pagination and mobile support were easy fixes with just a bit more prompting

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, logging in and upvoting were going to be more difficult, as we were now moving from a passive client to an active one.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Unfortunately, HackerNews's official API doesn't support authentication

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Lovable's first suggestion was to build our own authentication system and our own system for upvoting only within our client

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This didn't really work for me, as I wanted my upvotes (and future comments) to be reflected on the actual HackerNews website

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Again, this wasn't just being built for a demo; I wanted it to replace my current HN experience

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I kept trying different prompts to get Lovable to work it out, but it kept pushing back on this being possible

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is where a bit of independent thinking finally came in

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I realized there were definitely a lot of HackerNews clones out there (just look at all the clients on the iOS App Store)

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . How were they building it

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Well, unsurprisingly, HackerNews has an unofficial REST API for all of these POST requests

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The reasons Lovable was against using it were: Potential legal issues : I'm genuinely unclear of the risks here but figured because there are so many other HN clients, it wouldn't be an issue. This would be a different story for the New York Times, but I figure Y-Combinator isn't too worried about this (let me know if they are!). CORS problems : We can address this by adding a lightweight back-end layer for our client that makes the POST requests and returns them to the client. There was some negotiation with the Lovable agent, but I was able to get it to generate all the code for this

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For the back-end, it chose to use Supabase edge-functions (which I hadn't used before but it worked great as a lightweight serverless compute toolt)

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I needed to set up my Supabase account and link it with Lovable, but after a few approvals, it generated an hn-proxy edge function to handle authentication, upvotes, and favorites

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . With Supabase connected, I was also able to set up a serverless Postgres database with two tables, posts and events

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This would contain a cache of posts and user actions, both for performance and, later on, for building our "For You" feed

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Posts table schema, includes columns: url, score, title, author, published_at, number_of_comments, host, updated_at

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . All of these fields are used for display but also will be perfect as features to our ranking algorithms later on.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The client was feeling functional, so I reserved the rest of the day for polish

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I'm still not sure how Lovable's credit system works, but this is where I sent the most prompts

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I would do some QA, then go back and ask it to solve all the UX issues and bugs, like: Make sure all upvotes are colored, stored, and persist across all pages. Add skeleton UIs when loading. Make sure the feed loads smoothly. Make sure we're not storing duplicate posts in the database. And many more… Finally, I set up the DNS records for hn.shaped.ai , shared it with our team at Shaped for some extra dogfooding, and finished up for the day

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The polished HackerNews client

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Includes a user profile page, authentication, upvotes, and a top and new feed.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: There are many ways to build a "For You" feed

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The system for this doesn't need to be as sophisticated as Meta's or TikTok's

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . No recommendation problem is exactly the same, so we can't use the same system they're using either

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . News recommendations, in general, are quite different from social media and e-commerce

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . What makes something relevant for news

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? A simple way to think about it is with these two categories: Recency : It's more relevant if it's new. Popularity : It's likely more relevant if other people like it. In fact, this is exactly how HackerNews's ranking algorithm works, which Paul Graham explained in a comment here

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Basically, it works as follows: rank = (upvotes - 1) / (hours_since_post + 2) ^ 1.8 The intuition is that as upvotes grow, the rank grows, and as time increases, the rank decays

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here's an image of a post I made the other day that only got a few upvotes

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You can see the exponential decay on time pretty clearly

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If there were more upvotes, it would just spend more time on the front page and have a better chance to go viral.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: So how can we take this to the next level

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Personalization

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! There are two ways we can think about adding personalized relevance: Content-Filtering : What if posts rank slightly higher if they discuss similar content to what you've previously engaged with (e.g., favorited)? Collaborative-Filtering : What if posts rank slightly higher if they're popular within a segment of users that are similar to you? Ultimately, what I want is a feed that adds one of these as an extra term in the ranking function

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Something like this: rank = ((upvotes - 1) * (1 + content_similarity)) / (time_since_post + 2) ^ 1.8 For the first feed I built, I did exactly this and stuck with just content similarity

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The main reason is that content-filtering algorithms are more robust when there isn't much data

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It works perfectly fine with only my own interaction data

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Collaborative filtering, on the other hand, needs enough user data to find people who are actually similar to me.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Shaped is perfect for building these kinds of personalized feeds

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . At a high level, here’s what I needed to do: Connect the data : Get the posts and events tables from Supabase into Shaped. Create a ranking model : Define the objective function above in a Shaped model. Integrate into the client : Create a "For You" button that pulls results from Shaped. I created two Datasets in Shaped: a Postgres Connector that syncs from the Supabase database every 10 minutes, and a Custom API that provides an endpoint to push events like favorites directly to Shaped in real-time

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This real-time ingestion allows for in-session ranking , meaning the feed can react immediately after you favorite something

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . After creating those, I could see the posts start syncing

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . I went back to Lovable and asked it to push all favorite events to Shaped

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . High level diagram for Shaped powered "For You" feed

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Screenshot from the Shaped dashboard showing the posts dataset that's synced every 15minutes with the Supabase Postgres db.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Next, I needed to create the Shaped model that represents our objective

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Shaped uses a 4-stage ranking framework : Retrieval : Defines the initial pool of candidates. For us, this is the last 300 posts. Filtering : Defines items to filter out. Here, we'll filter out pages of data as the user scrolls, creating an infinite feed. Scoring : Defines the objective function we're optimizing for—our personalized rank score. Ordering : Assembles the final ranking. For now, we'll just sort by score. I created a Shaped model definition for this

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The definition is made up of two parts: Fetch and Model.

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: This section defines which datasets we want to pull data from (e.g

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . in this case the posts and events dataset)

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Shaped provides a SQL engine to make it easy to select the data we're going to need for any ranking algorithms

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In this case we're selecting everything from the database but deduplicating, for the events we're selecting all favorite events that haven't been subsequently unfavorited

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 📋 Copy 1 # Select all items features and dedupe 2 items: | 3 SELECT 4 item_id, 5 title, 6 url, 7 score, 8 by_author, 9 published_at, 10 descendants, 11 host, 12 updated_at 13 FROM ( 14 SELECT 15 id AS item_id, 16 title, 17 url, 18 score, 19 by_author, 20 published_at, 21 descendants, 22 host, 23 updated_at, 24 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) as rn 25 FROM 26 shaped_hackernews_posts 27 ) AS ranked_items 28 WHERE 29 rn = 1 30 31 # Select all favorite events unless they've been subsequently unfavorited 32 events: | 33 SELECT 34 user_id, 35 item_id, 36 published_at, 37 event_type AS event_value, 38 ( 39 CASE 40 WHEN event_type = 'FAVORITE' THEN 1 41 WHEN event_type = 'UNFAVORITE' THEN 0 42 END 43 ) AS label 44 FROM ( 45 SELECT 46 user_id, 47 item_id, 48 published_at, 49 event_type, 50 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id, item_id ORDER BY published_at DESC) as rn 51 FROM 52 shaped_hackernews_events 53 WHERE 54 event_type IN ('FAVORITE', 'UNFAVORITE') 55 ) AS ranked_events 56 WHERE 57 rn = 1 AND event_type = 'FAVORITE'

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The model section defines how our feed will be built exactly

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example it describes that we'll be pulling 300 items from the chronological retriever (one of Shaped's preset retrievers)

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It also defines the value model we're aiming for which we'll discuss afterwards

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . 📋 Copy 1 name : hackernews_for_you 2 3 language_model_name : Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base 4 5 pagination_store_ttl : 600 6 7 inference_config : 8 query : 9 retrieve : 10 - name : new 11 limit : 300 12 order_by : 13 order_type : COLUMN 14 columns : 15 - name : published_at 16 17 # Personalized retrieval using dense embeddings 18 policy_configs : 19 scoring_policy : 20 policy_type : score-ensemble 21 value_model : | 22 # Popularity 23 ( item.score - 1 ) 24 # Personalization 25 * ( 1 + cosine_similarity( 26 text_encoding( item ), 27 pooled_text_encoding( user.recent_interactions ) 28 )) 29 # Time Decay 30 / ((( now_seconds() - item.published_at ) / 3600 ) + 2 ) ** 1.8 A few extra notes: Content similarity model? I used Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base , a fine-tuned ModernBERT model great for this kind of task. How does the personalization term actually work? We look at the cosine-similarity of each item text embeddings, with the mean pooled text encoding of the last 30 previous interactions. This is providing a value between 0 and 1 that defines how similar the post is to previous favorites. Closer to 1 means more similar and the + 1 is to ensure the value is multiplicative to the popularity term. What events are we using? Just favorites and unfavorites for now. I tried using upvotes, but they were too noisy for a content-filtering algorithm, and debugging was tricky since you can't un-upvote. We can revisit this with more data. After registering the model and waiting about an hour, we had a workable ranking pipeline

author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! We can see the results on CLI with the following curl query

name: Building a HackerNews "For You" Feed
author: Tullie Murrell
