name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Collaborative filtering has become a popular choice for recommendation systems due to its ability to deliver personalized suggestions based purely on user behavior

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here’s why it’s so effective:

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Collaborative filtering is highly effective for delivering personalized recommendations at scale

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Analyzing historical data from all users can suggest relevant content or products based on patterns that similar users observe

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, it relies heavily on sufficient interaction data

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . While collaborative filtering excels with large datasets, it struggles to offer accurate recommendations for new or less active users—this is where the cold start problem comes into play

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Collaborative filtering may have difficulty making relevant suggestions for new users with little data or for items that haven’t been rated or interacted with yet

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This challenge is often addressed by hybrid systems that combine collaborative filtering with other techniques, such as content-based filtering.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: One of collaborative filtering's biggest advantages is that it doesn't require an in-depth understanding of recommended items

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Unlike content-based filtering, which relies on item features (e.g., genre, director for movies), collaborative filtering works purely with user interaction data

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This makes it easier to scale, especially in industries where detailed metadata may be sparse or unavailable.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Collaborative filtering systems adapt quickly to changes in user behavior

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The system continuously updates its recommendations as users interact with more content, providing fresh, relevant suggestions

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This dynamic feedback loop keeps users engaged by offering new items based on their evolving preferences.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: From e-commerce platforms suggesting products to streaming services recommending movies, collaborative filtering is versatile

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It can be applied across various sectors, including retail, entertainment, media, and healthcare

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . As long as user-item interactions are tracked, the system can suggest anything from products to content or services.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: While collaborative filtering is a powerful tool for making personalized recommendations, it does have its limitations and challenges that can impact its effectiveness

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Let’s take a look at some of the key drawbacks:

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Collaborative filtering relies heavily on the user-item matrix, but in many cases, these matrices are sparse

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This means that large portions of the matrix often have missing values, especially when many users and a wide range of items exist

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, if a user hasn't rated many products, there may be insufficient data to make accurate recommendations

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This data sparsity can reduce the accuracy of the predictions and may result in poor recommendations.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The cold start problem occurs when a system has little to no data about a new user or item

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . There may be no ratings or interactions to base recommendations on for new users, and for new items, there’s no user feedback to indicate which users might like it

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . While some hybrid models attempt to solve this by combining collaborative filtering with content-based methods, launching a new platform or product is still a significant challenge.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: As the number of users and items grows, the computational cost of calculating similarities and generating recommendations increases

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Memory-based collaborative filtering, in particular, can struggle to handle large datasets, as it relies on comparing all users or items against each other

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This can lead to slower performance and increased resource requirements, especially in large-scale applications like e-commerce or media platforms.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Collaborative filtering systems tend to favor items that are already popular, as they have been rated or interacted with by many users

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This can create a popularity bias, where niche or less well-known items are overlooked, even if they might be highly relevant to a specific user

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This can result in a lack of diversity in recommendations and limit the discovery of new content or products.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: There are inherent privacy and security risks because collaborative filtering often requires tracking and analyzing large amounts of user data

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Users’ behaviors, preferences, and interactions must be carefully managed to comply with regulations like the GDPR and CCPA

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Businesses must use appropriate data protection methods, such as anonymization or federated learning, to protect user privacy while providing personalized recommendations.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: While collaborative filtering remains a powerful method for personalized recommendations, the field is rapidly evolving

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Several trends and innovations are pushing the boundaries of what collaborative filtering can do

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here’s a look at the future:

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: To address the disadvantages of collaborative filtering, such as data sparsity and the cold start problem, many systems are incorporating hybrid models that combine collaborative filtering with content-based filtering and deep learning techniques

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These hybrid models take advantage of both user-item rating matrices and item-based filtering, allowing for more accurate predictions, even when user data is limited

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . By combining item metadata (e.g., product descriptions or movie genres) with user interaction data, these systems can overcome missing values in the user-item matrix and provide more robust recommendations, particularly when there’s insufficient data for a new user or new item

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Recent studies, such as " A Collaborative Filtering Approach Using Machine Learning and Business Intelligence: A Critical Review ," highlight the importance of integrating deep learning and reinforcement learning to enhance collaborative filtering systems

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . According to the study, these methods have led to a 35% improvement in recommendation reliability and a 25% increase in user engagement

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This research underscores the potential of machine learning and business intelligence tools to refine collaborative filtering, making it more effective for large-scale e-commerce and other platforms.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The rise of deep learning is enhancing collaborative filtering by enabling the model to learn more complex patterns in user behavior

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Neural collaborative filtering (NCF) and autoencoders are being integrated to capture non-linear relationships that traditional models might miss

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These techniques allow systems to understand user preferences better, improving the precision of recommendations, particularly in scenarios with complex user behavior or large datasets.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: As more data becomes available in real-time, there’s a growing demand for real-time personalization

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Collaborative filtering models are increasingly designed to update recommendations instantly based on user interactions

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This means that, for example, streaming platforms can instantly suggest a new show or movie as a user finishes watching something, ensuring the suggestions are always relevant.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The next frontier for collaborative filtering could involve generative artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance personalization

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . By using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) or similar models, businesses can go beyond just predicting what users might like; they can generate entirely new, customized content or products that might appeal to a specific user

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This could lead to even more personalized experiences, as generative models adapt to changes in user preferences in real time.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: As data privacy remains a key concern, advanced privacy-preserving techniques will likely be adopted in the future of collaborative filtering

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Methods like differential privacy and federated learning allow recommendation systems to personalize content without exposing sensitive user data

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These innovations will be crucial for compliance with stringent privacy regulations, such as GDPR and CCPA, while delivering highly relevant recommendations.

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Collaborative filtering is a driving force behind personalized recommendations across various industries

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . With over 45% of e-commerce platforms already using it to enhance product suggestions, its effectiveness in improving user engagement and boosting sales is undeniable

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . As the demand for more personalized, data-driven interactions rises, collaborative filtering will remain a cornerstone of recommendation systems

name: Collaborative Filtering Explained
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Advances in AI and machine learning will only enhance its capabilities, enabling businesses to refine their strategies and offer even more relevant suggestions

name: Boosting Revenue with AI-Powered Cross-Selling Recommendations
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Cross-selling is the practice of encouraging customers to purchase additional products that complement their original purchase

name: Boosting Revenue with AI-Powered Cross-Selling Recommendations
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Instead of focusing solely on attracting new customers, businesses increase revenue by enhancing the value of each transaction with relevant, supplementary items.

name: Boosting Revenue with AI-Powered Cross-Selling Recommendations
author: Tullie Murrell
content: While both strategies aim to increase revenue, they differ in approach: Cross-selling suggests related or complementary products that enhance the original purchase. For example, recommending a camera case when a customer buys a camera. Up-selling encourages customers to choose a higher-end or more expensive version of the product they are considering. For instance, promoting a premium camera model instead of the basic one. Both methods contribute to higher revenue, but cross-selling improves the overall customer experience by offering useful add-ons rather than just pushing for a bigger sale.

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide

content: Collaborative filtering is one of the most widely used techniques in recommendation systems

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It works by analyzing the behavior and preferences of many users to find patterns

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The assumption is that if two users have similar preferences, they are likely to enjoy similar items

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . There are two main types of collaborative filtering: User-based collaborative filtering: This method identifies users with similar preferences or behaviors and recommends products based on what similar users have liked. Item-based collaborative filtering: Instead of finding similar users, this approach focuses on items themselves. It recommends products that are similar to what the user has already interacted with, based on the behavior of other users. Collaborative filtering relies heavily on the idea of “other users” influencing recommendations

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This can be highly effective in large platforms where there are plenty of user-item interactions to learn from

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, it can suffer from the “cold start” problem, where recommendations are less accurate for new users or items with little interaction history.

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Content-based filtering focuses on the attributes of individual items

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Instead of looking at the behavior of other users, it recommends products based on a user's past behavior and the features of the items they’ve interacted with

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, if a user frequently browses electronics, the system will prioritize recommending other electronic products

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide

content: . While it doesn’t require data on other users, it can struggle to introduce new or diverse recommendations since it’s mostly limited to items similar to what the user already knows.

name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide

For example, when a user rates a product, the system gains insights into the user’s preferences, which helps refine future recommendations. Implicit Data : Unlike explicit data, implicit data is gathered from user behavior without any direct input from the user. This includes search history, browsing patterns, purchase history, and even time spent on particular items. For instance, if a user spends a significant amount of time viewing a particular category of products, the system can infer their interest and recommend similar items. name: AI-Powered Recommendation Engines: A Complete Guide

content: . Data Cleaning : This step removes any irrelevant, incomplete, or erroneous data that could distort recommendations. For example, outliers such as abnormally high ratings or purchases that don’t align with a user’s overall preferences are filtered out. Feature Extraction : This involves identifying key features from the data that help the system make accurate predictions. For instance, in a collaborative filtering system, the algorithm might focus on user-item interactions, such as the number of times a user has clicked on a product or added it to their cart. Data Transformation : Sometimes, raw data needs to be transformed into a more useful format, such as a user-item matrix, which represents interactions between users and products. This transformation helps the system efficiently analyze and extract valuable insights. By continuously collecting and analyzing diverse data sets, modern recommendation engines adapt over time, improving their ability to offer relevant content and personalized suggestions that drive user engagement and purchases.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Advanced ranking systems are designed to navigate this trade-off, offering personalized content while introducing fresh, engaging experiences

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Recent advancements have seen the widespread adoption of deep learning (DL) and neural network models, which enable more complex and nuanced recommendations by processing vast amounts of data and capturing intricate patterns

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Simultaneously, the emergence of large language models (LLMs) has opened new avenues for exploration, leveraging their world knowledge to suggest novel content beyond users' established preferences

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Let’s explore how these advancements are reshaping feed ranking, exploring the key techniques, practical deployment lessons, and opportunities and challenges they bring, particularly as demonstrated by LinkedIn's large-scale LiRank framework and recent work on LLM-powered exploration.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Feed ranking systems have evolved significantly from their simpler origins

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Early methods like collaborative filtering (recommending based on similar users' preferences) and content-based recommendations (recommending based on item attributes matched to user preferences) were foundational

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Still, they struggled with scale, cold-start problems, and limited diversity

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The shift to deep learning allowed for models that could handle more data, automatically extract features, and capture complex interactions

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A pivotal moment was the success of the Wide&Deep model in 2016, which combined a generalized linear model to capture explicit feature interactions with an MLP network for implicit interactions

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This spurred subsequent research focused on enhancing feature interaction capabilities

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn's experience with large-scale ranking models, captured in the LiRank framework, involved experimenting with and customizing various advanced architectures for various tasks, including Feed ranking, Job Recommendations, and Ad CTR prediction

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This process involved substantial effort and painstaking trial-and-error to integrate state-of-the-art (SOTA) architectures into production effectively

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Models like DeepFM, DCN, DCNv2, xDeepFM, AutoInt, AFN, and FinalMLP were explored

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Among these, DCNv2 proved to be the most versatile for LinkedIn's recommender tasks, leading to the development of Residual DCN as an enhancement.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The LiRank framework integrates several deep learning-based techniques to personalize content at massive scale.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: LinkedIn utilized DCNv2 to automatically capture feature interactions
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, DCNv2 added many parameters, especially with large feature input dimensions
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn adopted two strategies to enhance efficiency: replacing the weight matrix with "skinny matrices" resembling a low-rank approximation and reducing input feature dimension by replacing sparse one-hot features with embedding-table look-ups, resulting in a nearly 30% reduction
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . To further improve DCNv2's power, Residual DCN introduced an attention schema in the low-rank cross net
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The original low-rank mapping is duplicated for query, key, and value matrices, and an attention score matrix is computed and inserted
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Adding a skip connection was beneficial for learning more complicated feature correlations while maintaining stable training
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Paralleling a low-rank cross net with an attention low-rank cross net produced a statistically significant improvement on the feed ranking task.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "Residual DCN and Attention Layers for Feature Interactions"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Accurate model calibration, ensuring estimated probabilities align with real-world occurrences, is crucial for business success and impacts things like Ads charging prices

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Traditionally, calibration (using methods like Histogram binning, Platt Scaling, and Isotonic Regression) is performed post-processing after model training

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These methods have limitations for deep neural networks, including parameter space constraints and scalability issues when incorporating multiple features

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn addressed this by developing a customized isotonic calibration layer that can be used as a native neural network layer and is co-trained jointly within the deep learning model

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This layer bucketizes predicted values (converted back to logits) and assigns trainable non-negative weights for each bucket, which are updated during training

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Weights can be combined with embedding representations derived from calibration features to enhance power with multiple features

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Directly incorporating this layer improves model predictive accuracy significantly and ensures more accurate predictions in production.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Embedding tables, often comprising over 90% of a large model's size, can become bottlenecks due to large vocabulary and embedding dimensions, leading to storage and inference issues

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Vocabulary compression methods are employed to reduce memory usage

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The traditional approach uses static hashtables to map string IDs to integers, which can consume up to 30% of memory and are inefficient with continuous training requiring updates

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . QR hashing offers a solution by decomposing large matrices into smaller ones using quotient and remainder techniques, preserving embedding uniqueness

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This significantly reduces the number of rows needed

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . QR hashing is compatible with collision-resistant hashing like MurmurHash, potentially eliminating vocabulary maintenance and resolving the Out-of-Vocabulary (OOV) problem by generating embeddings for every training item ID

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This technique achieved a 5x reduction in the number of model parameters for Jobs Recommendations without performance loss

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Embedding table quantization reduces embedding precision and overall model size

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, 8-bit row-wise min-max or middle-max quantization can reduce table size by over 70% while maintaining performance and inference speed without extra training or calibration data

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Middle-max quantization is preferred as embedding values often follow a normal distribution, concentrating values in the middle and reducing quantization errors

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It also ensures reversible integer casting operations

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This technique led to a +0.9% CTR relative improvement in Ads CTR prediction, potentially due to smoothing decision boundaries and improving generalization.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Balancing exploration (recommending novel content) and exploitation (leveraging past behavior) is a fundamental challenge

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Traditional methods like Upper Confidence Bounds (UCB) and Thompson sampling are difficult to apply efficiently to large deep neural network models

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn tackled this using a method similar to the Neural Linear approach

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It performed Bayesian linear regression on the weights of the last layer of a neural network

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The posterior probability of these weights is acquired and fed into Thompson Sampling

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These updates are done incrementally at the end of each offline training period, allowing the timely capture of new information

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This approach has helped manage the exploration vs

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . exploitation dilemma, improving long-term user engagement.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: MTL is crucial for simultaneously optimizing various ranking criteria, such as user engagement metrics, content relevance, and personalization

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn explored multiple architectures, including Hard Parameter Sharing, Grouping Strategy, MMoE, and PLE

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Grouping Strategy, where tasks are grouped based on similarity (e.g., 'Like' and 'Contribution' together), showed modest improvement with only slightly increased parameters

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . While MMoE and PLE offered significant performance boosts (+1.19%, +1.34% Contributions respectively), they increased parameter count substantially (3x-10x), posing challenges for large-scale online deployment

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Grouping Strategy contributed +0.75% Contributions.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Understanding how long members interact with content provides valuable insights

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn introduced a 'long dwell' signal to detect passive, positive engagement

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Challenges included noisy data, difficulty setting static thresholds, and potential bias towards content with longer dwell times

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The solution was a binary classifier predicting if dwell time exceeded a context-dependent percentile (e.g., 90th percentile), determined based on contextual features like ranking position and content type

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This approach operates within a Multi-task multi-class framework, resulting in relative improvements in overall time spent (+0.8%), time spent per post (+1%), and member sessions (+0.2%).

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Modeling member interactions with platform content uses historical interaction sequences

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Item embeddings are learned and concatenated with action embeddings and the embedding of the currently scored item (early fusion)

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A Transformer-Encoder processes this sequence, using the max-pooling token as a feature

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The last five sequence steps can also be flattened and concatenated as additional features

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Ablation studies showed gains from adding encoder layers (largest from zero to one), increasing feedforward dimension, and increasing sequence length

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The optimal latency configuration was two encoder layers, feedforward dimension 1/2x embedding size, and sequence length 50, referred to as TransAct

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This technique contributed +1.66%.

author: Tullie Murrell
content: While LiRank's deep learning techniques significantly improved relevance, the balance with novelty remained challenging

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LLMs offer potential here by leveraging their world knowledge and reasoning capabilities to generate novel and relevant recommendations

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A recent thesis entitled “ User Feedback Alignment for LLM-powered Exploration ” proposes a novel approach combining hierarchical planning with LLM inference-time scaling
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Balancing Novelty and Relevance with Large Language Models (LLMs)"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This method decouples novelty and user alignment into two specialized LLM models: a novelty model and an alignment model
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Balancing Novelty and Relevance with Large Language Models (LLMs)"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The novelty model generates diverse, potentially novel, content suggestions
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Balancing Novelty and Relevance with Large Language Models (LLMs)"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The alignment model is trained specifically to rate the novelty model's predictions based on observed user feedback, ensuring the content remains relevant and engaging
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Balancing Novelty and Relevance with Large Language Models (LLMs)"}

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This allows for the independent optimization of each objective.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Recommendation systems face challenges in effectively using real-world human feedback, as they rely on noisy implicit signals (like clicks, dwell time) rather than explicit comparative judgments

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The alignment model is trained using collective user feedback gathered from live traffic interactions with LLM-powered recommendations to address this

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Feedback (e.g., positive playback, like, share, skip) is logged for each predicted cluster and the user's history

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This feedback is then aggregated for each ({C1, ..., CK}, Cn) pair (where {C1, ..., CK} is the user's historical cluster sequence and Cn is the predicted novel cluster) to generate an aggregated feedback score L(1,k),n

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Aggregating signals across user clusters helps reduce noise and bias

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The aggregated feedback is post-processed (normalized, filtered, rounded) to create training examples

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Both pointwise ({C1, ..., CK}, Cn , L(1,k),n) and pairwise (ranking different Cn for a sequence by score) training examples were tested for training the alignment model

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The alignment model, an LLM with a linear projection layer, is trained to score predictions using a cross-entropy loss against the aggregated user engagement

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In live experiments, the pointwise model slightly outperformed the pairwise model and was 2x faster to train, leading to its deployment.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The work introduced inference-time scaling to improve the system's ability to generate relevant novel predictions

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Instead of just taking one prediction from the novelty LLM, it repeatedly and independently samples multiple predictions (e.g., 5 times more) from the novelty LLM using a high temperature setting to encourage diversity

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The separate alignment model then acts as a selector, scoring these candidates based on user preference and choosing the best-of-n

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Crucially, this scaling, scoring, and selection happen offline, and the cost is amortized across bulk inference runs

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This ensures no additional latency impact on online serving, critical for large-scale real-time systems and addresses the Queries Per Second (QPS) challenge

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This dual-LLM setup avoids the challenge of teaching one model both novelty and relevancy, which can be competing objectives

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . By reflecting on the novelty prediction using an LLM aligned with user feedback, the system improves exploration efficiency by demoting predictions that are less likely to satisfy users

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The approach combines the personalization capabilities of traditional recommenders (constrained to items within the novel cluster) with the LLM's novelty-seeking behavior.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Deploying large-scale ranking models comes with significant practical challenges

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . LinkedIn shared several key lessons learned:

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Scaling the Feed training data pipeline from 13% to 100% of sessions caused significant delays due to a join between post labels and features

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The solution involved optimizing the join: exploding only post features/keys, joining with labels, then adding session features in a separate, smaller join, which reduced runtime by 80%

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Tuning Spark compression yielded an additional 25% reduction.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Adding DCNv2 introduced model training divergence issues

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These were resolved by increasing the learning rate warm-up (from 5% to 50% of training steps), applying batch normalization to numeric inputs, and using higher learning rates to compensate for fixed training steps when under-fitting was observed

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Different optimizers were needed for specific models; AdaGrad was crucial for models with numerous sparse features, where Adam was ineffective

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A generalized learning rate warm-up for larger batch sizes also improved generalization.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Constrained memory on serving hosts initially hindered deploying multiple large models

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . An initial external serving strategy for ID embeddings had iteration flexibility and staleness issues

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Transitioning to in-memory serving improved engagement metrics and reduced operational costs

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This was enabled by upgrading hardware, tuning garbage collection, and optimizing memory consumption through quantization and ID vocabulary transformation

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Minimal Perfect Hashing Function (MPHF) in TF Custom Ops initially reduced vocab lookup memory by 100x but slowed training 3x

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Hashing strings to int32 using Apache Commons Codec and fastutil map implementation reduced heap size by 93% without training degradation

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The latter QR hashing approach successfully eliminated the static hash table without performance drops.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Integrating deep learning techniques (LiRank) and LLMs has driven significant tangible results at LinkedIn

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The LiRank framework's advancements, including Residual DCN and other modeling techniques, have led to notable improvements across LinkedIn's core products: +0.5% member sessions in the Feed. +1.76% qualified job applications for Jobs search and recommendations. +4.3% for Ads CTR. Incremental training resulted in metric boosts and a 96% reduction in training time for both Feed ranking and Ads CTR models. Model parallelism reduced training time from 70 to 20 hours (71% reduction). The custom Avro Tensor Dataset Loader reduced e2e training time by 50%. Offloading last-mile transformations asynchronously reduced e2e training time by 20%. Prefetching datasets to GPU reduced e2e training time by 15%. For LLM-powered exploration, the user feedback alignment approach demonstrated a measurable impact on user experience and engagement

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . By balancing exploration and relevance through the dual-model system and inference-time scaling: Live A/B tests observed an increase in user interests and engagement metrics. The system simultaneously achieved high novelty and user satisfaction, described as a "rare combination". This resulted in a "significantly improved operating curve for user interest exploration" by ensuring content is new and aligned with user preferences.

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: As large-scale ranking models evolve, overcoming key challenges is essential, particularly regarding scaling efficiency, continuous adaptation, maintaining the novelty/relevance balance, and addressing ethical concerns

name: Advancements in Feed Ranking Systems: A Deep Dive into Large-Scale Models
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Scaling Models for Efficiency: As models grow more complex, especially with LLMs, further innovation is needed to balance accuracy with computational efficiency. Optimizing training infrastructure and improving model serving speeds are critical. Continuous Learning and Adaptation: User preferences are dynamic, requiring models to adapt continuously. While incremental training is useful, future systems will require more advanced lifelong learning techniques that can adjust in near real-time. Balancing Novelty and User Preferences: The exploration vs. exploitation dilemma persists. While LLMs are powerful for novelty, fine-tuning them to handle complex feedback and independently optimize novelty and relevance in real-time is a future challenge. Ethics, Bias, and Fairness: Integrating fairness-aware training and diversity-promoting strategies is necessary to ensure equitable and inclusive recommendations and avoid perpetuating stereotypes. Multimodal and Multidimensional Models: Future systems will likely integrate text, images, video, and other modalities, requiring models combining LLMs with vision and audio processing for richer, more personalized recommendations. By addressing these challenges, large-scale personalized recommendation systems can continue to enhance user experience and drive engagement effectively across increasingly diverse content and user bases.

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: This article unpacks how multi-armed bandits offer a smarter alternative to A/B testing for real-time personalization

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . By dynamically balancing exploration and exploitation, bandit algorithms adapt to user behavior on the fly—delivering more relevant content, faster

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Personalization has become the backbone of engaging user experiences across industries

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But delivering smart personalization isn’t easy

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits

content: . Traditional approaches like A/B testing can be slow, rigid, and resource-intensive

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Meanwhile, running complex machine learning systems requires expertise and infrastructure that many businesses don’t have

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This leaves many teams stuck in a cycle of guesswork or generic recommendations that fail to resonate

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Without fast, data-driven decision-making that balances trying new options with focusing on proven winners, companies risk losing users and sales

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Multi-armed bandits offer a solution to this challenge

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We’ll dive into how multi-armed bandits can transform your personalization strategy, unlocking more relevant content, better engagement, and measurable business impact.

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Imagine walking into a casino with a row of slot machines, each with a different, unknown payout rate

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You have limited time and coins to play, and your goal is simple: maximize your winnings

name: Beyond A/B Testing: A Practical Guide to Multi-Armed Bandits
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . But how do you decide which machines to try, and how long to stick with the ones that seem to pay off

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Traditional nearest neighbor search algorithms can identify the closest points by calculating exact distances, such as Euclidean distance, between vectors representing data points

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In exact nearest neighbor search, the system compares the query vector against every data point to find the closest matches

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . To address this challenge, approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms provide a faster alternative by sacrificing some precision for significantly improved search time

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Approach: Uses hash functions designed to maximize the probability that similar points hash to the same bucket. Accuracy & Speed: Provides fast lookups by drastically reducing the number of candidates, but accuracy depends heavily on the hash design and the number of hash tables. Memory: Requires storage of multiple hash tables, which can grow large. Best for: High-dimensional sparse or binary data where approximate similarity suffices.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Approach: Recursively partitions data space with axis-aligned splits, enabling efficient pruning during search. Accuracy & Speed: Provides precise results with rapid queries in low-dimensional data (typically fewer than 20 dimensions). Performance degrades sharply as dimensionality grows. Memory: Relatively low overhead; tree structure is compact. Best for: Datasets with low dimensionality and moderate size.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Approach: Organizes points into nested hyperspheres, allowing flexible space partitioning. Accuracy & Speed: Better than KD-Trees for medium-dimensional data; slower build times but efficient queries. Memory: Moderate memory footprint. Best for: Moderate dimensional datasets where KD-Trees falter.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Approach: Builds a multi-layer graph connecting points to neighbors, enabling rapid navigation to approximate neighbors. Accuracy & Speed: Near state-of-the-art recall and query speed; excels with very large and high-dimensional datasets. Memory: Higher memory usage due to graph edges. Best for: Large-scale, high-dimensional applications requiring fast and accurate ANN.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Approach: Compresses vectors by splitting into sub-vectors and quantizing independently, enabling search on compressed representations. Accuracy & Speed: Significantly reduces memory and speeds up distance calculations, but introduces quantization errors affecting accuracy. Memory: Highly memory efficient, suitable for billion-scale datasets. Best for: Massive datasets with strict memory constraints where some loss in precision is acceptable.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: When selecting an ANN algorithm, consider these core metrics: Recall (Accuracy): Measures how many true nearest neighbors are retrieved. High recall means results closely match exact search. Query Time (Speed): Time taken to return neighbors for a given query vector; critical for real-time applications. Index Build Time: Duration required to construct the data structure or index; important for datasets that update frequently. Memory Usage: Amount of RAM/storage needed to hold indexes and auxiliary structures.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Choosing the right tools and following best practices is crucial for successfully deploying approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search in real-world AI systems.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Tools, Libraries, and Best Practices for Implementing ANN in Production"}

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Faiss (Facebook AI Similarity Search): A highly optimized library supporting multiple ANN algorithms, including HNSW and PQ. Faiss excels at handling large-scale, high-dimensional datasets and offers GPU acceleration for faster indexing and querying. Annoy (Approximate Nearest Neighbors Oh Yeah): Developed by Spotify, Annoy uses forest of random projection trees to deliver fast and memory-efficient ANN search. It’s well-suited for read-heavy workloads with infrequent updates. ScaNN (Scalable Nearest Neighbors): Google's solution for efficient vector similarity search that combines quantization, partitioning, and graph search techniques. It balances accuracy and speed on large datasets. NMSLIB (Non-Metric Space Library): A versatile library supporting various ANN methods, including HNSW, with emphasis on high performance and flexibility.

name: A Comprehensive Guide to Approximate Nearest Neighbors Algorithms
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Index Management: Build indexes carefully, considering dataset size and update frequency. For dynamic data, incremental updates or scheduled reindexing can help maintain performance without full rebuilds. Latency Optimization: Monitor query latency closely. Use batch processing, caching, or approximate pre-filtering to reduce response times in real-time applications. Resource Allocation: Balance CPU, memory, and GPU resources based on workload. GPU acceleration (available in Faiss) can significantly accelerate large-scale vector search. Hybrid Approaches: Combine ANN with traditional ranking or machine learning models. Use ANN to generate candidate sets, then apply more precise re-ranking for final results. Monitoring and Alerts: Implement robust monitoring for index health, query accuracy, and latency to ensure optimal performance. Set up alerts for anomalies to catch regressions early. Testing and Validation: Regularly benchmark your ANN implementation against accuracy and performance goals. Use representative datasets and query workloads to validate real-world effectiveness.

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: TL;DR: LLMs are powerful, but making them use collaborative filtering (CF) signals effectively for sequential recommendations is tricky

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . AdaptRec proposes a self-adaptive framework where the LLM actively selects which similar users to learn from (via a "User-based Similarity Retrieval Prompt") and then uses their histories as demonstrations in a "User-Contextualized Recommendation Prompt." Results show significant HR@1 improvements (7-18%) over traditional and other LLM-based methods, especially in few-shot scenarios

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into sequential recommendation systems (LLM4SRec) is a hotbed of research right now

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . We're all seeing the potential of LLMs' world knowledge and in-context learning abilities

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . However, a core tenet of traditional RecSys is leveraging collaborative signals – learning from the behavior of similar users

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Translating these rich, often numerical or ID-based collaborative signals into a format that LLMs can understand and truly reason with remains a significant hurdle

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The authors of AdaptRec: A Self-Adaptive Framework for Sequential Recommendations with Large Language Models by Zhang, Wang, Li, et al

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . pinpoint a key issue: while some recent approaches try to feed similar user sequences into LLM prompts, the selection of these "demonstrations" is often based on static, numerical similarity (like cosine similarity on embeddings) and doesn't truly align with the LLM's own reasoning process

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . It's like giving a brilliant student a pile of notes without teaching them how to pick the most relevant ones for a new problem

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . AdaptRec proposes a "self-adaptive prompting framework" to bridge this gap

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The core idea is to make the LLM an active participant in selecting and utilizing collaborative information

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . It's a multi-stage process designed to be more dynamic and aligned with how LLMs learn.

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec

content: Traditional sequential recommenders (GRU4Rec, SASRec, etc.) excel at capturing patterns from user-item interaction sequences

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The paper categorizes current LLM4SRec prompt strategies (Figure 1 in their paper is a great visual for this): User-Agnostic Prompts: General instructions to the LLM on how to recommend, without specific user history. (e.g., "Recommend a romantic movie from this list...") Single User-Specific Prompts: Focus on the target user's own history, either "isolated" (just their sequence) or "implicit" (using pre-learned embeddings of their history within the prompt). Multi-User Collaborative Prompts: The emerging area where sequences from other, similar users are incorporated as demonstrations. This is where AdaptRec operates. Overview of Prompt Design Strategies for Sequential Recommendation Systems: User-Agnostic Prompt, Single User-Specific Prompt, and Multi-User Collaborative Prompt
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Challenge: Making LLMs Understand Collaborative Filtering Intuitively"}

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The problem with current multi-user prompts, as AdaptRec identifies, includes: Assessing Demonstration Quality: How do you know if a similar user's sequence is actually a good example for the LLM to learn from for this specific target user and this specific recommendation task? Handling Large Search Spaces: Finding the "best" few similar users from millions is computationally intensive. Adapting Demonstration Selection: Similarity isn't static. As the LLM learns or as user preferences evolve, the "best" similar users might change. Existing methods often use a fixed set of similar users.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "The Challenge: Making LLMs Understand Collaborative Filtering Intuitively"}

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: AdaptRec tackles these challenges with an iterative, three-stage framework (beautifully illustrated in their Figure 2): The Self-Adaptive User-Contextualized Sequential Recommendation Framework

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . (1) User Similarity Retrieval extracts relevant sequences

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . (2) Self-Adaptive User Selection refines similar user pool

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . (3) Contextual Prompt-based Recommendation generates personalized suggestions

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . An iterative feedback mechanism continuously improves user selection and recommendation accuracy

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Stage 1: User Similarity Retrieval (Coarse Filtering) Problem: LLMs have token limits. You can't feed in thousands of user histories. Solution: Start with a traditional, efficient CF method. They use cosine similarity on item sequence title embeddings to find an initial Top-N set of potentially similar users. This prunes the vast search space. Equation (2): sim(v, u) = (e_v ⋅ e_u) / (||e_v|| ||e_u||) where e_v , e_u are sequence embeddings for target user v and candidate user u. Stage 2: Self-Adaptive User Selection (LLM-Powered Refinement) Problem: The Top-N from Stage 1 are just numerically similar. Are they demonstratively useful for the LLM? Solution: This is the clever bit. They introduce a User-based Similarity Retrieval Prompt (Figure 3 in the paper). User-Based Similarity Retrieval Prompt This prompt essentially asks the LLM: "Given the target user's watch history and the watch history of these N candidates, rank the candidates by similarity (from the LLM's perspective of how well they'd serve as an example)." The LLM (using its understanding of sequence patterns, item semantics, etc.) re-evaluates these N users and selects a smaller Top-M subset (U₂). Key Idea: The LLM actively participates in choosing its own demonstration examples. This selection process isn't static; as the main recommendation model is fine-tuned (using LoRA for parameter efficiency), its understanding of what constitutes a "good similar user" can evolve, leading to better demonstration selection over time (hence "self-adaptive"). Stage 3: Contextual Prompt-based Recommendation (LLM Does its Magic) Problem: How to actually use these M refined similar user histories for the target user's recommendation? Solution: They construct a User-Contextualized Recommendation Prompt (Figure 4 in the paper) Contextual Prompt-based Recommendation This prompt includes: Demonstrations from the M similar users: "{Similar user M} has watched... Based on this, she/he chose {next item}." These are translated into natural language. The target user's history: "#Task: The {Target user} has watched... Please recommend the next movie for this user..." The LLM is then fine-tuned (using LoRA) to predict the next item i_{n+1} based on this rich, collaboratively-informed prompt, minimizing a standard negative log-likelihood loss. Equation (6): P(i_{n+1,t} | [i_1, ..., i_n], {H_u}_{u∈U₂}, i_{n+1,<t}) – probability of the next item token given target user history, similar user histories, and previously generated tokens of the next item. The "Self-Adaptive" Loop: The crucial part is that the LLM used for Self-Adaptive User Selection (Stage 2) and the LLM used for Contextual Prompt-based Recommendation (Stage 3) are essentially the same underlying model being fine-tuned

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . As the model gets better at recommendations (Stage 3), its ability to judge which users are truly "similar" in a way that's helpful for its own reasoning process (Stage 2) also improves

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: AdaptRec was evaluated on MovieLens100K, LastFM, and GoodReads datasets against: Traditional Sequential Recommenders: GRU4Rec, Caser, SASRec. LLM-based Models: Vanilla LLMs: Llama2-7B, GPT-4 (zero-shot). Specialized LLM Recommenders: MoRec (encodes item modality), LLaRA (hybrid prompting with item textual/behavioral signals). AdaptRec also uses Llama2-7B as its base.

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Performance comparison of different methods." Highlight AdaptRec's scores, especially HR@1, and the "Improv." row

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . AdaptRec consistently outperforms all baselines across HR@1, NDCG@5, and NDCG@20 on all three datasets. HR@1 Improvements over the next best method: MovieLens: +7.13% (AdaptRec 0.4736 vs LLaRA 0.4421) LastFM: +18.16% (AdaptRec 0.5327 vs LLaRA 0.4508) GoodReads: +10.41% (AdaptRec 0.4432 vs LLaRA 0.4014) Traditional models lag significantly , highlighting the benefit of LLMs' semantic understanding. Vanilla LLMs (Llama2, GPT-4) show limitations , especially Llama2 in controlled generation (low ValidRatio). Specialized LLM recommenders (MoRec, LLaRA) improve stability but are still beaten by AdaptRec. This suggests that simply applying LLMs or doing basic LLM enhancement isn't enough; how collaborative signals are integrated matters.

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Effectiveness of User Similarity Retrieval (RQ2, Table 3): Comparing AdaptRec's coarse-grained retrieval (Stage 1) against random user sampling shows massive drops in performance if Stage 1 is omitted (e.g., HR@1 on MovieLens drops from 0.4736 to 0.3224). Simply increasing candidate pool size without smart filtering is detrimental. The results of ablation study on AdaptRec," showing rows for "w/o retrieval", "w/o self-adaptive", "w/o demo"

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Impact of Self-Adaptive User Selection (RQ3, Figure 7): Comparing Self-Adaptive selection (Stage 2) against just randomly sampling from the retrieved pool ("Static Selection") shows consistent improvements for Self-Adaptive across different numbers of demonstrations (M=1,3,5,7,9). The LLM choosing its own examples is better than random choice from a pre-filtered set. Performance comparison of static and adaptive selection strategies on MovieLens dataset

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Impact of User-Based Contextual Prompts (RQ4, Table 4 & Figure 6): Introducing demonstrations (even just M=1 ) significantly boosts performance over a baseline without any demonstrations. Performance exhibits an inverted U-shape with the number of demonstrations (M). For these datasets, M=5 demonstrations was optimal. Too few, and there's not enough collaborative signal. Too many, and the LLM might get confused by excessive or noisy contextual information, hindering its ability to focus on the most relevant patterns. HR@1 drops sharply when increasing demos from 5 to 7 on LastFM and MovieLens. Impact of varying demonstration numbers on HR@1 across three datasets" AND Figure 6 from arXiv:2504.08786v1 - "Performance with Different Numbers of Demonstrations across three datasets

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Few-Shot Performance (GPT-4 without fine-tuning, Table 5): AdaptRec's User-Contextualized Prompt (UCP), even without fine-tuning (using GPT-4 zero-shot with UCP), significantly outperforms Basic Recommendation Prompts (BRP) and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. MovieLens: UCP (0.2460 HR@1) vs CoT (0.2240) vs BRP (0.2000) -> +23% over BRP, +9.82% over CoT. This shows the strength of providing explicit, relevant collaborative examples even for powerful, un-tuned LLMs. Performance comparison of UCP, CoT, and BRP across datasets

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Illustration of User-Contextualized Prompt, Chain-of-Thought Prompt and Conventional prompt The qualitative analysis in Figure 8 is particularly insightful, showing how UCP can lead to non-obvious, cross-genre recommendations (e.g., recommending Lord of the Rings after Titanic , Notebook , Pride and Prejudice ) because similar users exhibited that pattern, whereas BRP sticks to genre matching and CoT might over-rationalize.

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: LLM-in-the-Loop for Demonstration Selection: This is the core novelty. Instead of just feeding pre-selected similar users, the LLM actively refines this selection. This makes the collaborative signal more "digestible" and aligned with the LLM's reasoning. Dynamic and Adaptive: The framework allows the model's understanding of "similarity" to evolve during training, potentially leading to more nuanced and effective collaborative filtering over time. Strong Empirical Results: The significant improvements over both traditional methods and other LLM-based approaches, especially in HR@1 (which is critical for many RecSys applications), are compelling. Effectiveness in Few-Shot Scenarios: The UCP prompting strategy shows value even when full fine-tuning isn't feasible, making it relevant for quickly leveraging powerful foundation models. Addressing a Core LLM4SRec Challenge: It provides a structured and effective way to inject explicit collaborative signals into LLMs, which often struggle with the implicit, ID-based nature of traditional CF.

name: Bringing Collaborative Filtering to LLMs with AdaptRec
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Reduced effectiveness with multilingual content (seen on MovieLens with its diverse titles). Computational overhead of the iterative self-adaptive framework (though LoRA helps). ValidRatio (ensuring LLM generates items from a candidate set) is high (0.96) but not perfect like traditional models.

name: A/B Testing Your Rankings: Metrics That Matter in the Real World
roles: Engineer ML Engineer Data Scientist Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Static vs. Dynamic: Historical logs don't reflect how users react to new rankings or items. Presentation Blind: UI/UX, latency, and visual appeal aren't factored in offline. Feedback Loops Missing: Live interactions influence future recommendations, a cycle absent in offline tests. Implicit Assumptions: Offline metrics might assume unrealistic user examination patterns. Online A/B testing overcomes these limitations, allowing you to measure the actual effect of your changes.

name: A/B Testing Your Rankings: Metrics That Matter in the Real World
roles: Engineer ML Engineer Data Scientist Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: When evaluating ranking systems via A/B tests, metrics generally fall into these categories: Engagement Metrics: How are users interacting directly with the recommendations or search results? Click-Through Rate (CTR): (Clicks / Impressions). A fundamental measure of immediate appeal. Interaction Rate: Broader than CTR; includes clicks, add-to-carts, saves, likes, etc., directly from the list. Clicks/Interactions per User/Session: Average engagement intensity. Session Depth/Duration: Time spent or pages viewed post-interaction (interpret cautiously). Specific Examples (from practice): Daily Active Users (DAU), Engagers (users performing specific valuable actions), TimeSpent (on platform or with content). Conversion Metrics: Are recommendations leading to valuable downstream actions? Conversion Rate (CVR): (Key Actions / Sessions or Users). Measures impact on core goals like purchases, signups, leads, content completion. Add-to-Cart/Save Rate: E-commerce/discovery specific intermediate actions. Business Goal & North Star Metrics (NSMs): What's the impact on overarching business objectives and core customer value? North Star Metric (NSM): This crucial metric (or set of metrics) encapsulates the core value delivered to customers and acts as a leading indicator of long-term success and revenue. Examples: Spotify's "Time spent listening," a SaaS company's "Trial accounts with >3 users active in week 1." A strong NSM reflects customer value, predicts revenue, is actionable, and balances acquisition/retention. Your primary A/B test metric should ideally be or directly drive your NSM. Revenue Per User/Session: Direct top-line impact. Average Order Value (AOV): Value per transaction influenced by recommendations. Purchase/Subscription Frequency: Impact on repeat behavior (requires longer tests). User Experience & Quality Metrics (Guardrail Metrics): Are we inadvertently harming the experience? Latency: Critical – how quickly are results returned? Slower variants often lose, even if more relevant. Zero-Result Rate (Search): Frequency of users getting no results. Bounce Rate/Exit Rate: Are users leaving more quickly?
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Key Categories of Online A/B Test Metrics"}

name: A/B Testing Your Rankings: Metrics That Matter in the Real World

author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Define: Primary Metric: The single key metric (often aligned with your NSM) determining success. Decisions hinge on statistically significant changes here. Secondary Metrics: Other important metrics providing context. Guardrail Metrics: Metrics you must not harm (e.g., Latency). Statistical Power & Errors: Simply observing a difference isn't enough

name: A/B Testing Your Rankings: Metrics That Matter in the Real World
roles: Engineer ML Engineer Data Scientist Product
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You need statistical rigor: Statistical Power: The probability of detecting a true effect if one exists (Power = 1 - β, where β is the Type II error rate). A power of 80% is a common target. Low power means you might miss real improvements. Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE): The smallest change in your primary metric you deem practically significant and want your test to be able to detect reliably. Power Analysis: Conduct before the test to determine the required sample size based on your desired power, MDE, significance level (α), and baseline metric values. Tools like G*Power or online calculators can help. Type I Error (α, False Positive): Concluding there's an effect when there isn't (controlled by your significance level, e.g., p < 0.05). Running A/A tests (comparing identical versions) helps validate your testing setup and ensure your Type I error rate is behaving as expected. Type II Error (β, False Negative): Failing to detect a true effect (reduced by increasing power, e.g., larger sample size or larger effect). This is particularly risky when testing significant system changes where missing a real win (or loss) is costly. Research (like ShareChat's) shows combining multiple well-chosen metrics can sometimes reduce Type II errors and required sample sizes. Type III Error (Sign Error): Correctly detecting an effect but concluding it goes in the wrong direction (e.g., saying B beat A when A actually beat B). Usually less common but important to consider. Practical Significance: High power might detect statistically significant but tiny, practically meaningless effects. Balance statistical rigor with real-world impact when interpreting results.
