name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: The blog explores "Retrieval-Augmented Generation" (RAG), which melds information retrieval with language generation, to evaluate its promise for recommendations

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . ‍ “Retrieval Augmented Generation for Large Language Model in Watercolor” via DALL-E 3 The quality of AI driven recommendations has witnessed remarkable advancements in recent years, enabling hyper personalized experiences in e-commerce, social media, and discovery applications

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Even more recently there's been another breakthrough advancement in the AI community: large language models (LLMs)

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . These models introduce a new paradigm of machine learning that involves coming up with prompts to instruct the agent to perform tasks without having to fine-tune them on your domain specific dataset

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Naturally one has to wonder what this new paradigm means for the recommendation system (RecSys) community

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And to motivate this direction I want to give you a thought: Imagine a system that doesn't generate recommendations from looking at only your domain specific dataset but also possesses the wisdom to tap into a vast sea of existing knowledge before crafting its response

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This knowledge isn't contained in a linear sparse matrix but instead a high dimensional latent space that contains rich information about your users and recommendation documents

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This is the inspiration of what an LLM can do for recommendation system and the key to making it work is: retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Today we'll talk about why RAG is helpful, and back it up with experiments against more traditional recommendation system baselines

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Let's dive in!

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: When we think about using an LLM as a recommendation model, an obvious question arises: why not just directly prompt the model with what we want to achieve

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? E.g

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . why not just ask ChatGPT to "Recommend documents that are going to most engage users?"

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In our previous blog post , we found that recommending in this zero-shot, zero-context setting does not result in good performance compared to traditional recommendation baselines

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . There are several inherent problems with that approach, notably: 1

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Context memory and context length LLMs have a limit on how many tokens one model can ingest, this is determined by the underlying architecture, here by context I mean all the prior information that the model ingests along with a prompt to craft an appropriate response

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If the context is too long the model will start forgetting the input given prior 2

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Hallucination LLMs can and do hallucinate

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Every other month you may spot a Twitter thread on a new prompt that broke even the best models available

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And really if you try it out for yourself you will sometimes get the result you did not ask for

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Bias LLMs are notorious for biased responses as the quality and content depend on the prior dataset the model was pretrained on

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Since these datasets are so large, they get cleaned via automation but this could be better

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In a race to achieve the best performance other important metrics get eclipsed, the result however is not always satisfactory

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Inference speed As we discovered in our previous blogpost inference depends on decoding strategy and the amount of data required to decode, picking a greedy strategy results in messier final results but gives a great speed

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . On the other hand, using something like beam search allows for neat output, but will generally take longer

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In a world of recsys, the response time has to be in milliseconds

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, saying that LLMs are bad at ranking is unfair, as evidenced by many recent approaches trying to utilize the models in different roles

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . You can read more about the overview of the role of LLMs in recess and their benefits here

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Enter "Retrieval-Augmented Generation" (RAG), a groundbreaking paradigm that seeks to harmonize the strengths of retrieval and generation models.

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: RAG as a concept comes from the paper Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks by Patrick Lewis et al

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . At the center of this approach is the following scheme: source: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.11401.pdf The part we mostly care about here is the Retriever

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Regarding LLMs, frameworks like LangChain all utilize a form of RAG to create a ”long-term” memory for the LLM

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . More importantly, unlike accepted fine-tuning methods for some downstream tasks, this approach is less expensive to train and relatively straightforward to implement

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Looking at the Retriever we can note the query encoder

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This is a module that reduces our query to a vector of numbers encoded in relation to a certain latent space

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The second component here is MIPS or Maximum Inner Product Search , but really in this case it can be any form of search over encoded documents

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We then can retrieve the relevant context for the model out of the vast space of possibilities

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This allows us to efficiently utilize the model’s context length and vastly improve the quality of our response

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The Generator module in the scheme above can be viewed as our end LLM

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . As we can see to create the best kind we need to finetune them together

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . With that being said no rule says that the retriever model has to be the same, in practice, you can train and use a smaller LLM for retrieval and a larger one for the final generation

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . See the representative diagram from AWS below: Source

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: To build RAG, we need a way to store and retrieve candidate items/documents that will be used within the context of the LLM ranker.: 1

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A way to ingest candidate items 2

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A way to search over those ingested items and retrieve the most relevant ones Vector search can help us do both at the same time

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you don't know what vector search is I recommend taking a look at our previous post

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In short, we encode information as meaningful, high-dimensional vectors in dense latent space and then search through them based on a similarity measure appropriate for vectors

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Naturally, if the information between two vectors is semantically similar they will be closer e.g

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . encoded "apple" and "banana" vs

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . "apple" and "Gandalf", because the first two are fruits, so they are semantically closer

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To do so we will use two tools

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For encoding I will use sentence BERT, however, I will utilize its implementation from the Hugginface library

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Currently, there are libraries like lancedb , that will allow you to extend your embedding powers beyond just text, giving you the potential to search and provide enriched context to your LLM

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . I will use the Movielens25M dataset to create this example, you can follow along with your data

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However keep in mind that your data must be searchable , in my case I convert strings to semantic vectors and use similarity search

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For many multimodal data formats, autoencoders, and other ML architectures that perform embeddings will work best to provide a suitable numeric representation

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Remember that the key here is extracting a semantic vector from a user query

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In the case of a dataset of movies, the user may ask: "Recommend me a drama or romance movie to watch tonight?"

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . These keywords will affect the resulting query vector making it more similar to a vector of an entry that is a drama and romance movie (better yet if it has these keywords in the description)

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Let’s first load the models

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . I suggest specifying a cache directory (model files will go here) as you will have greater control over where specific project files will live

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . I already combined three different movielens CSV sheets into a pandas data frame

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Each resulting entry has the name of the movie, genre, and tags that users described the movie with

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . What we want to do is combine these into a single sentence and make sure that we have unique records, as many users like the same movie we want to encode the record once if there is no difference between entries for each user

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So what’s next

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? We need to make an embedding function, using the model and tokenizer loaded from Huggingface I do it like so: Due to the way sentence BERT works we need to create a mean poling operation to combine the attention mask and actual token embeddings we receive from the model to produce final sentence embeddings

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We then can write a simple loop to embed all our data: Then it is a matter of searching over the embeddings and corresponding records

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To do so I use LanceDB and similarity search

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We can create the table and perform a search like so: This way we can retrieve any number of records for our context and improve our LLM response.

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Naturally, we have a set of questions: how do we measure the benefits of RAG

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Is the benefit worth it against the engineering effort

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Are there extra considerations and “underwater stones” we might need to be aware of

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Let’s go through them one by one.

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: I decided to do some performance tracking using models you can find in every recsys toolbox

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Essentially I will use a sample of the Movielens dataset on a few baselines

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The dataset in question is 5-core (meaning removal of users with less than five or items that are interacted with less than 5 times) split in training and test using “global temporal split” which in essence amounts to splitting by timestamp in proportion 9:1 for train:test

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We then also want to make sure that item sets between two splits are equalized, some models we will employ operate using sparse matrices so we want to make sure that the test set possesses the items in train

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This isn’t an issue with deep learning models and if we are using encoded input, which is one of the other benefits of using RAG and DL models like LLMs for your recommendation pipeline

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Now back to the models

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We will compare ALS and LogMatrix models against popular list and random list

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For random we would randomly recommend N items for a user from the test set, in this case, N=100; this is done to ensure that the model is learning something

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Next is the popular list model, to construct this one I take all the items and sum their relevance scores across all users, this ends up giving me a measure of popularity for all users that I can sort

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you want to understand ALS and LogMatrix factorization better you can read about them at their respective links

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For RAG we want to retrieve the top 100 relevant items for ALS and LogMatrix, then we will ask those models to perform a rerank task and measure HR@10 and NDCG@10

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For GPT-3.5 which will serve as our reranker LLM, I do a bit of prompt engineering and construct the query in the following way: We want to pass watch history as common sense and existing literature evidence would suggest that there should be a way to describe a user, so naturally based on the most liked movies you want to get new ones that will match your preference

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . You can expand this concept to describe detailed user profiles from a multitude of characteristics

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The next step is just querying the API and fitting/measuring all models

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Here are the results: Results speak for themselves in that there is evidence of performance gain by combining RAG and LLM

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Specifically, RAG allows for performance increase on all models

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But for an LLM RAG is particularly suitable to cut down on the tokens required to produce reranking and as a stable pipeline for long-term data insertion

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Additionally, keep in mind that I have not pretrained GPT for this specific task, it is relying on movie titles alone to produce a recommendation

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Adding pretraining, a better model, and better task definitions along with an expanded user profile potentially will superboost these performance numbers.

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: I would say so, RAG’s' ability to ingest multimodal data as well as different data objects are given a suitable encoder represents the most flexible way anyone can address long-term data collection and relevance search

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . You hypothetically could construct an embedded model that will ingest video as well as its short description and produce a semantic multimodal embedding vector, the limit here will lie in the ability of trained architecture

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We can create a live memory structure for an LLM that can recall the best items in advance, thus avoiding issues with context length and forgetting

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We can also update the vector database on the go if the user discovers new items and rates them higher, essentially the best interactions are also dynamic in this case

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . I must add though that for RAG to work well you need to do some careful training along with your model

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For production, retraining the whole model often means high costs and it is not very clear how a good pretrained embedding model will compare to a small one that is getting constantly updated as new online data comes in

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This is a question for future research but I’m willing to bet that in the case of a good embedder frequent retraining won’t be required

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It is also worth mentioning that most of the RAG cost comes upfront from fitting it on a specific dataset and making it work with the LLM ranker in question, whereas down the line it is amortized as the updates are generally not done.

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Long context models are what you will need if you want to fit in a lot of data to rerank, but this comes at a cost. A limitation of all transformer architectures is their autoregressive nature. For input, you can feed in a lot of data rapidly, for the output however you will be generating all of your data token by token, as the new prediction requires maximum likelihood measurement over other tokens( this is subject to the sampling strategy you are using aka beam search, top-p, etc.). Hence a lot of data=slow output, and slow output is what we can’t have for a recommendation system. Minimizing this tradeoff is a special engineering problem on its own. Hallucination is a constant problem. Yes, I said it. In fact, one thing I avoided mentioning in the results is that @10 metrics worked well because model with a 100 items to return is very likely to give me back at least 10. In practice, if you are not careful with your sampling parameters like temperature , and allow the model to get a bit more creative you will end up with fewer or more items than needed, or items that do not exist. I expect this can be generally resolved with some finetuning on the dataset. For my experiment, I kept the temperature at 0 and used fuzzy string matching that matched the movie title to the closest corresponding title in the dataset to translate this into an item ID. You can’t use streaming for everything. If you use ChatGPT you are used to it printing a line out, this is a clever trick called streaming, meaning tokens are outputted as soon as they become available, this makes it seem like the response is coming out just as you requested and there is no latency. Obviously, this does not suit the case where we need a complete model output, so for each set of items you will have to wait for the full output time to get the complete reranked list.

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: RAG might not be a perfect solution to every case but it is still a formidable approach

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Recent papers like PALR: Personalization Aware LLMs for Recommendation demonstrate the benefit of using RAG for LLMs oriented for recommendation

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . One shortcoming that RAG cannot address is the structure of your data

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . As we see the concept of similarity is very important here, hence to get the best match of the embeddings that hold the representation of your data it has to be the best as well and that is largely model-dependent

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Hence the failure of RAG might be related to your embedding model not learning a good semantic meaning of your data

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Largely the research into the effectiveness of representation in RAG is missing

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Additionally, we currently don’t have an idea of the usefulness of RAG and LLMs in multimodal datasets combining text and images or text and video

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Overall RAG shows great promise in enhancing future LLM-oriented applications

name: RAG for RecSys: a magic formula?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Stay tuned for our new posts where we explore LLMs as recommendation systems in greater depth!

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: As the digital landscape continues to evolve, search is moving beyond simple keyword matching to understanding the context and intent behind user queries

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Personalized semantic search, powered by state-of-the-art artificial intelligence, embeddings, and machine learning technologies, is revolutionizing traditional keyword-based search, transforming the way we find and access information online

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In this blog post, we will delve into the history and types of search, discuss the technical aspects, advantages, and disadvantages of each approach, and explore real-world examples of personalized semantic search in action, along with its impact on business metrics such as conversion, retention, and engagement.

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Personalized semantic search is an advanced search technique that couples understanding the meaning, context, and intent behind user queries with personalization from past user behavior

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . By leveraging machine learning, artificial intelligence, and natural language processing technologies, personalized semantic search can deliver more accurate, relevant, and personalized search results, vastly improving the user experience

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This approach enables search engines to move beyond mere keyword matching and offer a more intuitive and seamless information retrieval process

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . One way personalized semantic search is often characterized is helping you “search the way you think”

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Although you’re almost certainly using personalized semantic search already everyday in products from big tech companies, you can get a unique feel for what it’s like with search engines like You.com and Same.Energy

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ Example of visual search engine results using semantic understanding

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Keyword-based search relies on explicitly matching keywords from user queries to the data with rules

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . These rules typically include factors like keyword frequency, location, and the presence of related terms.

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Building upon keyword-based search, semantic search employs AI, machine learning, and NLP to understand the meaning and context behind user queries, providing more accurate and relevant results

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Techniques such as tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, and named entity recognition help analyze text, while machine learning algorithms identify patterns, draw connections, and make predictions based on the data.

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Personalized semantic search aim to balance the strengths and weaknesses of both approaches whilst taking into account past user behavior

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . It starts by conducting a keyword-based search to quickly identify potential matches

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Then, it incorporates semantic analysis techniques to better understand the meaning and context of the user's query and the content of the documents

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Finally it personalizes the results by re-ranking them based on past user behavior

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This enables the search system to refine and rank the search results more accurately, consider the presence of keywords, the semantic relationships between the words and user interests.

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: The e-commerce giant has implemented semantic search to improve the accuracy and relevance of search results, leading to increased conversion rates and customer retention

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Semantic search enables shoppers to find products more easily and delivers personalized recommendations, enhancing the overall shopping experience

name: Search the way you think: how personalized semantic search is disrupting traditional search
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . https://assets.amazon.science/95/2f/51e4ebdb4347990fedc1815d7327/semantic-product-search.pdf ‍

content: By leveraging AI-powered semantic search and embeddings, Spotify can better understand user preferences and provide better results for artists, podcasts and songs even if many of the keywords in the search query are not present

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: This blog post discusses the importance of novelty in recommendation systems and how it can improve user experience by providing diverse and unexpected suggestions

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Have you ever received a recommendation for a product or service that was completely new to you, but ended up being exactly what you needed

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: ? That feeling of discovering something unexpected and useful is what the novelty metric in recommendation systems aims to capture

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . In a world where we are inundated with choices and information, the ability to discover new and interesting items can be a valuable feature for users

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . In the previous post, we talked about serendipity as one of the ways to measure how a recommendation system can find unexpected but useful items, we looked into how similarity can help us, this time we will look into how to use dissimilarity instead

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . As recommendation systems become more sophisticated, it's important to evaluate not just their ability to suggest relevant items, but also their ability to suggest novel and diverse items

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . In this post, we'll dive into the world of novelty metrics in recommendation systems, exploring what they are, why they matter, and how they can be used to evaluate the effectiveness of recommendation algorithms

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . We'll also take a closer look at some of the challenges involved in measuring novelty, and the different approaches that have been proposed to address them

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . By the end of this post, you'll have a deeper understanding of why novelty is such an important factor in recommendation systems, and how you can use novelty metrics to improve the user experience of your recommendation system.

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: As mentioned before the key difference between serendipity from Part 1 and novelty are: 💡 Novelty tends to focus more on the degree to which recommended items are dissimilar to items that the user has already interacted with, while serendipity may take into account factors like the user's preferences or interests

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . 💡 Additionally, serendipity may involve a stronger emphasis on the unexpectedness of the recommendation, whereas novelty may be more concerned with the diversity of the recommendations overall

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . To understand how we can mathematically extract concepts like diversity and dissimilarity we should start with the essence of both - a measure of how two items or sets can be similar.

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: An old-school way of determining a novelty of an item is through similarity or rather its inverse

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Recalling from Part 1 we learned about Cosine Similarity as one of the basic ways to define how two items in a recommendation system can be considered similar: Where A and B , are two vectors that can represent two items in a recommendation system, say an anime edit you saved and a new action movie trailer

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . What we did not dive into last time is the importance of choosing the right similarity metric

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . 💡Topology of data matters

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: ! Try to think about your dataset and your users, if we are getting feedback in form of categorical ‘yes’ or ‘no’ variables that can’t be represented in a continuous manner (say in the range from 0-1)

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Our data can be binary and the dataset may become sparse

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . This makes density-focused metrics like cosine similarity ineffective and costly to compute

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . As you can tell measuring something as clicked on the movie using a continuous range is not possible

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . TikTok’s recommendation engine for example relies on sparse features

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . For cases like these, a different similarity metric may be used called Jaccard Similarity

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Let’s see it in action, picture our features as geometric shapes: We can use union operation to find similarity between two items like so: 💡 The alchemy of features is real

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: ! In practice, different sets of components of your product may give you both continuous and categorical variables as user feedback

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . So in real-world applications, a combination of different scores is used to accurately determine similarities between items, items in combination are often weighted.

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: The novelty of a recommended item may be calculated based on its similarity to previously recommended items, such that items that are dissimilar to past recommendations are considered more novel: Where r is recommended item and i is each previously recommended item

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . 💡 This approach is not as common as using popularity-based methods to calculate novelty, as it relies on user-specific information and is much more complex to implement in practice

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Popularity-based methods are often preferred in recommendation systems because they are simple and easy to implement, and they do not require any information about individual users and their preferences, making them particularly useful for cold-start situations where little or no user data is available

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Moreover, popularity-based methods can often provide good recommendations for popular items that are likely to be of interest to many users, while also ensuring diversity in the recommended items, being particularly useful in scenarios where the goal is to provide recommendations that are likely to be widely accepted and generate high overall satisfaction among users

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . Two common ways of defining it are: But what if the item in question is already trending and was interacted with by all users, say most users on Netflix already got recommended Squid Game , can it still be considered novel

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: ? What if a year has passed

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: ? One better approach could be to consider user interaction instead, e.g

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: . if the user clicked to watch for example:

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: So why even use novelty

name: Not your average RecSys metrics Part 2: Novelty
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
categories: Data Personalization AI/ML Product Learn Tutorial
content: ? There are 3 main reasons: Firstly , in a world where we are constantly inundated with information and options, the ability to discover new and interesting items can be a valuable feature for users. Recommending only items that are similar to ones the user has already interacted with may not provide the user with a diverse and interesting set of options to explore. Secondly , recommending only popular or well-known items may lead to a phenomenon known as "filter bubbles," where users are only exposed to a narrow range of content and perspectives. This can limit their ability to discover new and diverse viewpoints and experiences. By incorporating novelty into recommendation systems, we can help users break out of their filter bubbles and explore a wider range of content. Finally , from a business perspective, incorporating novelty into recommendation systems can help to increase user engagement and satisfaction. Users who are constantly discovering new and interesting items are more likely to continue using the recommendation system and may even become loyal customers.

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: If you’re interested in recommendation systems but not sure whether you have enough data this blog post is for you

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ! If you haven't read Part 1, a link is below

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Welcome back to the second installment on data requirements for recommendation systems

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ! In part 1 , we looked at the types of data used, the importance of high-quality interactions, and strategies for improving interaction signals

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . We highlighted that there is no minimum amount of data required for a recommendation system; instead, what matters is the quality of interactions and contextual information about users and items being ranked

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In part two, we will explore the challenges posed by sparsity, discuss the significance of contextual information for enhancing recommendations, and examine the latest advancements in machine-learning techniques that are reducing data requirements for businesses of all sizes.

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Sparsity refers to the amount of available data or the density of data points in a dataset

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In the context of recommendation systems, sparsity can refer to the number of ratings or interactions that users have had with items

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . The sparsity requirements for recommendation systems can vary depending on the type of system and the goals of the recommendations

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Some recommendation systems may be able to function effectively with relatively little data, while others may require a larger, denser dataset in order to make accurate recommendations

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In general, it is generally easier to make higher quality recommendations when there is more data available

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . One way you can unpack why higher quality recommendations are roughly proportional to interactions / (users * items) is looking at a classic collaborative filtering method: matrix factorization

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In matrix factorization, you have a feedback matrix, where rows are users, items are columns and the cells contain the event label (e.g

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . positive event as 1, negative event as 0)

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . You can think of the recommendation task as one where you need to predict the missing cells of this matrix

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Matrix factorization solves this by learning a lower dimensional latent space that represents the feedback we do know, to predict the feedback we don’t

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . As you can imagine, the more sparse this feedback matrix is, the harder it is to predict the missing values

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . E.g

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . if 99% of the feedback matrix is complete with data then it should be much easier to predict what that 1% is

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . If we only have 0.1% then it becomes much harder

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Matrix Factorization is a simple embedding model One rule of thumb that’s quoted as an ideal minimum anecdotally is that you need less than 99% sparsity of interactions relative to the user and item matrix to make good recommendations

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Sparsity doesn’t necessarily change when you add any type of data

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . If you increase more users and items you’ll need exponential amount of interactions to have equivalent sparsity

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ! For example: 1000 users and 1000 items you need > 10,000 interactions. 100,000 users and 1000 items you need > 1M interactions. 1,000,000 users and 10,000 items you need > 100M interactions. 1,000,000 users and 100,000 items you need > 1B interactions. But is this the whole story

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ? Not at all

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Minimum thresholds of data are a misnomer

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In the example above, we set each row to represent a new unique user and each column as a new unique item, but this doesn’t consider all the shared attributes of the user and item entities — contextual information

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . These extra attributes provide another feature to represent similarity between users and between items

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . 💡Minimum thresholds are a misnomer.

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Intuitively there are two ways we think about the improvement here: Having a prior on the similarity of entities (users or items) based on the similarity of features, gives us more information about the relationship between users and items before they’ve made many interactions. For example, if an anonymous user is added, and they click on an item that’s popular with women in their mid-30s, we can start off by recommending them something that we know other female’s in their mid-30s like. If an item is added, and we know it’s red, and a type of shoe, can we recommend it to people that like things that are red, or shoes! Having extra user or item features means there’s more ways to relate the interaction relationships together. If we take the matrix factorization example again, one way to handle these attributes is to just concatenate them to the sides of the matrix (by the way, this is why user and item attribute features in recommendation systems are often called “side-information”). If we now fill in the feedback matrix of the new attribute rows and columns with their respective interaction values, assuming the cardinality of the features is less than the number of interactions (which is guaranteed), and we use the same number of interactions, this feedback matrix must be more dense then the original feedback matrix without the attributes. Fig

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Example of contextual or 'side information' excerpted from Movielens dataset This all comes with a lot of caveats, which is why there’s never an answer of exactly how much data you’ll need

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . But what we can conclude is that quality of recommendations is correlated with the number of high quality interactions and amount of high quality contextual information

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . One recent advancement in recommendations systems is big tech companies using deep learning to extract high quality contextual information from the content itself

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For example, their recommendation systems understand whether a video is dancing (see below), keyboard cats or sports highlights without any additional metadata

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . An example of a video understanding model we use at Shaped to add high quality contextual information to recommendations As you’d expect deep learning has high initial data requirements for model training

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For example, foundational large language models (LLM) like PaLM and GPT-4 required billions of data points, many machine-learning engineers and huge compute power to train over many months

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . With that in mind, it might seem as though the bar to deploy a modern recommendation system with deep learning into production is only getting higher.

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Thankfully the opposite is occurring

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ! 🙃 These innovations have reduced the minimum data requirements and made it easier than ever to get started

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . LLM have enabled transfer learning to other contexts and use cases — which is likely to include whatever you’re building

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ! For example, a pre-trained model on out-of-domain data (for example public or purchased datasets) means you need less unique domain specific data to get good results

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . In an effort to build community, companies like Meta are even open-sourcing their advanced video deep learning models on github or publishing them on Hugging Face

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Transfer learning means we can literally stand on the shoulders of these giants

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . We no longer need gigantic datasets (or technically any data at all) to use deep learning in production

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . At Shaped we use a combination of pre-trained models, traditional, and deep learning techniques to get the best performance possible for each customer

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This means anyone can get started today with much less data than was required previously!

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: It's essential to recognize that the data you need for your recommendation system might already be at your fingertips, hidden within various tools and platforms
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Unlocking the potential of your existing data"}

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For example, tools like Google Analytics and Segment are often underutilized as sources for recommendation systems
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Unlocking the potential of your existing data"}

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . By tapping into these rich data sources, you can uncover valuable user interactions, such as page views, clicks, and dwell time, that provide crucial insight into user preferences and behavior
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Unlocking the potential of your existing data"}

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Moreover, you can leverage other data sources such as CRM systems, which hold a wealth of customer information including demographic data, purchase history, and engagement with marketing campaigns
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Unlocking the potential of your existing data"}

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . By integrating this data into your recommendation system, you can enhance the user experience with personalized recommendations based on a more holistic understanding of their preferences and interests.
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Unlocking the potential of your existing data"}

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: In conclusion, the age-old question of "How much data do I need for a recommendation system?" doesn't have a straightforward answer

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . However, what we do know is that the quality of recommendations is closely tied to having high-quality interactions and rich contextual information

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . As machine learning and deep learning innovations continue to advance, the data requirements for building powerful recommendation systems are becoming increasingly accessible for businesses of all sizes

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . So, don't let the fear of not having enough data hold you back from implementing a recommendation system that could significantly boost your conversions and user engagement

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . By leveraging pre-trained models, transfer learning, and existing analytics tools, you can harness the power of your data to create personalized and effective recommendations for your users

name: Part 2: How much data do I need for a recommendation system?
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . You likely have much more data than you think, and the benefits of a recommendation system are just waiting to be unlocked!

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: This blog post explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) as powerful recommendation systems, highlighting their ability to understand context and meaning to provide personalized suggestions, particularly focusing on their application in movie recommendations

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Today’s recommendation systems are often incredibly complex, akin to a large machine with many moving parts carefully engineered to provide your users with the best suggestions possible

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It is hard to design right and even harder to tune, and so not surprising that recommendation systems are their own field of research

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . After all we all unknowingly or not heavily rely on recommendations and this existing paradigm

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, this preexisting status quo might be about to change

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you were awake for the past 6 months you saw how AI came forth from research labs and universities straight into the mainstream for everyone

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . At this point it is very likely your mom has tried ChatGPT

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . At the forefront of widespread adoption are large language models or LLMs

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Specifically: a large parameter count of foundational models that were pre-trained by research communities, large private and non-profit labs and companies

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . With their ability to ingest background knowledge from large datasets scraped from the internet it is no wonder that researchers have thought about emerging capabilities of AI trained on such vast amounts of information

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And it is precisely this theory that inspires this post.

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Okay, so what

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Language Model Machines (LLMs) have been making waves in the tech industry for their ability to generate natural language and respond to user input, but can they be more

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? LLMs have the potential to be powerful recommendation systems and change the way we consume information and products

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The secret to LLMs' success lies in their ability to understand the context and meaning behind words

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Unlike traditional recommendation systems which are statistical linear models that rely on keywords and metadata, LLMs can analyze the entire text of an article or video to understand its topic, tone, and sentiment

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This allows them to make recommendations that are not only relevant but also aligned with the user's interests and preferences

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And unlike current approaches LLMs due to their central idea of being a general tool, are capable of very good generalization and customization, this partially comes from emergent properties of language models of scale

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Here is some extra spice: LLMs are also capable of learning from user feedback

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you interact with an LLM's recommendations by clicking on a link, for example, the system will take note and use that information to improve its future recommendations

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This feedback loop allows LLMs to continuously refine their recommendations and provide an even better user experience over time

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A research team behind the paper Is ChatGPT Good at Search

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Investigating Large Language Models as Re-Ranking Agent , discovered that two key pieces that make LLMs a good candidate for RecSys

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . First is the way to meaningfully encode information: the sheer vastness of LLM’s latent space allows it to produce a better representation of the ingested information (this also allows it to effectively address cold-start cases) , whereas other approaches often cannot recommend anything unless you provide some starting data

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Second is a constant ability to update the latent space using user feedback

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This happens through repeated interaction with the LLM, as user provides more information the latent space adjusts to give appropriate tokens better probability of being selected

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Let’s briefly look at those two closer:

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Embeddings are frequently employed in the context of search systems to transform textual content into numerical representations or vectors

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . These numerical representations effectively compare and analyze the text while capturing its semantic content

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Semantic embeddings enable a deeper understanding of user preferences by capturing the subtle nuances in expressed or implied intent

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Unlike traditional approaches that rely on simple keyword matching or basic metadata, semantic embeddings allow recommendation systems to comprehend the underlying meaning of queries or user profiles

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This understanding goes beyond the surface level, taking into account the context, synonyms, related concepts, and even the sentiment behind the user's interactions

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . By leveraging semantic encodings, recommendation systems can provide more accurate and contextually relevant suggestions, enhancing the user experience and increasing the likelihood of engagement

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To simplify the better the model is better in producing these semantic vectors the better understanding of the items it possesses and therefore likely the better recommendation we can get

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If we know that LLMs are trained on large datasets with various types of content then we can assume they possess a good amount of knowledge on various topics and things that we might want to recommend

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you were to picture every item for your user as a vector then all items exist in latent space with mathematical relationships between them

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If we measure the distance between those we can predict how similar they are, this being said this is just one of the ways to do rankings

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In theory LLMs can utilize the concept of similarity of fit given that they understand spatial relationships in the latent space they learned.

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: To test our theory we will be using LLMs to recommend us movies

author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Why not

author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Spotify, TikTok, Netflix we all use them to recommend us content so let’s see if we can do better

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For this article motivated by previous experiments in the community and recent emergence of open source AI I want to focus specifically on open source models

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . On the menu today for you I have LLAMA (7B,13B,30B,65B), GPT-J

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Since these models generally work in a prompt continuation (which is different from QA model of ChatGPT), we need to construct a prompt that would fit our requirements of returning the recommended movies, preferably in some form of a parsable sequence Two key parameters like temperature and sequence length need to be adjusted to reduce model hallucination. Temperature - refers to how “creative” the model should be, the higher the value the more freedom the model would have to generate something different from your prompt. Max sequence length - is the length of the output sequence of tokens you will receive upon inference. We can also adjust sampling parameter top-p , which determines the amount of less likely words to exclude from the sampling pool, but since probability distribution of words changes with change in temperature values this has a similar effect as changing top-p . We also need a way to determine if a model performs better or worse, hence we also need a way to parse the results from the output and compare them to the dataset. For LLAMA you can find code provided by Meta here , which will help you run this experiment

name: LLMs - a paradigm shift in RecSys?
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For GPT-J we wrote custom code but it is very straightforward and simple nonetheless

content: . To start off we want to test zero shot performance of the model for example: Ideally we want the model to give us a specified amount of results (n) similar to items in item_list, and to queue results via a special symbol for this purpose I chose =>

author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For starters lets try to run the prompt above on all the models as a zero shot example and see how they do: So some mixed success here and there

author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But we can still nitpick, for example I chose a specific movie collection to prompt because they are all Studio Ghibli films, that all are anime and in fantasy genre, most importantly they made a few movies so their titles will be easy to recognize
