content: . Before I explain why, let’s discuss three reasons why it’s so difficult to act on analytics with machine-learning today.

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: “How much data do I need for machine-learning to work?” is one of the top questions we get asked at Shaped
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Uncertainty around whether you have enough data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Almost all companies we talk to are collecting analytics and user interaction data but there is still a deep seated fear that there isn’t enough of it for machine-learning to work
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Uncertainty around whether you have enough data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This is a legitimate concern because traditional machine-learning techniques required extremely large data sets to overcome the cold start problem
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Uncertainty around whether you have enough data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This uncertainty typically results in pushing machine-learning projects to next quarter or year when of course, there will be more data and users than there are today
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Uncertainty around whether you have enough data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ Broad data requirements for different models from http://blog.easysol.net/building-ai-applications ‍
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Uncertainty around whether you have enough data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: The actionability of analytics is slow because there are many hurdles between the initial analysis and the product change

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Machine learning systems allow these hurdles to be skipped by immediately taking data insights and driving product change

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Whereas utilizing analytics data sometimes feels like pushing a rock up a hill — there is a significant amount of inertia

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . To determine what to improve, a project needs to be set-up and time needs to be dedicated for formal investigation

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For example, this might look like a few days of SQL analysis to develop a story, convince a product manager, organize the engineering resources and then several weeks to design and implement the changes into production

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ Pushing a rock up a hill is how I feel sometimes about analytics

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Most companies are aware of the huge opportunity that utilizing analytics presents to personalize their product experience and improve conversion and engagement
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . However after looking into what would be required to DIY it becomes clear that it’s a gargantuan task
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . A team of people are needed to build, experiment and maintain machine-learning systems in production
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Typically that looks like a combination of data engineers, data scientists and machine-learning engineers
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Plus a 12+ month initial upfront investment
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Will it pay off
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ? How many models and experiments will we need to try out before landing on something that works
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ? In addition, machine-learning engineers are costly and hard to hire -- accounting for just ~1% of all software developers
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Another problem is that off-the-shelf solutions like AWS Personalize or GCP Recommender aren’t all that easy to use
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . They require a lot of work to coerce all of your data (e.g a customer data platform like Segment or Mixpanel) into their data stack, a surprising amount of maintenance, struggle with the cold-start problem and are a black box — companies tell us they’re not really sure what’s going on with their models
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ Building a model is only 5% of the work of productionizing machine-learning ‍ The good news is that all three of these issues are going away quickly
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Building and maintainingmachine-learning systems is challenging"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Transfer learning lets us stand on the shoulders of giants
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Irrespective of the size of your dataset, transfer learning and newer machine learning techniques enable a higher start point, slope and asymptote
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . The models we use at Shaped are pre-trained so our customers don’t have to worry about the cold-start problem being a limiting step
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Once we’ve connected to a customers data source we then re-train and fine tune our models so that they’re customized
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For those looking to tinker, huggingface is a wonderful community of open sourced machine-learning models to explore
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . All in all, transfer learning means that the minimum data required for excellent machine-learning results has shrunk considerably over the last decade
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ Transfer learning is a game changer for performance
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "1.Transfer learning means companies don\u2019t need as much data"}

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Machine-learning systems for use cases like ranking and recommendations are by design anti-inertia — they are constantly improving the end-users experience with every piece of data collected

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . The monitoring and analysis of machine-learning embeddings (numerical representations of data — see the appendix for a graphic) can also reveal complex trends in your product that low-level analytics dashboard are incapable of providing

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For example, visualizing your embeddings can show the similarities of your user cohorts or break down the dimensions of importance of your content

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This has huge potential to be a source of business intelligence for many companies that is currently untapped

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Another game-changing possibility is that embeddings can generate new products or content ideas and even predict the demand for it

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . More on that for discussion in another post

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ It’s fascinating to visualize embeddings of the Netflix library of movies and their genre

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . T-SNE visualization of embeddings learned from content categorization task from Netflix technology blog ‍

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: Companies like Shaped , Pinecone , Mage and Continual have made it considerably easier to experiment, vectorize and productionize machine-learning

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This is saving months or years of build and maintenance time

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Still, the machine-learning ecosystem is young and emerging

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . It could be compared to the state of early 2000s cloud infrastructure as AWS was entering the market

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . ‍ The machine learning eco-system is rapidly expanding

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This graphic by Leigh Marie Braswell from her excellent Startup Opportunities in Machine Learning Infrastructure blog post ‍

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: You can build a ranking model with Shaped and go from 0-1 in a few hours

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . You’ll likely be pleasantly surprised how far you can get with little data and effort

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Once you have results from your first model it’ll become clear where opportunities to iterate are

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Some of our smallest customers are pre-launch, private beta or pre-seed companies with <1000 users

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . When these companies scale, their feeds and recommendations will be personalized from day 1

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . This is becoming the norm because products like TikTok have dramatically lifted users expectations of personalization

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . Even Amazon is testing a new TikTok style feed in their app

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . For the team at Shaped it’s exciting that we are able to help all companies big or small utilize their analytics data to personalize their product experiences with machine-learning

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: . What do you think

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ? Has your company got analytics data sitting idly in a data warehouse

name: From Analytics to Action
author: Daniel Camilleri
content: ? Or have they thought about implementing machine-learning but decided to wait because it seemed too difficult

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: OpenAI has released its latest natural language processing system, GPT-4, which promises to be even more advanced and capable than its predecessor, GPT-3

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . GPT-4 is built on the same deep learning approach as the previous models but leverages more data and computation to achieve greater sophistication and accuracy

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI has recently announced the creation of its latest deep learning model, GPT-4

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . It is a large multimodal model that accepts image and text inputs and outputs text

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . While GPT-4 is not as capable as humans in many real-world scenarios, it has shown human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks.

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: GPT-4's text input capability is now available via ChatGPT Plus and the API, with a waitlist

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI is also collaborating closely with a single partner to prepare the image input capability for wider availability

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Additionally, OpenAI is open-sourcing OpenAI Evals, their framework for automated evaluation of AI model performance, to allow anyone to report shortcomings in their models to help guide further improvements.

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: GPT-4 is a multimodal model that can accept both image and text inputs and generate text outputs

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . While it is not as capable as humans in real-world scenarios, it has achieved human-level performance on several academic and professional benchmarks

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI tested them on a variety of benchmarks, including simulating exams that were originally designed for humans

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . They tested GPT-4 using the most recent publicly-available tests (in the case of the Olympiads and AP free response questions) or by purchasing 2022–2023 editions of practice exams

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI did no specific training for these exams

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . A minority of the problems in the exams were seen by the model during training, but they believe the results to be representative

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . GPT-4 has shown better performance than GPT-3.5 on the benchmarks, exhibiting human-level performance on various professional and academic exams, such as passing a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . In contrast, GPT-3.5's score was around the bottom 10%

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI has also shared the estimated percentile lower bound among test-takers for each exam

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . The results showed that GPT-4 performed better than GPT-3.5 in all the tests

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . For example, GPT-4 scored 298 out of 400 on the Uniform Bar Exam (MBE+MEE+MPT), which is around the 90th percentile, while GPT-3.5 scored 213 out of 400, around the 10th percentile

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . The results demonstrate the significant improvement that GPT-4 has achieved over its predecessor

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . GPT-4 scored high on traditional machine learning benchmarks, outperforming existing large language models.

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: In addition to its advanced language processing capabilities, GPT-4 is designed with safety and alignment in mind

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI spent six months making the model safer and more aligned, resulting in a system that is 82% less likely to respond to requests for disallowed content and 40% more likely to produce factual responses than GPT-3.5 on internal evaluations

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI achieved this by incorporating more human feedback, including feedback from ChatGPT users, and working with over 50 experts in domains such as AI safety and security.

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: OpenAI has released some information about companies that are already integrating ChatGPT in their product, some of them are: Duolingo Be My Eyes Stripe Morgan Stanley Government of Iceland

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: GPT-4 is the latest achievement in OpenAI's efforts to scale up deep learning

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . It is a large multimodal model that has achieved human-level performance on various academic and professional benchmarks

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Although it is still far from perfect, it exhibits improved factuality, steerability, and adherence to guardrails, making it more reliable, creative, and able to handle nuanced instructions than its predecessor, GPT-3.5

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . We are excited to see what GPT4 brings after seeing the hype and incredible amount of products that raised from ChatGPT

name: GPT-4: A New Milestone in Scaling Up Deep Learning
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: Explainable AI is increasingly important as it helps users understand the decision-making processes of machine learning models, ensuring fairness, addressing potential biases, and complying with regulations.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: It’s common to do your daily tasks and not stop to realize how technology is part of society

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . There are many situations in which AI is involved: when you are going somewhere but using Google Maps, if you don’t know what film to watch, Netflix helps you, or even in health-related fields

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Most of these AI applications are not determinants

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . For instance, I will not suffer if Spotify recommends a song I don’t like

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . However, there are professional usages where it is decisive, such as diagnosis or trials

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Should we know why AI has decided on a particular result

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: ? Is the process for a result always necessary?

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: All those examples are involved in the new technological field which tries to extract information from data, and it has lots of phases: data management, which acquires, stores, and cleans the data; creation of models to accomplish an aim, such as prediction or analysis; and sometimes visualization to explain which is the obtained information or the results from the data and model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . The problem given in the introduction is done in model creation.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: When a Machine Learning (ML) engineer or a Data Scientist has to decide which model fits better with the proposed goal, there are many models, and each has its features

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . ML models are divided into three types: Unsupervised, Supervised, and Reinforced

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . However, that’s not the only way to classify the models

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . They can be distinguished between Black boxes and White Boxes.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: First, white boxes are named to those models which receive input, and after its training, you can know all the decisions taken to an output given
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Let’s imagine there is a model that predicts when it's going to rain
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . It receives data related to humidity, temperature, speed, wind… And it says which is the probability of precipitation
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . In this model, the user could see if the decision was made because the temperature was low, the humidity was high, or perhaps it was due to many conditions
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . On the other hand, a black box is a system where the only visible part is the input and output
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . As its name says, the decision-making process is hidden from the user
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Continuing with the previous example, the model receives the same information about the weather in this case
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Still, you cannot see the exact mechanism of what features are more decisive or which ones are not influential
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Black boxes vs White boxes (ML models)
chunk_metadata: {"Header 2": "Which are the differences between these two systems?"}

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: Once the two sorts of “boxes” are explained, it’s time to return to the post's beginning

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . As it is said, many uses of AI are just for making life easier or enjoyable

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Nevertheless, other areas where AI is starting are delicate due to different factors

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . These factors are the reason why explainable models are needed:

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: Let’s suppose a trial for a crime

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . We have acquired data from the last years, including information about the type of previous crimes, the subject, and details about what happened, to decide whether the subject is innocent or the punishment

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . What would the result be if that court tends to punish black people rather than other races due to the proportion in the population

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: ? In this situation, the model is biased and will be more likely to predict black people as criminals

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Then, having a black box as a model, the prediction can’t be supervised, and justice will be in jeopardy.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: Fairness is not the only aspect compromised

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . When you are training models for a particular purpose, there are variables you don’t feel can affect a model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Now, you are trying to distinguish between land animals and birds

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . It seems to be easy

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . However, ML models learn patterns, and one of them for this classification is the background

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . When you think about birds, they are flying or in a tree, and that’s what the model can learn

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . But it isn’t always true because a bird can go on shore

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . This case can be detected using interpretable methods, but you can make the model more robust by modifying the images

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . That’s called data augmentation for image classification.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: Nowadays, many countries are regulating AI usage

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . One of the cases is in Europe, where individuals can ask about algorithmic decisions based on Art

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . 12 GDPR (data protection law)

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . How can black boxes be interpreted

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: ? First, we need to know which methods aren’t explained by themselves

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . To make figure it out quickly, here is a figure: The complexity of the ML methods Ways of interpreting black boxes:

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: The basic technique to understand an ML model is ranking the different features

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . This is common in interpretable methods, but it is essential to understand

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . When simpler models are used, like linear regression or decision trees, the variable importance can be known by the coefficients (linear regression), or thanks to visualizing decision trees, it is possible to see how the decisions are taken

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . However, it is tough to comprehend what’s happening when many features are involved

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . That’s why there are different measures: Once common in decision trees are Gini gain: Information Gain formula

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: This method is useful when we need to explain an opaque model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . When you have your model trained and prepared to work, you may wonder what’s the next step to discover its decision-making

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . The idea here is to create a secondary ML model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . How does it work

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: ? Once your next move is creating that secondary model, you should choose an interpretable model and train it with the same data as you did with the primary model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Still, the target variable is the predictions of this prior model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . So, this surrogate model is interpretable and tries to behave as the black box model does

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . The more accurate this surrogate model is, the better you should explain the black box model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . In summary, you choose an interpretable model, get predictions from the black box model, and use them for training the interpretable model selected

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Once done, you will measure the accuracy of this surrogate model and interpret it to understand the black box behavior.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: Those prior methods to interpret models are global, and you can learn how a model works in general, such as features' importance

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . However, occasionally you are wondering about a specific subject and why the model has taken a particular decision over a user

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . What should we do if we want to figure it out

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: ? That’s the time for LIME

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . It is a technique focused on local interpretable agnostic model explanations

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . This method works as follows, LIME produces lots of samples following the normal distribution and modifies the input data

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . It calculates the distance between the original and created observations and tries to predict the new points

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . After that, it selects the best features that describe the permuted data and fits a linear model on that data

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . This fitted linear model is now how we can explain the decision for that specific subject.

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: We have explained how AI is making decisions in our daily lives

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Moreover, we named how the models are classified and explained the differences between interpreted and not interpreted, white and black boxes, respectively

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . Answering the beginning questions is not always compulsory to reach a model functioning

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . However, each day it is more legislated and vital in business aims

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . The users are more aware of how ML models can affect their lives and ask how decisions are made

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . That’s why we should prevent and learn specific techniques to achieve a transparent model

name: Explainable AI
author: Daniel Oliver Belando
content: . In this post, we have explained many techniques for this transparency and interpretability: Feature importance, Global surrogate models, and LIME.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: This blog post explores the potential of using large language models in recommendation systems, optimal integration points and challenges in real-world applications such as training efficiency, inference latency and bias

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In the previous post we experimented with using LLMs as a recommendation systems

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This showed promising results but wasn’t without its challenges

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Recently more and more people began exploring the potential of language models as a new way to suggest information

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In a recently published paper titled How Can Recommender Systems Benefit from Large Language Models: A Survey a research team attempted to codify and summarize this potential as well as challenges that will arise with running LLMs as recommendation systems

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Welcome to another paper digest where we dive deep and summarize the survey, discussing the new exciting potential of LLMs

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: The explosion of recommendation systems coincides with development of online services and the work to address users overload with information and the need for its higher quality

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The common learning objective for a deep learning-based recommender system is to estimate a given user's preference towards each candidate item, and then arrange a ranked list of items presented to the user

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This is true despite the various forms of application tasks (such as top-N recommendation or sequential recommendation)

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . At the same time large language models (LLM) have demonstrated significant emergent capabilities in the field of natural language processing (NLP), including reasoning and in-context few-shot learning, as well as a vast repository of open-world information compressed in their pretrained model parameters

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Even while LLM is achieving tremendous success in a variety of deep learning applications, it is natural to ask the following question: How can recommender systems benefit from large language models for performance enhancements and user experience improvements

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? So to address this, this blog will be split into 4 parts: In the first one we will talk about where we can integrate the LLMs as there are sensible limitations to inclusion of new models/pipelines. There are places where they make complete sense and there are others where a simpler solution is preferred. In the second part we talk about how to integrate LLMs into the existing recsys pipelines. There are multiple modes of inclusion for example you can tune and not tune the LLM on your data, as well as include CRM (conventional recommendation methods) as part of your pipeline. We also mention challenges that arise from the industry to apply these new paradigms. And discuss potential future directions to improve the inclusion of LLMs into the recommendation systems of the future.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: So where can we even adapt the LLMs, we have already talked about the potential they have, but with so many possibilities we need to think about their place in the pipeline

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In a figure below we can see how many approaches just in the past 2 years were developed with the goal to integrate large language models as a means to improve existing recsys pipeline

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To understand its specifics I will briefly explain what each sector means: ‍ User data collection is a process which gathers user input from online services by recommending products to users. This feedback might be explicit (ratings) or implicit (click signals). Feature engineering is the process of choosing, modifying, enhancing, and changing the unstructured data gathered online (such as one-hot encoding) into structured data. In the subsequent stage, the feature encoder creates the neural embeddings for the scoring/ranking functions using the structured data as input. The embedding layer for one-hot encoded categorical features is how it is often formulated. Another basic component of recommendation is the scoring/ranking function , in which several machine learning techniques are created to choose the most pertinent items to meet users' information needs. The aforementioned recommendation pipeline's operations are monitored and managed by a pipeline controller . It can provide fine-grained control over various stages of recommendation (such as matching, ranking, and reranking). So now that we know what they do let’s talk business and discuss how LLMs can be integrated into those.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: What LLM can do heere is take the original data input and generate additional textual features as a way to augment the data

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This approach was demonstrated to work well with tabular data , and was further extended by using the LLMs to align out of domain datasets on the shared task

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . They can also be used to generate tags and model user interest.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: For conventional recommendation systems the data is usually transformed into one-hot encoding + an embedding layer is added to adopt dense embeddings

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . With LLMs we can improve the feature encoding process in two ways: we can add better representations for downstream models via the semantic information extracted and applied to the embeddings, achieve better cross-domain recommendations where feature pools might not be shared

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For example UNBERT uses BERT as a way to improve news recommendations via better feature encoding

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And ZESREC applies BERT in order to convert item descriptions into a zero-shot representations of a continuous form.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: A common approach explored is to use the LLM as a means to rank the items based on their relevance

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Many methods use a pipeline where the output of LLM is fed into a projection layer to calculate the score on the regression or classification task

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But recently some researchers proposed to instead use the LLM to deliver the score directly

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . TALLRec for example, uses LLM as a decoder to answer a binary question appended to the prompt, other team used LLM to predict a score in a textual manner and formatted it with careful prompting

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . LLMs can also be successfully used for direct item generation

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This would be similar to our approach in the previous blogpost

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . These approaches also can be hybridized and used in tandem.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: This approach largely stems from the notion that LLMs possess emergent properties, that is they can perform tasks that smaller models could not, these can be in context learning and logical reasoning

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, you should be aware that many researches a ctively dispute the claims that LLMs possess any emergent abilities and imply that these are instead a product of imperfect statistical methods that bias the evaluation, suggesting it may not be a fundamental property of scaling AI models Some researches even suggested a full framework that utilizes the LLM to manage the dialogue, understand user preferences, arrange ranking stage and simulate user interaction

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . You may have noticed that the user data collection piece is missing

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It is true, not a lot of work has been done to explore the LLM’s potential in this domain

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . LLMs here can be used to filter biased, hateful data and select best representations, or find meaningful, relevant information from a sea of input

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . They can be used in surveys as customer experience collectors and many more.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Now that we know where we can include the models into our pipeline let’s talk about how we can do so

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Generally we can have 4 cases

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . From the diagram above we can see how the current approaches are distributed given the choice of tuning and not tuning the LLM during training phase (this includes using efficient methods like adapters and LoRA ), and whether to use CRM as a recsys engine or not

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . By quadrants (in the figure models approaches by performance): Here we can see the approaches that both utilize LLM tuning and CRM inference. What is notable here is the model size. Approaches here use LLMs as feature encoders for semantic representations, this allows for lightweight setup but the key abilities of larger models (reasoning, instruction following) remain unexplored. Inferring with CRM but not tuning the LLM utilizes different abilities of LLMs (reasoning, richer semantic information) and a layer of CRM to either prerank items before inserting information into LLM or as a layer for LLM output. These approaches investigate zero-shot performance of LLMs and here they are all largely reliant on bigger LLM sizes and the idea behind it being that larger models have better latent space. This being said these approaches lag behind in performance and efficiency compared to light-weight CRM tuned on training data, indicating the importance of domain knowledge These approaches are similar to 1 in a way that they use lighter model sizes but they also go beyond the simple econder paradigm and use LLMs in greater capacity in the recsys pipeline.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: From the diagram above we can observe the performance difference between groups in 3 and 1,2,4, indicating that while 3 had the largest model sizes, the task of recommending items requires specialized domain knowledge

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Therefore finetuning indeed increases the performance

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Which means you can either tune the LLM during training and inject in-domain collaborative knowledge, or during inference inject this information via CRM from a model centric perspective.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Although as demonstrated, larger models with zero-shot performance do not work as well in a context of a recsys

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Researchers found that they are surprisingly good at reranking hard samples

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . They introduce the filter-then-rerank paradigm, which uses a pre-ranking function from conventional recommender systems to pre-filter simpler negative items (e.g., matching or pre-ranking stage in industrial applications) and creates a set of candidates with more difficult samples for LLM to rerank

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This should improve LLM's listwise reranking efficiency, particularly for APIs that resemble ChatGPT

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This discovery is useful in industrial settings, where we may want LLM only handle hard samples and leave other samples to light-weight models to reduce computational expenses.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: It is difficult to tell

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Given finetuning on the domain data, all models large and small give comparatively good performance

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . As there is no unified recsys benchmark to measure the performance of larger and smaller models and their relative success, this question is still up for evaluation

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . I would argue that depending on your application and where in the pipeline you want to include the LLM you should select different model size.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: But this is still all in an academic setting, there are serious specific engineering challenges that come from the industry that I want to mention here

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . First is training efficiency

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Recall the articles about training cost of the GPT-3 and 4, and you can already start to get a headache about the cost of repeated finetuning of your LLM for a recommendation data pool that is constantly shifting and expanding

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So you have expanding data volume + update model frequency (day-level, hour- level, minute-level) + underlying LLM size = trouble

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To address this parameter-efficient methods are recommended for finetuning

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The benefit to using larger model sizes lies in producing more generalized and reliable output via just a handful of supervisions

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Researchers suggest adopting the long-short update strategy, when we leverage LLM for feature engineering and feature encoder

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This cuts down the training data volume and relaxes the update frequency for LLM (e.g.week-level) while maintaining full training data and high update frequency for CRM

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This way LLM can give the CRM aligned domain knowledge and CRM can be used as a frequently updated adapter for the LLM

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Second important part is inference latency , something I have dealt with myself in the past.Recommendation systems are usually real-time services and applications that are extremely time sensitive, where all stages (matching, ranking, etc.) should be done in tens of milliseconds

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . LLMs famously possess large inference time, so this creates a problem

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To address this we recommend using caching and precomputing, which has proven to be effective , hence you can cache dense embeddings produces by an LLM

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Another good strategy is reduction in model size for final inference via techniques like distillation and quantization, this introduces a bit of tradeoff between model size and performance so a balance has to be found

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In other ways LLMs can be used for feature engineering which does not bring extra burden of computation to the inference phase

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Third is a challenge of dealing with long-text inputs

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For LLMs we need to often use prompts and given that a lot of user data is collected the general industry recsys requires longer user history

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But LLMs don't perform well with large textual inputs

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This can be partially because the original training corpus contained shorter inputs and the distribution of in-domain text is different from the original training data

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Additionally, using larger text sizes can induce memory inefficiency and break the limits of context window causing LLM to forget information and produce inferior output

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In the same category ID indexing should be mentioned

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Recall that large amounts of data for recsys possess no semantic information

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Here approaches are divided into 2 camps

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . One completely abandons non-semantic IDs and instead focuses on building interfaces using natural language alone, this seems to improve cross-domain performance and generalization

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, other choose to potentially sacrifice these gains in favor of im domain performance, by introducing new embedding methods that account for IDs like P5

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Or cluster related IDs together, or attach semantic information to them

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The last but not least important considerations are fairness and bias

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . An underlying bias of LLMs is an active research area

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Further finetuning and the foundation model choice have to account for bias in the data to make recommendations fair and appropriate

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Careful design considerations need to be made to address impact of sensitive attributes (gender, race) and focus model on historical user data, possibly with filtering and designed prompting.

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: In this post we covered the landscape of current LLM approaches in recsys

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This area of research is very fresh and no doubt in the coming years we will see new developments addressing challenges and potential mentioned in this blogpost

name: Exploring the benefits of Large Language Models for Recommendation Systems
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For takeaway the 2 great directions for the future of LLM in recsys can be: A unified benchmark which is of urgent importance and need in order to provide convincing evaluation metric to allow fine grained comparison among existing approaches and it is expensive to reproduce many experimental results of recsys with LLMs A custom large foundation model tailored for recommendation domains, which can take over the entire recommendation pipeline, enabling new levels of automation in recsys. ‍ References 1 For more reading or if you are curious please visit this great repository that hosts the papers about recys LLMs and stay tuned for more from our blog 2 Images are sourced from the paper

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: Problems with bias in recommendation systems and what you can do about them.

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: When it comes to watching YouTube videos, I often categorize myself as part of that “silent majority” group

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . As one of the 1.5 billion viewers of BTS’s most viewed music video , I managed not to smash that like button even though I played it probably more than 100 times

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . In the dictionary of AI bias, my unconventional user behavior is a perfect example of selection bias , a common bias in recommendation system applications such as YouTube

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Given recommended videos, the user can choose whether to rate and what to rate, making the observed rating distribution less representative of the hidden true rating distribution.

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: Besides the selection bias, many other biases can emerge in the recommendation system

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . The following table summarises the seven typical biases in recommendation systems, which follow the taxonomy of this latest survey paper

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . The illustrating examples in the context of recommendation systems are also provided to help you understand these biases more concretely

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . ‍ Depending on the specific generation stage, these biases can be further clustered over the following feedback loop , which is an abstracted lifecycle of recommendations with three stages

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Specifically, stage 1 (data collection) aims to collect the data from users, leading to the generation of data-associated biases such as selection bias, exposure bias, conformity bias, and position bias

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Once data are collected, Stage 2 (model learning) learns the recommendation model from the data with model assumptions, i.e., inductive bias

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Finally, in Stage 3 (recommendation), the learned model will return its recommendations to the users, which may involve recommendation-associated biases such as popularity bias and unfairness

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . These same three stages will keep iterating along the loop, collecting the latest user data for model updates and more recommendations

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . ‍ The feedback loop of recommendations, where different biases occur in three stages, i.e., the “data collection” stage, the “model learning” stage, and the actual “recommendation” stage.

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: However, there is a growing concern regarding the effect of feedback loops

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Google’s @DeepMind warned people back in their 2019’s tweet that feedback loops can amplify biases along the loop, leading to filter bubbles and echo chambers that can shift users’ views

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . ‍ ‍ What are filter bubbles and echo chambers

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: ? And why are they so undesirable

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: ? An illustration of filter bubble, where users are isolated from new and different content outside the bubble The concept of the Filter Bubble was initially proposed and discussed in 2011 by @Eli Pariser in his book “The Filter Bubble: What The Internet Is Hiding From You” , where he raised concerns regarding the increasingly personalized internet

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . He claimed that the recommendation algorithms of search engines and social networks, such as Google and Facebook, have created a distorted “bubble” world for users by filtering their search results based on relevance

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . For example, back then, Google utilized as many as 57 “signals” such as search history or geological location to better deliver the most “relevant” and customize content for users

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . By restricting access to information outside, filter bubbles can further enhance the similar viewpoints to be shared and reinforced among homogenous groups with similar opinions

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . For example, in the 2016 US presidential election, Twitter information flows, such as liking and sharing posts, are shown to be more frequent among individuals with similar political backgrounds

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . This phenomenon is often termed Echo Chambers , which is a good analogy for describing the information echoing effect within the closed bubbles

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Both filter bubbles and echo chambers can be extremely harmful

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . From the perspective of users, overexposure to homogeneous content or viewpoints can make them feel bored as it doesn’t always align with what they want

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Users may also want to be challenged from time to time with some opposing views for learning purposes

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Hence limiting users within the bubbles and chambers can decrease the long-term user satisfaction and loyalty to the associated platforms

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Moreover, filter bubbles can also harm the benefits of content creators who deliver new content for these users

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . For new creators who just enter the platform such as TikTok, the “lack of relevance” caused by filter bubbles makes their work less recommended and less likely to go viral

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Consequently, many talented content creators who could have contributed good content for the platforms may be driven away, further damaging user satisfaction and deteriorating the platform’s “ecosystem” in the long run

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . ‍ Eli Pariser’s TED talk on Filter Bubbles back in 2011 ‍ Moreover, echo chambers and filter bubbles can create more damage beyond individuals (users and content creators) and worsen society-level issues such as the spreading of misinformation

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . In a recent article published by Misinformation Review of Harvard Kennedy School, researchers analyzed news articles shared by more than 15K Twitter accounts

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . By visualizing user retweets and quotes as a network, the echo chamber effect is apparent - in the red “chamber”, conservatives tend to retweet and quote other conservatives more, and the same phenomenon appears in the blue liberal “chamber” as well

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Moreover, the spreading frequency of misinformation, measured by the node size, is generally higher within each chamber, indicating a positive correlation between echo chambers and the spreading of misinformation (also validated statistically)

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Without promptly addressing echo chambers and filter bubbles, such social issues can eventually make users and society feel frustrated, damaging the user loyalty and reputation of Twitter as a platform

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . ‍ Visualizing the network structure of Twitter followers behavior: the node color indicates the follower’s partisanship while the node size represents the spreading frequency of misinformation, i.e., sharings from low-quality sources ( source )

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: Given the problems of filter bubbles and echo chambers, what can we do about them to alleviate the negative consequences

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: ? To find an answer, researchers from DeepMind conducted detailed simulations of various recommendation system algorithms, which differ in their priority of accurately predicting users’ interests or randomly promoting new content

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . The simulation result reveals that algorithms valuing more random exploration tend to have less system degeneracy, i.e., less severe effects of filter bubbles and echo chambers

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Therefore, they conclude that the best remedy for both phenomena is to design recommendation systems with more random exploration, e.g., offering users more diverse and unexpected recommendations

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Meanwhile, boosting the candidate item pool where recommendations are drawn can also help

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . This remedy essentially brings us back to the well-known concept of trade-off between exploration vs exploitation in the recommendation system

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Here exploitation refers to making recommendations that are seemingly optimal based on known user behavior data collected in the past

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Exploitation is always safer due to its relevance, but it can also limit the model from discovering better options if they exist

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . By contrast, exploration overcomes this limit by recommending more random items, enabling the model to obtain more optimal recommendations from the larger pool of usage data

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . However, exploration may suffer from poor decisions made, resulting in wasted resources spent on exploring

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . As we can see here, there indeed exists a fundamental dilemma between exploration and exploitation

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . To most effectively alleviate both filter bubbles and echo chambers, the goal is to find a strategy with a good trade-off between exploration and exploitation

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Different exploration strategies are available, with the most popular ones being Epsilon-Greedy Method , Optimistic Initialization Method, Upper Confidence Bounds (UCB) Method, and Thompson Sampling Method

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . We won’t go into too much detail here but if you are interested, highly recommend this medium article by @Joseph Rocca

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . It’s pretty well-written

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: ! Here at Shaped , we address the trade-off between exploration and exploitation through Thompson Sampling in the ordering stage of our ranking engine

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Specifically, some indeterminism is added into the final ranking (e.g

name: Exploration vs. Exploitation in Recommendation Systems
author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . placing random candidate items towards the top of the rankings) to mitigate filter bubbles and echo chambers that bias the ranking algorithm

author: Jazlyn Lin
content: . Does it sound relevant to you
