name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: You probably have heard of terms like ROC, AUC, and Precision-recall, they show up in data science articles on Medium, machine learning tutorials, and academic papers are full of them

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But why are they so important and what do they actually mean

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Today we will dive into the specifics of those essential metrics, and explain how they work and their importance in the world of machine learning and recommendation systems.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: The first thing you need to know is that all these metrics are used to provide a quantifiable measure of performance

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Let’s imagine that you are a machine learning developer, building an app for the delivery of bubble tea, these days there are many different vendors offering a wide variety of options

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But you want to make sure your users will buy the tea from your app, to make it happen you want to suggest the best bubble tea options based on their preferred flavors, tea type, sugar level, and time of delivery (gotta keep it fresh)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . All of this can be framed as a typical recommendation problem

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And for simplicity let’s assume that you are just starting out so you have only two types of bubble tea, one that has tapioca balls and another coconut jelly

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . After tracking and recording user orders you build a dataset of customers who prefer these two types of tea

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Next, you want to classify them so that your general recommendation model can infer from user data that it would prefer bubble tea chains and products that contain tapioca

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This type of problem is known as binary classification , in simple RecSys terms the two things you are trying to predict are users’ likes and dislikes

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In the real world, this task gets more complex but these evaluation metrics actually work in the same way for a multitude of options and scenarios

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So let’s take our example and explain all the metrics using it.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: We have trained our model and now we need to test it out, so where do we start

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? We begin at ROC

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . ROC stands for Receiver Operating Characteristic

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It's a graphical representation of the performance of a binary classification model

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It plots the true positive rate (TPR) against the false positive rate (FPR) at different threshold settings

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To break it down let’s explain those terms: TPR is the percentage of correctly predicted positive examples out of all the actual positive examples

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Here our model will be correctly predicting that our user likes the type of bubble tea we selected

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . From the equation above: TPR = TP(True Positives) / P(All Positives) Now what about FPR

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? FPR is the percentage of incorrectly predicted positive examples out of all the actual negative examples

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So in our case, the model will predict the wrong type of bubble tea that the customer likes

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . From the equation above: FPR = FP(False Positives) / N(All Negatives) As we can see both FPR and TPR relate to each other and can be calculated in different ways

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A perfect model would have a ROC curve that hugs the top-left corner of the plot, meaning that it would have a high TPR and a low FPR at all threshold settings

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A model that makes random predictions would have a ROC curve that is a diagonal line from the bottom-left to the top-right corner of the plot, meaning that its TPR and FPR would be equal at all threshold settings

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A threshold in this case is the value above which the prediction becomes positive or negative depending on your setup

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For example threshold >= 0.5 means that every sample that gets above 50% for the target class becomes this class

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Threshold settings are used to adjust the balance between true positives and false positives by changing the criteria that determine when an example is classified as positive

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . These adjustments are reflected in the ROC curve which is a graphical representation of the performance of a classification model

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Here we can see the ROC curve and a dashed line labeled random

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This represents ROC curve of a classifier that makes random predictions.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ROC seems sufficient so why use AUC

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? AUC or Area Under the Curve summarizes ROC across all thresholds and is therefore the area under the ROC curve

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . AUC is calculated by finding the area under the curve of the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve, which plots the true positive rate (TPR) against the false positive rate (FPR) at different threshold settings and combining them into a single score

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A perfect model would have an AUC of 1, meaning that all the positive examples would be ranked higher than all the negative examples, while a model that makes random predictions would have an AUC of 0.5

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This detail is important as this makes AUC a better metric than a plain accuracy score which is just a percentage of correct predictions against all the possible inputs in the dataset

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . AUC can be interpreted as the probability that a randomly chosen positive example will be ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative example

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Below we can see how AUC looks like when plotted, it is the shaded blue area under the ROC curve

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If we were to shade everything below random line we would get AUC of 0.5 → a result signifying random predictions coming from our classifier model

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This understanding of AUC is traditional and is very suitable for classification

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, this approach is not ideal for most recommendation systems and requires adaptation

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you were to look up implementations of AUC online, you would likely find that two things the method would require are ids and scores

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In essence this would be the true ids of your items, and the scores meaning how likely the item was picked or predicted (note how the idea of prediction scores is more relevant for classification objective)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For ranking, instead, we often get the predicted ids of items in order that the model also attempts to predict (from most relevant to least) and the true ids which is the true ranking, i.e

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . user preferences

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So to redefine relevance we need to incorporate the measure of relevant items in correct order

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We can do it like so: In the numerator we have a sum over an indicator function that equals 1 if the score of irrelevant item t 0​ is less than the score of relevant item t 1 , and 0 otherwise

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Note that the score s(t) is calculated based on the inverse rank of the item in the predicted list

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Higher rank (closer to the top) results in a higher score

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . M 0 is the set of irrelevant items that are present in the predicted list but not in the actual relevant set, M 1 ​ is the set of relevant items that are present both in the predicted list and the actual relevant set

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Hence, in our version, the AUC value is computed by counting how often a randomly selected relevant item is ranked higher than an irrelevant item, normalized by the total possible pairs of relevant and irrelevant items

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The formula defaults to 0.5 when no relevant or no irrelevant items are found in the predicted list, indicating no discrimination between relevant and irrelevant items.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: We can clearly see now that all of these metrics are related

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It is directly because they all rely on the same common variables like TP, TN, FP, and FN

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So what’s so different about precision-recall

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? In essence, the task PR fulfills is very similar but with a slight difference

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . While ROC and AUC look to measure the ability of the classifier to separate positive and negative examples and are a good choice when the dataset is balanced (equal number of both classes), PR is looking to measure a model's ability to identify positive samples while minimizing false positives at the same time

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . It is considered a better choice for imbalanced datasets and a good option when you are more interested in positive examples

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Precison-Recall in the data To better understand this concept let’s recall the equations for TPR and FPR above and see the difference between them and equations for precision and recall : And for recall: Notice anything common

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? That’s right

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ! TPR and Recall are the same

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . There is one more important detail, notice how true negatives are missing from the equations above

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? As mentioned PR focuses on the positive examples as under this metric they are of the bigger interest to us

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A perfect model would have a precision of 1 and a recall of 1, meaning that all of the positive examples are correctly predicted and all of the actual positive examples are predicted as positive

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . In practice, there is a trade-off between precision and recall, and a model with high precision might have a low recall and vice versa

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . PR helps to understand how well the model is able to identify relevant examples while minimizing the number of irrelevant examples

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (ROC, AUC, and Precision-Recall)
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This sums up our journey into popular ML metrics!

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Evaluating recommendation models is notoriously difficult and there is rarely a silver bullet approach

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . This article walks through different model evaluation methods, the common pitfalls when evaluating recommendation models, and how to avoid them

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . A typical evaluation workflow involves two main stages: offline and online evaluation

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Offline evaluation uses historical data to predict user interactions and measure model performance with metrics like precision and recall

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Once the model performs well offline, it moves to online evaluation, where it is tested in a live environment using A/B testing to track its impact on real user behavior and business objectives such as impressions, clicks and conversion.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Offline evaluation assesses a model's performance using historical data in a controlled environment to predict user interactions and measure various metrics without impacting live users

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . This method is essential for tuning and improving models before deploying them into a live environment.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: During offline evaluation, algorithms are quantitatively assessed by how well they predict relevant user interactions on a hold-out set of data using metrics such as precision, recall, mean average precision (MAP), and normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG)

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Qualitative evaluation also plays a role, involving an examination of the descriptive analytics of the recommendations, such as the distribution and diversity of recommendations in the top-k results

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . What’s a hold-out set

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: ? A hold-out set is a subset of your data that you deliberately avoid training on so that you can test the model's performance on unseen data

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . For production machine-learning use cases like recommendation systems, it's important to split this hold-out set chronologically to test the model's performance on future data and avoid time-based data leakage

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Biases in Offline Evaluation Metrics Offline evaluation metrics are a great way to get a sense of how well your model is performing; however, they can sometimes be misleading

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The biggest problem is that predicting a hold-out set of interactions is not the same as predicting what your users will actually interact with

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Offline evaluation is observational —we're evaluating how well we fit logged data—rather than interventional —evaluating how changing the recommendation algorithm leads to different outcomes (e.g

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . purchases)

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . If the logged data is biased in any way, this can lead to misleading results

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Here are some examples of bias commonly seen: Data Delivery Bias : Your interactions will be biased towards the historic delivery mechanism used to surface recommendations. For example, if you've only been showing users the most popular items for the last year, your interactions will have a significant bias towards popular items. In this case, typically the best algorithm on the hold-out set will be the same one you're using to serve the data; however, this doesn't mean it's the best algorithm for your users. Cold-start bias : Related to data delivery bias, but it's so common it deserves its own point: Your interactions will be biased towards older or newer items. For example, new items may have fewer interactions, which means they're not weighted as highly within the hold-out set. Observational bias : Even in a perfect world with no data delivery biases, where all items were historically served completely randomly, the algorithms will still be biased towards an environment that isn't affected by the candidate recommendation itself. Once deploying the algorithm to production, the way users interact with items will change and, therefore, the model's performance will change. Mitigating Biases in Offline Evaluation Several techniques have been developed to address the above biases: Counterfactual Evaluation: Counterfactual evaluation aims to estimate what would have happened if a different recommendation policy had been used. This involves modeling the biases and adjusting the evaluation metrics accordingly. Inverse Propensity Scoring (IPS) : A method to adjust for exposure bias by weighting interactions based on their propensity scores, which estimate the probability that an item was seen by a user. The corrected metric provides an unbiased estimate of the true performance of the recommendation algorithm. Debiasing Techniques: These techniques aim to correct for biases present in the data: Popularity Strata: Segregating test data into different strata based on item popularity ensures that evaluations do not disproportionately favor popular items. Equal Sampling: Ensuring an equal number of interactions for each item type, thereby reducing the impact of popularity bias. Unbiased Data Collection: Collecting random samples of user interactions can help create an unbiased dataset. However, this approach is resource-intensive and challenging to scale.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: To address the complexities of offline evaluation, several techniques and methodologies are employed: Data Partitioning: Random Sampling: This involves randomly splitting the data into training and test sets. While simple, this method can ignore temporal dynamics in user interactions, which are crucial for evaluating recommendations. Temporal Sampling: Data is split based on time, with earlier interactions used for training and later interactions for testing. This approach helps simulate the real-world scenario where models predict future user behavior based on past interactions. It also avoids temporal data leakage, ensuring that the evaluation is realistic. Candidate Item Set Subsampling: Evaluated systems are often required to rank a subset of items rather than the entire catalog. This subset can be determined by various factors: Training Set Exclusion: Excluding items seen during training to avoid overfitting. Popularity-based Sampling: Including a mix of popular and less popular items to ensure that the model's ability to recommend diverse items is tested. Dynamic Subsets: Using contextually relevant subsets, such as items that have recently become popular or those that align with current trends. Metrics Beyond Accuracy: Traditional accuracy metrics like precision and recall are necessary but not sufficient for a holistic evaluation of recommender systems. Other important metrics include: Novelty: Measures how unexpected the recommendations are. High novelty can enhance user satisfaction by introducing them to new and interesting items. Diversity: Evaluates how varied the recommendations are. Diverse recommendations can cater to multiple user interests and prevent the over-concentration on a narrow set of items. Serendipity: Assesses the ability of the system to recommend items that are not only relevant but also pleasantly surprising. We recommend looking at some of the attached resources at the end of the article to understand common metrics for evaluation.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Considering all the issues with offline metric evaluation, how do we interpret the results

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: ? We like to think of offline metric evaluation as a compass rather than a map

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . You can use it to understand characteristics of the model relative to baseline algorithms; however, you can't interpret these metrics too literally

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . For example, a precision of 10% doesn't mean that 10% of the items within a slate size will be relevant in a live test; however, if it's 1% better than a trending baseline, it's a good sign it's worth evaluating in an online setting

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Note: even if it is 1% worse, it might still be worthwhile evaluating in an online setting if the results are more diverse than the baseline or you know the sampled data is biased towards the baseline in some severe way.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Within the offline evaluation stage, it's also critical to qualitatively evaluate the candidate model by closely examining a sample of recommendations from different users

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . For example, for a book recommendation model, you might find a user who has only interacted with romance books and confirm that the model is recommending mostly romance books to that user

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Evaluating the model in this way can help sanity check that everything is working as expected

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . If we see unexpected qualitative results despite seeing good quantitative results, it may mean the objective used to train/evaluate the model is incorrect

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . The Problems With User Drill Down Analysis The biggest issue with user drill down is the human biases that come in when evaluating the results

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . This typically happens in two ways: user-selection biases and product biases

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . User-selection biases: Say you're evaluating a recommendation model and instead of a random user, you pick your own internal user. You know your interests best, so it might seem obvious to try yourself first. The problem is you are likely biased in ways related to being an employee at the company. You might have internal features that result in a different user experience than the average user, and maybe your interactions don't reflect your true interests because you test the product constantly. Sometimes even choosing a random "power user" can be misleading as these power users are actually employees or have some other bias that makes them less useful to manually evaluate. We suggest choosing several random users when evaluating. Product biases: The other human bias that's common comes from preconceived product biases of what you might think users are interested in compared to what they're actually interested in. For example, assuming that a user's demographic is a good predictor of their interests when in fact it's not. Sometimes it's best not to be overly prescriptive about what you expect users to see, and as long as the results aren't majorly wrong, let the online metrics speak for themselves.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: Online evaluation occurs after you've deployed your model to production and are serving end-users with results from your algorithm

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . This is the gold-standard of evaluation as you can objectively track the impact of your model on your target business objectives (e.g

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . clicks, purchases) in an interventional way.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: A/B Testing: Typically when first deploying a new algorithm to production, you'll run an A/B test where you serve the new algorithm to a subset of users and compare the results to a control group that's served the old algorithm. This is the best way to understand the impact of the new algorithm on your business objectives relative to the old and removes confounders that might affect the evaluation metrics (E.g. seasonality may affect purchase rates in a way that's not related to the recommendation algorithm). Multi-Armed Bandit Testing: Multi-armed bandit testing is a sophisticated approach to model evaluation that dynamically allocates traffic to different models based on their performance. This method balances the need for exploration (trying out different models) and exploitation (favoring the best-performing models). In practice, algorithms such as epsilon-greedy, UCB (Upper Confidence Bound), or Thompson Sampling are employed to determine which model to present to users at any given time. By using these algorithms, the system can efficiently identify and prioritize the most effective recommendation models, thereby optimizing user experience and engagement. This approach not only enhances the performance of the recommender system but also ensures that the best models receive more exposure and testing opportunities. Interleaving: Interleaving is another technique used in online model evaluation where recommendations from different models are presented together to the same users. This can be achieved by interleaving items from different models within the recommendation list. By tracking user interactions with these interleaved lists, it becomes possible to determine which model's recommendations are more preferred by users. Interleaving offers a direct comparison between models under identical conditions, providing clear insights into their relative effectiveness. This method is particularly useful for fine-tuning models and making informed decisions about which model to deploy broadly based on actual user preferences and behaviors.

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online

content: The main problem with online evaluation is that it's time-consuming

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . Despite this, as an objective measure of uplift, it's nearly always worth it once you feel confident the offline results are at least comparable with a baseline

name: Recommender Model Evaluation: Offline vs. Online
author: Nic Scheltema
content: . That all being said, there can be several pitfalls during online evaluation that are worth mentioning: Looking only at one metric: If you only look at one metric, you may be optimizing for that metric at the expense of others. For example, if you're optimizing for click-through rate, you might end up recommending the same popular items to everyone, which might not be the best for your business in the long run. We recommend looking at a suite of metrics to understand the full picture. Looking at only the aggregate data: If you only look at the aggregate data, you might miss important sub-populations that are being affected by the algorithm in different ways. For example, if you're optimizing for purchases, you might miss that the algorithm is actually decreasing the number of purchases from your most loyal users. We recommend looking at the results of the A/B test across different user segments. Focusing on short-term signals: If you only look at short-term signals like clicks, you might miss the long-term impact of the algorithm, such as 30-day retention. Even if the algorithm is increasing clicks in the short term, it might be worthwhile holding a long-running experiment indefinitely that keeps a baseline algorithm shown to a small subset of users (e.g. 5%).

If you’re thinking what the relevance of this silly story from my childhood is, it is that I believe that embeddings have the potential to be the Flash ability of modern companies, a way of illuminating the landscape beyond the limited flashlight view of traditional Data Science methods of the past

author: Zac Weigold
categories: Learn LLMs Technology Data AI/ML Tutorial
content: . Typically, companies utilize well-known Data Science methods to analyze segments of their business, whether it be customer data, marketing research, or even administrative tasks, in an isolated manner; meaning that they draw segregated conclusions from each individual relevant task related to data they possess

name: Embracing Embeddings: From fragmented insights to unified understanding
author: Zac Weigold
categories: Learn LLMs Technology Data AI/ML Tutorial
content: . Embeddings aims to change this whole paradigm, by allowing businesses to gather insights from the collective viewpoint of all their data rather than inferences made by snapshots of singular datasets

author: Zac Weigold
categories: Learn LLMs Technology Data AI/ML Tutorial
content: . Embeddings create universal understanding of users that can power all AI systems within companies Embeddings allow companies to achieve this by essentially acting as a numerical translator from unstructured data types to numeric vector representations, thus unlocking the potential of any unstructured data that a business may have, which was once thought irrelevant to numerical Data Analysis and left on the cutting room floor

content: . In many senses, it acts as the bridge between unstructured human-enforced data and the technical powers of machine learning algorithms

content: . By acting as a translator from unstructured data to an appropriate vector space, embeddings can enable AI to perform nuanced, linguistically adept analyses on the entirety of a company's data pool—essentially a ‘Zoomed Out’ view that encompasses building holistic customer personas, cohort analysis, and understanding user psychology, thus replacing simple keyword searches with a system that understands context, sentiment, and subtle differences within data points that from a traditional Data Science perspective would be perceived to be numerically similar

name: Embracing Embeddings: From fragmented insights to unified understanding

categories: Learn LLMs Technology Data AI/ML Tutorial
content: . This in turn, allows for the creation down the line of a shared workspace for continuous, contextually aware insights that evolve from the static snapshots of the past to dynamic, universally comprehensible environments, streamlining everything within a business from marketing and research to strategy and administrative tasks into a unified, continuously updating analysis system

name: Embracing Embeddings: From fragmented insights to unified understanding
author: Zac Weigold
categories: Learn LLMs Technology Data AI/ML Tutorial

author: Zac Weigold

author: Zac Weigold
categories: Learn LLMs Technology Data AI/ML Tutorial
content: . By bucketing users into discrete categories through the analysis of a few features within their data, these traditional methods are highly prone to stereotyping users into groups they may not necessarily belong to

name: Embracing Embeddings: From fragmented insights to unified understanding

content: . According to tech research firm Gartner , unstructured data now accounts for an estimated 80-90 percent of all data stored online

With embeddings you can use all of your data to power AI systems With access to the benefits of modern AI in tandem with the conversion of unstructured data to a format that machine learning models can understand, the true power of this shift lies in the ability to ask more powerful and revealing questions concerning the nature of your data

content: . Embedding your unstructured data still allows you to preserve the original intricate relationships between data points, allowing businesses to delve deeper into patterns, correlations, and outliers that might otherwise remain elusive

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Imagine you’re shown two ordered feeds of product recommendations from separate algorithms

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In the first one (A) you’re shown: Nike sneakers, Adidas shorts, and an Apple Watch

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In the second one (B) you’re shown the order: Apple Watch, Adidas shorts, and Nike Sneakers

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . -- Which feed is more relevant to you

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Considering both of these lists have the same items, the question of relevance becomes a question of what order is best

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Typically we assume the more relevant list is the one that has more relevant items closer to the top/start of the list

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is because for feed like use-cases where an item is surfaced one after an other (e.g

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . like TikTok), it’s important that the top items of the feed are the most relevant to keep the user engaged

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It’s equally important for carousel recommendation use-cases (e.g

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . like Netflix), where the items to the left of the carousel are often the first looked at as the audience gazes of the page

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In our first post on evaluating recommendation systems we looked at evaluating Precision@k, Recall@k and R-Precision metrics using a test set of relevant items

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If you compute them for the example two recommendation feeds, you’ll see they’re not too useful — they’re equivalent for both lists

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is because they’re not capturing anything about the relative order of the rankings, only how many relevant matches are found

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Below we discuss two evaluation metrics that are typically used for recommendation system use-cases where ranking order is important

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . To motivate these metrics, let’s assume a user has actually purchased: Apple watch, and Adidas shorts, and we’ve put these items in a test set that wasn’t used when training the recommendation algorithms.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Mean average precision [1] averages the precision@k metric at each relevant item position in the recommendation list

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For recommendation list A and using our example user, the relevant items are at position 2 and 3

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Therefore, we compute precision@2 and precision@3 and average the results

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The mAP values for algorithm A and B are below: Algorithm A, mAP = (precision@2 + precision@3) / 2 = (1/2 + 2/3) / 2 = 0.58 Algorithm B, mAP = (precision@1 + precision@2) / 2 = ( 1/1 + 2/2) / 2 = 1 As you can see from the example, this metric rewards the recommendation algorithm that puts more items at the top of the list

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This is because any non-relevant items at the start of the list are factored into the aggregation at each subsequent precision@r computation

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Mean Average Precision (mAP)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Where Rel(r) is an indicator that specifies whether the item at rank r is relevant

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Note that the normalization factor of the varge can either be the total number of recommendations or the total number of relevant items (or the minimum of both).

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ‍ Mean Reciprocal Rank quantifies the rank of the first relevant item found in the recommendation list

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The only complexity is that it takes the reciprocal of this “first relevant item rank”, meaning that if the first item is relevant (i.e

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . the ideal case) then MRR will be 1, otherwise it’ll be lower

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For the example above, the first recommendation list has a first relevant item at rank 2 (Adidas shorts)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The second recommendation list has a relevant item at rank 1 (Apple watch)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Therefore: Algorithm A, MRR = 1/2 = 0.5 Algorithm B, MRR = 1/1 = 1 ‍ Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ‍ Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain is the other commonly used ranking metric

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Its best explained by first defining Cumulative Gain (CG) as the sum of relevant items among top k results

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Note that this value for the binary case is the numerator of Precision@k and Recall@k and doesn’t take into account any ordering

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Cumulative Gain (CG) Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) is where the ordering comes into play

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This metric discounts the “value” of each of the relevant items based on its rank

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The problem with DCG, is that even an “ideal” recommendation algorithm won’t always be able to get DCG@k = 1

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Discounted Cumulative Gain (DCG) Normalized DCG (NDCG), the final iteration, it normalizes DCG by the “ideal” recommendation algorithm (IDCG@k)

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . That is, an algorithm where every relevant item is ranked at the start of the list

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . IDCG@k NDCG@k So looking at our example user, lets compute NDCG@k for both recommendation lists

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We can first compute IDCG because it’s a constant: IDCG@k = (1/log(1 + 1) + 1/log(2 + 1)) = 5.417

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Then we’ll compute DCG and put it altogether for each algorithm: Algorithm A: DCG@k = 1/log(2 + 1) + 1/log(3 + 1) = 3.756 NDCG@k = NDCG@k / IDCG@k = 0.693 Algorithm B: DCG@k = 1/log(1 + 1) + 1/log(2 + 1) = 5.417 NDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k = 1 As you can see, Algorithm A has a higher NDCG@k, which is what we should expect

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: mAP and NDCG seem like they have everything for this use-case — they both take all relevant items into account, and the order in which they are ranked

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, where MRR beats them across the board is interpretability

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . MRR gives an indication of the average rank of your algorithm, which can be a helpful way of communicating when a user is most likely to see their first relevant item using your algorithm

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Furthermore, MRR might map better to your final use-case better, for example if you care more about the “I’m Feeling Lucky” search result, than the standard “Search” ranking

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . When should we use mAP vs NDCG

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? mAP has some interpretability characteristics in that it represents the area under the Precision-Recall curve

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . NDCG is hard to interpret because of the seemingly arbitrary log discount within the DCG equation

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The advantage of NDCG is that it can be extended to use-cases when numerical relevancy is provided for each item.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ‍ To motivate where NDCG reigns supreme, let’s say we have another user who has previously purchased: 1x Apple watch, 5x Adidas shorts and 3x Nike sneakers

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We may conclude that the relevancy of each item is weighted by how many items were purchased

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . So let’s define: relevance(Apple watch) = 1 relevance(Adidas shorts) = 5 relevance(Nike sneakers) = 3 Then recomputing the NDCG metrics: IDCG@k = 5/log(1 + 1) + 3/log(2 + 1) + 1/log(3 + 1) = 24.55 Algorithm A: DCG@k = 3/log(1 + 1) + 5/log(2 + 1) + 1/log(3 + 1) = 22.104 NDCG@k = DCG@k / IDCG@k = 0.9 Algorithm B: DCG@k = 1/log(1 + 1) + 5/log(2 + 1) + 3/log(3 + 1) = 18.78 NDCG@k = NDCG@k / IDCG@k = 0.764 Therefore, we can see that Algorithm A is better in this case

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Note that unfortunately obtaining this 'ground-truth' relevance score in practice can be tricky so you don't see it used as much in practice.

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Finally, mAP, MMR, and NDCG are great offline metrics for evaluating recommendation algorithm relevancy given historical data but what about measuring these algorithms in the online production setting

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Furthermore, what about evaluating more than just relevancy

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? You may want to ensure your algorithms aren’t biased, surface a diverse range of items and optimize for differently for different actors on your platform

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We’ll dive into these questions in the next posts

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Stay tuned!

name: Evaluating recommendation systems (mAP, MMR, NDCG)
author: Tullie Murrell
content: For simplicity of the post we’re defining the average precision (AP) metric as the mean average precision (mAP). The only difference is that the mean will compute AP over all users in the test set. ‍

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), enabling significant advancements in language understanding, text generation, and more

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . With the help of memorization and compositionality capabilities, LLMs can perform various tasks like never before

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . They're already at the core of several products used by millions of people, such as Google's search engine, Github's Copilot, and OpenAI's ChatGPT

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: ! Title image from Xavier Amatriain (2023) Despite their groundbreaking capabilities, people argue whether these language models are still missing fundamental parts that make up general intelligence

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . The question is whether these language models, when the parameters are scaled up, could match human-level intelligence

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Or are these language models just understanding the statistics of language, so that they can pattern-match output well enough to mimic understanding

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: ? In the recent paper: “Augmented Language Models: a Survey” from Meta AI, the authors argue that statistical language modeling is a fundamental defect of LLMs

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Notably, the issue of having one single parametric model (rather than an ensemble of models working together), and a limited context of typically n previous or surrounding tokens, is a severe limitation

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . And although the scaling up for the models and their context will always improve things, there’s a need for research to solve these issues

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . The survey paper goes on to explain that language models need to develop reasoning skills (rather than just statistical language modeling)

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . With reasoning capabilities, these models can output a plan of how to solve a task with easier sub-tasks, which can be solved easily by other tools (e.g

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . APIs, programs, or task-specific models)

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Furthermore, these models typically become more interpretable as the causal means of how an LLM came up with an answer is captured.

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: The authors define reasoning in the context of LLMs as the following: Reasoning is decomposing a potentially complex task into simpler subtasks the LM can solve more easily by itself or using tools

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . There exist various ways to decompose into subtasks, such as recursion or iteration

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . In that sense, reasoning is akin to planning

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . So for the LLM to be reasoning in this context, we expect it to output an instruction set of how to complete a task when given a prompt

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Below we discuss several of the mentioned strategies in the ALM paper to augment LLMs to achieve reasoning including: Eliciting reasoning with prompting and Recursive prompting.

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: As opposed to “naive” prompting that requires an input to be directly followed by the output/answer, elicitive prompts encourage LMs to solve tasks by following intermediate steps before predicting the output/answer

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Prompting typically takes one of two forms: Zero-shot, where the model is directly prompted. You can think of this as the case when you’re using ChatGPT ’s playground tool and asking it questions it hasn’t seen before. Few-shot, where the model is first fine-tuned on task-specific examples before being prompted. Zero-shot Kojima et al

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . (2022) investigated reasoning in the zero-shot scenario by simply appending “Let’s think step by step” to the input question before querying the model

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Although this doesn’t do as well as the few-shot counterpart (explained next), considering this does actually work, it’s an argument for “just scaling these models up” as enough to have a general intelligent model that can reason

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Few-shot Wei et al

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . (2022) was the paper that initially introduced chain-of-thought (CoT), a few-shot prompting technique for LMs

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . They propose to train LMs on a prompt consisting of examples of a task, with inputs followed by intermediate reasoning steps leading to the final output, as depicted in the diagram below

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Wang et al

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . (2022c) further improve CoT with self-consistency: diverse reasoning paths are sampled from a given language model using CoT, and the most consistent answer is selected as the final answer

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: The idea behind recursive prompting is to explicitly decompose a problem into sub-problems in order to solve the problem in a divide-and-conquer manner

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . These sub-problems can either be solved independently, where the answers are aggregated to generate the final answer or solve sub-problems sequentially, where the solution to the next sub-problems depends on the answer to the previous ones

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . For instance, in the context of math problems, Least-to-most prompting ( Zhou et al., 2022 ), first employs few-shot prompting to decompose the complex problem into sub-problems, before sequentially solving the extracted sub-problems, using the solution to the previous sub-problems to answer the next one

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . From Zhou et al. (2022)

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: The prompt strategies above can be computationally expensive and require significant human effort to discover the right prompts for a given task
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Several recent works suggest using a scratchpad to train LMs to perform multi-step tasks by seeing input tasks and associated intermediate steps during training, and then predicting the steps and answer at test time
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Scratchpads differ from prompts in that they are fine-tuned on example tasks with associated computation steps
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Comparison and limitations of reasoning Reasoning can be thought of as breaking down a problem either iteratively or recursively
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . However, there are potentially infinite ways to break down these problems and when the LLM models predict each one there’s no guarantee that the chosen reasoning is valid
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . In fact, by having to predict each intermediate step, there may be more of a chance of error because each step needs to be correct rather than just the final output
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . For example, mistakes in nontrivial mathematical operations in a reasoning step may lead to the wrong final output
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Finally, a reasoning LM seeks to improve its context by itself so that it has more chance to output the correct answer
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . To what extent LMs actually use the stated reasoning steps to support the final prediction remains poorly understood (Yu et al., 2022)
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . Conclusion This post discusses the "Augmented Language Models: a Survey" paper and talks about several research directions to coerce, prompt and supervise LLM models to reason about the tasks they’re solving
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . The advantage of this reasoning is that the model breaks down the problem into smaller easily solvable sub-problems, and provides interpretability to the human using the LLM to evaluate how the model came to an answer
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . One thing that we mentioned earlier — and that is the main motivation of the paper we’ve been discussing — is that these sub-problems can not only be solved by the LLM model that generated them, but also by an external model or computation engine
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris
content: . We encourage you to take a look at the paper and stay tuned for more posts about this from us soon
chunk_metadata: {"Header 3": "3. Explicitly teaching language models to reason"}

name: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) reason?
author: Nina Shenker-Tauris

Results for MovieLens 20M: Million Song dataset: The In order to achieve these results multiple iALS hyperparameters are tuned, they provide recommendations on what values to use: Num iterations: How many times it trains on the data, typically converged in 16-20 iterations. Embedding dimensions: Controls capacity of the model, if it's too small it will negatively affect model performance. Training cost scales in d^3. Standard deviation: not too sensitive to this parameter, the typical value 1 / sqrt(embedding dimensions) Unobserved weight (weight of unobserved value) and regularization weight: Crucial, important to tune carefully, recommend to search on a logarithmic grid to determine the appropriate scale, then do a more refined search. Regularization regularization exponent: Reparameterization to decouple lambda and v, their optimal value was frequently 1. ‍
