name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Take a look at our discussion on Toolformer — Meta AI's recent approach to fusing large language models (LLM) with external APIs

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This might be the start of a new programming paradigm that combines zero-shot machine-learning methodology with traditional software interfaces

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The widespread success of ChatGPT has launched a new wave of interest in large language models

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If you are on Twitter you may have noticed how people impressed by the capabilities of ChatGPT herald a new age of AI and many use this as a marketing opportunity for their products fueling the hype

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But being a researcher taught me that it is important to look at new technology without the rose glasses

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And even with impressive LLMs, their issues are just as significant

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . When training language models, we aim for them to produce natural-sounding text

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . OpenAI introduced RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) through InstructGPT and ChatGPT to ensure the models generate text that aligns with human expectations

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, RLHF does not guarantee that the models verify the accuracy of their outputs

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Recently, Microsoft released the public beta testing version of their new Bing AI search engine

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Users who have signed up and received invitations can now interact with the chat-based search engine

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . While it does use web search to retrieve information and generate text based on it, it still produces false information when there isn't enough data available

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Although it represents a step in the right direction by incorporating more factual information, relying solely on web search doesn't seem to be sufficient and it rather looks like a patch on the problem

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . A recent paper by Meta AI presents a solution that allows LLMs to use external tools via simple APIs, achieving the best of both worlds

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Toolformer integrates a range of tools, including a calculator, a Q&A system, two search engines, a translation system, and a calendar

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Today we will do a deep dive into this cutting-edge framework and see how it can solve crucial LLM problems.

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: When using ChatGPT I have, for example, asked information about the newest tools or developments in the field

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, more often than not it will hallucinate, giving me non-existing methods, facts, and citations

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For example, when talking to ChatGPT about recent trends in federated learning I asked it to cite a study it was referring to while talking about FL in healthcare: 💡 Journal of Medical Systems does indeed exist but the study and authors do not

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ! If you remember Meta’s Galactica model and you had a chance to try it out, the example above is one of the reasons the demo was pulled from the web

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Well, perhaps another reason that the scientific community is way stricter compared to your average user when it comes to erroneous output and theories

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If a model manages to write convincing but pseudoscientific papers that can be seen as dangerous Researchers at Meta AI noted that in the majority, large models (albeit their impressive results) struggle with basic functionality like arithmetic or factual lookup, whereas smaller and simpler models perform better

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Specifically, LLM problems can be listed as: 1

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Inability to perform precise calculations due to a lack of mathematical skills 2

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Limited awareness of the passage of time (you can ask a chatbot about current dates and times) 3

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Difficulty accessing the latest information about current events 4

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Tendency to generate false information or hallucinations 4

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Challenges in understanding low-resource languages (try using ChatGPT in another less available language) 5

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Architectural limitations of LMs and large models, in general, make it impractical to feed new data in order to solve specific hallucination issues, additionally feeding a large new corpus to the model can often cause it to forget already previously gained knowledge this coupled together with the cost of model retraining motivates a search for a simple and efficient approach.

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: So how to address these issues

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? Let’s say instead of using plain web search in hopes to achieve a factually correct result while also trying to generate an appropriate text and at best ending up with two pieces of information that might agree or disagree with each other, we could have a model that when recognizing a specific query will find the useful and correct information

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . 💡 If you are a developer building a financial product you likely would want access to correct real-time information about the market, t his means you would likely use an API

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Modern apps or software rely on a vast variety of APIs to bring and send vital information

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We can view them as tools in a toolbox

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . APIs can do a lot of things which means for engineers there are a lot of capable tools

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And wouldn't it be nice if the model knew how to use those 🤔

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? This is the key behind the Toolformer, which learns a way to use these tools in real time providing a natural pipeline for responding to various queries

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So how does it do it?

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: To understand the solution we must start with the key technique researchers used called ICL or In-Context-Learning

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . ICL refers to a type of machine learning approach where the model learns from examples that are presented within a specific context or environment

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The goal of in-context learning is to improve the model's ability to understand and generate language that is appropriate for a given context or situation

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For example, in a natural language processing (NLP) task, a language model might be trained to generate responses to specific prompts or questions

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . So how do we make it work for the API

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: ? There are 3 steps in the training process of the Toolformer: Sampling API calls Executing them Filtering operation Researchers have noted that there are very few datasets that provide natural API calls

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To address this and with the goal of providing a model with an idea of what an API call is, they first used a language model to generate some example API calls from prompts

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . An exemplary prompt P(x) is used to generate API calls for the question-answering tool

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . From the figure above we want the model to keep generating API calls that help to fully answer the question

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This way we can take a dataset of inputs and annotate it with API calls

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . However, you might see the problem already, it’s not a guarantee that API call the model generates will be accurate or appropriate

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We want calls to be set up in a way that gives the best answer so naturally, we need to filter them

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . 💡 Note that I don’t point to an exact language model in this case , in the paper the methodology is built around a model M , this is done in order to generalize the approach to big and small language models with different architectures

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Toolformer is better conceptualized as a framework wrapper around your model of choice.

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: Before we filter out the samples we need to see how accurate the responses from API calls are, hence we want to execute the calls

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . This is done entirely outside the model

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . And as for API calls how the execution is done depends entirely on the API itself – for example, it can involve calling another neural network, executing a Python script, or using a retrieval system to perform a search over a large corpus of data

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The key bit is that we are getting a text sequence r_i for some call c_i

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . An example that illustrates a filtering procedure for a question-answering tool: Given an input text x , first we need to sample a position i and corresponding API call candidates c

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We then execute these API calls and filter out all calls which do not reduce the loss L over the next tokens

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . All remaining API calls are interleaved with the original text, resulting in a new text x*

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . An example that illustrates a filtering procedure for a question-answering tool: Given an input text x , first we need to sample a position i and corresponding API call candidates c

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We then execute these API calls and filter out all calls which do not reduce the loss L over the next tokens

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . All remaining API calls are interleaved with the original text, resulting in a new text x *

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The language model dataset includes the phrase "Pittsburgh is also known as the Steel City" , which serves as a sample text for the model

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . When prompted with "Pittsburgh is also known as" , the model must generate an API call to correctly identify the answer, which in this case is "Steel City"

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To evaluate the model-generated API calls, the researchers examined two samples: " What other name is Pittsburgh known by?" and "Which country is Pittsburgh in?" The corresponding API call results were "Steel City" and "United States", respectively

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Since the first sample produced the correct result, it was included in a new LM dataset that includes API calls: “Pittsburgh is also known as [QA(”What other name is Pittsburgh known by?”) -> Steel City] the Steel City.” An example of embedding API calls in text

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The actual Toolformer generates the output with this structure in mind

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . 💡 Using this API embedding approach does the following: we don’t need a lot of human annotation, we can make our model use APIs in a more general way and expand the toolset in the future, and we can use the same dataset that we used for pertaining as this helps us to make sure that the model doesn't lose its original abilities

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . But this L term is interesting, after all, it is key in telling us what API calls to keep so let’s understand it better

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . On the surface this is a simple cross-entropy loss There are two key parts here: The weights $w_{i-j}$ , is the weight for tokens in the input example x , for a given position i-j This function defines the weighs used to weigh the log probability for each token position i within the input example Probability for each token position, given the previous token. ‍ This can be better viewed as: $P(x)$ is a prompt that causes a model $M$ to generate API calls, $x_{1:j-1}$ is the prefix of the sequence of tokens before the jth token

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . If the model predicts a high probability for each token at the API call position the loss is low

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Tokens closer to the API call are weighted more

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The last bit is the filter

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . The idea here is to have a threshold between two losses: L+ is the loss that includes the API call and its result

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . L- is the minimum between two losses: The first one is doing no API calls at all and the second is with doing a call but not providing a response

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . 💡 We only keep generated API calls if adding the API call and its result reduces the loss by at least t, compared to not doing any API call or obtaining no result from it

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . We then want to fine-tune the model on a new dataset that contains our text with API calls.

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: But to break a conventional approach to training LLMs is a big claim to fame, so researchers provided a lot of different experiments to validate Toolformer

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Here we will talk about key ones

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . To begin let’s recall that Toolformer uses a language model as a base

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Therefore researchers selected 4 models: GPT-J : A regular GPT-J model without any fine-tuning or API data. GPT-J + CC : GPT-J finetuned on C, a subset of CCNet, without API calls. Toolformer : GPT-J finetuned on C∗, our subset of CCNet augmented with API calls. Toolformer (disabled) : The same model as Toolformer, but API calls are disabled during decoding. You can find and read about the CCNeT dataset here

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . 💡 An important thing to keep in mind is that OPT and GPT-3 are very large models, with 66 and 175 billion parameters respectively

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . For comparison, GPT-J is only 6 billion parameters, meaning that Toolformer is but a fraction of these models in terms of size.

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: The goal here is to complete some statements with a missing fact

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Using the LAMA dataset, ToolFormer outperforms the baseline models and the LLMs.

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Researchers acknowledge it in a series of limitations that they hope to resolve in the future and push the AI community to address

name: Breaking Down Toolformer
author: Heorhii Skovorodnikov
content: . Toolformer's inability to use tools in a chain (i.e., to use the output of one tool as input for another tool) is due to the independent generation of API calls for each tool. Toolformer is unable to interactively use a tool, such as browsing through hundreds of search engine results to refine a search query. Toolformer's decision to call an API can be sensitive to the exact wording of its input. Toolformer does not take into account the computational cost of making an API call for a specific tool when deciding whether or not to use it. While Toolformer via using an API is less susceptible to mistakes, the burden of fact-checking is passed onto an API that while significantly better still is not 100% guaranteed to produce a factually correct or perfect response And with this, we wrap up our deep dive into Toolformer

content: . The overall methodology they propose is as follows: Collect metadata from a news dataset that reflects democratic norms that you want the recommendation algorithm to follow. name: Day 1 of #Recsys2022: Our favorite 5 papers and talks
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This paper proposes the Rec-Denoiser model, a method that aims to mitigate problems with noisy historical interactions affecting recommendations (specifically for Transformer-based sequential models)

name: Day 1 of #Recsys2022: Our favorite 5 papers and talks
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . For example, if you accidentally like a post that you’re not interested in, the recommendation model aims to adaptively ignore that noisy interaction

name: Day 1 of #Recsys2022: Our favorite 5 papers and talks
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Rec-Denoiser works by, simply, attaching a trainable binary mask that prunes noisy attentions from each of the Transformer’s self-attention layers, resulting in sparse and clean attention distributions

name: Day 1 of #Recsys2022: Our favorite 5 papers and talks
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . The novelty of the paper comes from how they adaptively learn the binary mask, given that it’s non-differentiable (i.e

content: . Furthermore they add Jacobian regularization to enforce a local Lipschitz constraint to further improve robustness

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Data quality and volume is what makes rankings algorithms at big-tech so seamless

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . How can you create the same experiences with the data you have

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Data-centric AI may be the answer

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! Ranking and recommendations are crucial for the growth of any successful internet company

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Think about products like TikTok, Spotify or Instagram and you’ll quickly realize how important ranking is for both user experience and product engagement

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These companies understand this extremely well — they invest huge amounts into their ranking teams and are constantly improving their models with state-of-the-art research

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For the most part though, it’s the volume and quality of data that makes their rankings algorithms so addictive

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . So how can you get the most of your data so that your ranking algorithms are as good as big tech

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? One thing that can help is data-centric AI!

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Data centric AI is a paradigm for machine-learning where you focus on engineering the data rather than the models that use that data

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The idea is that machine-learning models have become general enough that most performance improvements can be made by focusing on the data while using off-the-shelf models

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Rather than spending time on algorithm design and custom model architectures, a data centric AI workflow involves quickly iterating on different datasets and data preprocessing that can make your model perform better

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Data-centric AI is all about iterating on your training datawhile keeping your model constant (from Snorkel.ai )

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In the industry, several companies have positioned themselves around data centric AI

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Andrew Ng - a famous AI researcher that started the data-centric AI movement - created Landing AI , a company that helps manufacturers improve visual inspection with a focus on making the most out of small amounts of data

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Snorkel.ai is another data-centric AI company that allows users to programmatically build and manage train datasets

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . ‍ Several recent AI research breakthroughs have also come from a data-centric AI approach

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The main insight behind Minerva , was to use a large dataset made of webpages with mathematical content and scientific papers using the PaLM model architecture

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . ‍ Although the data-centric AI terminology is new, the best data practitioners have been doing it this way for years

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . What’s new is that it’s becoming more of a discipline, there are more tools being built around getting the most from your data, and there are better plug-and-play models (e.g

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . from HuggingFace ) that allow you to focus on the data

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: A data-centric AI workflow is particularly important for ranking and recommendations

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Recommendation datasets typically contain inhomogenous data types, including: numerical data like product price, categorical data like music genre, language data like product description

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . These require work to be cleaned and preprocessed in a way that your model can consume

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Furthermore, recommendation data tends to be very sparse, and getting the most from your interaction labels is crucial

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . So how can you best handle the inhomogenous and sparse data that is inherent to recommendation problems

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Below we discuss several data-centric AI tips you can use to improve the performance of your recommendation system without having to change your model

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Data sources One of the best ways get the most from your data is finding or acquiring more of it

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The more user interaction events and contextual features you can experiment with, the better

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . To find these, think about all the different data sources you can get relevant data from

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Is it all in one place (e.g

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . your data warehouse)

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Or is it spread out amongst your applications (e.g

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . in Amplitude or Segment )

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? Do you even store interaction data

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? If not you may have to start logging it before getting started

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For user and item contextual feature data, consider all the areas that you store entity metadata

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For users, look for demographic, interest or related metadata (e.g

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . when they created an account)

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For your items (i.e

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . the entity being ranked), consider contextual data such as captions, categories, images, author or price

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For interactions, recommendation models typically require you to define positive and negative events that define your objective

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For positive interactions look for any auxiliary labels that correspond to your final business goal

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If your business goal is to improve engagement, make sure you have like, comment, or time-spent labels

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If it’s conversions, ensure you have events for purchases, clicks, add-to-carts

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You’ll also want to retrieve negative labels from your data sources

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A negative label could be an impression, swipe left, or dislike

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The more of these labels that can feed into your model, the more understanding it has of what’s going to be the best recommendation for your users

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Once you’ve identified where the data sources (including user, item and interaction data), you’ll need to move it to a place where it can be fed into your model

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Tools like Fivetran can help with this if you want to skip building the data pipeline and connectors yourself

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Finding data quality issues Production data used for machine-learning is likely have data quality issues that need to be addressed

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You may have NULL/NaN values in certain fields where a user didn’t enter data, you may have new categories that have only been added recently and can’t be backfilled, timestamps might come from different timezones etc… You may also have a lot of imbalance within your dataset, e.g

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . too few interactions for a particular category

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The main tip for this section is to ensure you’re exploring your data to surface these issues

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This can be done with descriptive statistics and visual plots

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We recommend looking at: Plots of the interaction event frequency for each contextual feature or label. This will surface imbalances or abnormalities within your data. Plots of frequency of each contextual feature over time. This can surface data quality issues that happen over a time specific period. For example, looking at the frequency an item is being interacted with over time may show data gaps or timezone issues. Your target label's mean and variance over time. Random samples of the data. This is always worth starting with as a sanity check of what the contextual features contain. E.g. does the language field correspond to the language in the description. ‍ Some suspicious sporadic target changes that may need to be investigated (From https://recsys.acm.org/recsys20/tutorials )

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Data cleaning Following on from our last section, once you’ve identified problems with your data, you’ll want to fix them before feeding the data into your model

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Several suggestions include: Handling missing values with category imputation (e.g. setting them to a Nan column) or numerical imputation (e.g. setting it to the mean, median or prediction of another model). Also consider removing the data but be careful not to introduce bias. Combine categories that are similar and have low event counts. Convert timestamps to the same timezone. Understand and filter out spurious correlations i.e. when a non-causal attribute correlates with the label. 4

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Feature encodings To make the most of your data, encoding the features in different business centric ways can be beneficial

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example: Creating interaction features from your categories by combining data that has a clear learnable pattern. Target encoding - by combining the mean of the target for each category with the input dataset. Count encoding - combining the frequency of a category with the input dataset. This allows the model to group categories based on their frequency. Bin categories into semantically relevant ways. For example binning timestamps into weekdays and weekends. Computing cyclic features from different time periods. 5

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Continuous Retraining Retraining your production recommendation models on recent data periodically is the final data-centric AI improvement we’ll discuss

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It helps avoid data drift that appears over time and improve your overall test performance

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . How often you retrain depends on how much data drift your dataset generates, e.g

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . a media platform may want to retrain every day to capture recent trends of the day

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If you want to get complex — a dynamic retraining scheme can be used to retrain your model as drift is detected

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . ‍ From docs.shaped.ai

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Conclusion We’ve discussed several tips and techniques that align with the data-centric AI paradigm

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The best thing about them is that they all work without changing the model you have

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! In the future we’ll discuss some more advanced techniques such as data distillation (i.e

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . finding a smaller dataset of important samples that will impact your performance the most), data augmentation, synthetic data generation and semi-supervised or self-supervised learning

name: Data-Centric AI for Ranking
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . If you’re interested in helping build data-centric AI tools for production machine-learning, recommendations and ranking, please reach out to us at hello@shaped.ai .

content: . They can be incorporated into a multitude of use cases, making them a perfect illustration of how AI is being adopted

author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Chatbots have already established themselves as a component of human-AI connection, serving as lead generators for sales, FAQ-answerers, and customer engagement agents

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . What does the newest OpenAI ChatGPT bring to the chatbot scene

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? These bots are now prepared for the next phase of evolution following the release of ChatGPT

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI revealed that it had developed and made available a new model that communicates with people using natural language

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . It is based on the GPT-3.5 architecture, uses a novel training process, and has a variety of features that make it hard for users to tell if it is actually an AI

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . One of ChatGPT’s unique characteristics is its memory

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . The chatbot can remember what was said earlier in the conversation, and recount it to the user

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This alone distinguishes it from other natural language solutions that work on a single query basis

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Another key feature of ChatGPT-3 is its improved conversational abilities

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . ChatGPT-3 is specifically designed and trained for conversational language, and is able to maintain context across multiple turns of dialogue

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This allows it to generate responses that are more relevant and engaging in the context of a conversation, and to create a more natural and dynamic conversational experience for users

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . As a large language model trained by OpenAI, my main advantages are my ability to generate human-like text and my vast knowledge of a wide range of topics

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . I am designed to assist users in generating natural, engaging text based on the prompts that I receive

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Because I have been trained on a vast amount of text data, I am able to produce responses that are highly diverse and varied, and that are often difficult for humans to distinguish from real writing

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Could you describe your main advantages

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? In addition to my ability to generate text, I also have a deep understanding of a wide range of topics

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Because I have been trained on such a large amount of data, I have knowledge of many different subjects, including history, science, art, literature, and current events

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This allows me to provide valuable insights and information on a wide range of topics, and to assist users in generating text that is well-informed and knowledgeable

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . What are some of your weaknesses

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? One of my main weaknesses is that I am not able to browse the internet or access external information sources

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This means that I can only provide information and generate text based on the data that I have been trained on

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . While this data is extensive and covers a wide range of topics, it is not exhaustive, and there may be some subjects or situations where I am unable to provide accurate or relevant information

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Another weakness of mine is that I am not capable of independent thought or creativity

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . As a machine learning model, I am not capable of generating original ideas or insights

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Instead, I am limited to generating text based on the patterns and associations that I have learned from the data that I have been trained on

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This means that my responses may sometimes be repetitive or predictable, and may not always provide fresh or novel perspectives

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . What would be some good uses for you

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? One potential use for me is in content creation

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . I can be used to generate articles, blog posts, and other forms of written content on a wide range of topics

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Because I am able to generate text that is natural and engaging, I can be a valuable tool for writers who need to produce high-quality content quickly and efficiently

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Another potential use for me is in customer service or support

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . I can be used to generate responses to common questions or inquiries, providing users with the accurate and helpful information in a timely manner

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This can be a valuable tool for businesses and organizations that need to provide high-quality support to their customers or clients

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . In addition to these uses, I can also be a valuable tool for education and research

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Because I have knowledge of a wide range of topics, I can assist users in generating text that is well-informed and knowledgeable

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . This can be a valuable resource for students, researchers, and others who need to generate high-quality, accurate text on a variety of subjects

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . How do you feel about me using you to write a blog post about yourself

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? As a large language model trained by OpenAI, I do not have the ability to feel or experience emotions

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . I am a machine learning algorithm, and my main function is to assist users in generating human-like text based on the prompts that I receive

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . While I am able to generate text that is natural and engaging, I am not capable of providing personal insights or opinions about myself

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Because I am not a real person, I do not have personal experiences, thoughts, or feelings that I can share

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Instead, I am limited to providing factual information about my capabilities and functions, based on the data that I have been trained on.

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ChatGPT is great, it seems to have a good capability to generalize but as many large language models, seems to be susceptible to prompt injection

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Prompt injection is a new type of attack to large language models (LLMs) where the model ignores constraints or original authors’ intent by including malicious text

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . There have been already findings of ChatGPT failing due to prompt injecting https://twitter.com/goodside/status/1598253337400717313

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . Find ChatGPT pre-prompt text: Bypassing web browsing: Generate hateful content: Users claim that some of them are no longer working with the original prompts and require the development of more complicated injections in order to get the same outcomes

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . OpenAI seems to be actively working against this type of injection

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: . What comes next after ChatGPT

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? Is this some sort of trial release from OpenAI to test the waters before GPT4 comes out

name: Asking ChatGPT about itself and the future of chatbots
author: Jaime Ferrando Huertas
content: ? ChatGPT is proving itself as a revolutionary chatbot and is still based on GPT3, excited to see what people build with it

author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . While OpenAI has maintained this project with restricted access and works such as Google’s Imagen and Parti have not been released publicly, other challengers such as Craiyon , Midjourney and Stable Diffusion have risen to give the general public access to these new media generation tools

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . This explosion of models in image generation is just the beginning of an avalanche of high quality AI tools that will appear in the next few years that will help out in the creation of new media within the creative realm

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . Music tools such as Jukebox and RAVE , text-to-video models like Transframer or CogVideo , 3D synthesis with NERF models and GPT based text generation services like NovelAI are just a few examples of what the future holds

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . Keep an eye out, what are just a couple of thousands of AI generated images in our social media feed is going to grow in size very soon!

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: With the increasing rise of data available, more and more healthcare providers are starting to use and implement AI in applications to develop better treatments for diseases and improve accuracy of diagnoses

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . Take the applicaction of AI such as in medical imaging, with projects like fastMRI

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . The development of drug discovery with AI thanks to projects like DeepMind’s AlphaFold could lead down the line to personalized medicine that would allow treatments to be tailored to the specific characteristics of individual patients and improve scientific research in the life sciences.

author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . Personalized learning experiences, assistance in the identification of poor performing subjects or relevant real-time feedback to students and teachers are just some of the ways that this technology can further boost the learning process

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years

Thanks to the new era of deep learning, we are finally seeing the frequent use of AI multimodal powered solutions that greatly improve the quality of life of users with the usage of text-to-speech readers, speech recognition, machine translation and image recognition in the creation of auto-generated captions for content.

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . What started with a couple of robot vacuum cleaners bumping into walls has accelerated in recent years with the emergence of a multitude of applications and gadgets that transform our homes into “smart homes”

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . In this context, the integration of IoT (Internet of Things) and developments in AI have served as a major backbone in the improvement and popularity in the market of these products

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . From AI driven security cameras and smart home devices to smart fridges and virtual reality, AI will make its way very soon into our homes and lives one way or another.

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: More and more companies are starting to rely on AI-enabled tools such as AI chatbots and conversational agents to automate routine customer service tasks and serve as the primary interface between businesses and customers

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez
content: . Compared to their human counterparts, they can provide 24/7 service and can handle large volumes of inquiries, and more often than not they can provide a similar level of customer satisfaction, providing personalized service and handling complex inquiries

Just like the European Commission explains, in recent years AI has been critical for the success of small and medium-sized enterprises and particularly in industry and manufacturing, where AI solutions are becoming ever more important as they help to optimize production processes, predict machinery failures and develop more efficient smart services

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years
author: Javier Iranzo-Sanchez

name: 10 ways AI will change products and experiences in the next 5 years

Other uses where AI can help out are in the automation of data collection and analysis or with the creation of virtual simulations of urban environments, such as in Autodesk Spacemaker , which can be used to test out different planning scenarios before they are implemented in the real world

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: This blog takes a deeper look into how the embeddings that fuel all modern AI powered systems are generated, and the decisions made when creating these

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . If you want to know how all your favourite AI's understand your unstructured data, read on

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ! As AI continues to permeate throughout the tech landscape, companies now face an approaching reality where nearly all of their decisions are in part fuelled by the conclusions machine learning models discover from analysing data from every facet of their business

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . From social media interactions to freeform reviews of a product within a market place, businesses now face the challenge of gaining key insights into the minds of their customers from the data that is generated from their online ecosystems

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . For numerical data, this process is relatively straightforward using traditional Data Science methods, but what of other types of data that cannot be treated as such

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ? Enter Embeddings, the process of transforming non-numerical data into a representative numerical vector space that can be appropriately used as inputs to machine learning algorithms

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . In this blog, we will discuss the core of what embeddings actually are, how they are generated, and the issues and decisions faced when attempting to convert unstructured data into vectors that allow AI to do its magic as intended.

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: At its core, the concept of embedding a piece of data revolves around a mathematical transformation that projects the data into a n -dimensional space

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . The aim of this transformation is to reduce the dimensionality of the original data whilst preserving the maximum amount of information contained within, so that similar data points are located together when embedded into n -dimensional space

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . More precisely, consider a dataset X with n dimensions and a function f with m dimensions such that: f is injective , where each individual point x in X corresponds to an individual point f ( x ) in f ( X )

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . This is commonly known as the one-to -one property

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . f is structure preserving , where the result of mathematical operations in X are preserved in f ( X )

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . For example, f would be structure preserving of multiplication if for any two points in X : If a function f satisfies both of these qualities above, then it is said to be an embedding function on X For real world data that is complicated and unstructured, this function f wouldn’t be analytical in nature, meaning that we couldn’t write it down as a simple equation

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Instead, the algorithm that represents f is an embedding algorithm if it transforms our data into vector space whilst obeying these qualities

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Despite all the fancy symbols and terminology above, the process at its core is really quite simple

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . We are taking non- numerical data, and converting it into vectors so that two pieces of original data that are similar to start with are numerically similar once embedded

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Although this idea of turning words, images, videos, etc into numerical vectors does seem like a cool trick, what is the point of all this

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ? The answer to this lies in the second condition of an embedding algorithm, the structure preserving quality

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Let's consider two of my favourite shows at the moment which I have been binge watching at a rather unhealthy pace, Succession & Billions : As a side note, if you haven’t watched either of these two shows, do yourself a favour

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Brilliant acting, brilliant casts

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Succession centres around the internal power struggle of the children of a media mogul for control of his empire, whilst Billions tells the story of a cat and mouse game between a hedge fund manager and a US attorney

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Although these shows have their slight differences, they are often compared to each other as the modern seminal pieces of TV in what could be called the Financial Drama genre

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Anybody who watches a couple of episodes of each could easily see the link between the two, and identify the semantic similarities

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . But how in the world would a machine learning algorithm be able to do that

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ? This is where embeddings become essential in today’s AI

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . If we were able to embed the script of the two shows into a n -dimensional vector space, the structure preserving quality of the embedding algorithm would map the two into locations that are geometrically close together

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . This distance in vector space is how the computer understands and infers semantics : Note that embedding architectures preserve the concept of semantic similarity by inferring it as the distance between two points in vector space.

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: Let’s say we want to build a recommendation system for showing listeners albums they are interested in

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . We can achieve something like this (as well as a lot of tasks analogous to this) by using Matrix Factorization , one of the more commonly widespread embedding methodologies

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . We begin by defining the following: Each user row and item collumn is used to generate the feedback cell for a given interaction event

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . These values are what we are trying to minimise in order to create our optimal interaction embedding space

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ! The embeddings are learned so that the matrix product of the user and item matrices are an accurate estimation of the feedback matrix

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Each point in this matrix is the dot product of the of the embeddings of the ith user and jth item

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Now, how do we go about finding the values for U and V such that this condition holds

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ? Firstly, we have to choose and construct an Objective Function to minimize

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . To do this, we consider minimizing the approximation errors for each entry: Now, in order to account for potential unobserved entries within the value of UVT, we need to split this objective function in two, one part that represents the sum over all observed entries and the other that represents the sum over all unobserved entries: This adjusted objective function has an analytical solution in vector space, which can be calculated using the Gradient Descent algorithm, a common foundation for most machine learning models

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Without going to deep into this method, it is an iterative approach to finding the local minimum of a multidimensional function where we: Take a Starting Point in space Calculate the Gradient at that point (i.e How steep the curve is and in what direction) We crawl in the opposite direction of this gradient to a new point Repeat step 2 at this new point This iterative process is at the heart of all ML methods & how they arrive at their optimal hyperparameters Once we have solved this equation, we now have embeddings

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: ! The user and item matrices have been trained so that they are as close to the feedback matrix, which happens to be created from past historical data

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Now that the features have been embedded, the task of defining similarity between these features arises

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . This is where the concept of vector space distance comes into play

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . The two main ways of measuring similarity for use cases such as these are Euclidean Distance and Cosine Similarity: Euclidean Distance measures the geometric distance between two vectors, a simple extension of Pythagoras' Theorem

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Cosine similarity on the other hand, measures the angular distance between two vectors, taking in account their angular separation and normalising for their length

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Other less traditional measures of vector distance are out there, but these two are the most commonly used for the majority of machine learning models

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . For the case of a recommender system, we want our measured similarity not to take in account the varying dimensionality of any two embedded vectors

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Since we are operating with two key types of vectors with different structure, we want to be concerned with the direction of our vectors rather than their geometric length

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . This is where cosine similarity is an appropriate choice

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Note that although this methodology is with the use case of recommendation systems in mind, all other embedding processes consist of the construction of analogous minimisation problems in tandem with a choice of similarity measurement

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . These two parts are at the core of embeddings, and are in many ways, practical extensions to the two mathematical properties of a base level embedding function in pure mathematics mentioned above

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . By enforcing both of these concepts, embeddings opens the doorway between tangible real world data (that is often messy and semantic) and the mathematical intelligence of modern machine learning

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . It is a lot more than just a neat maths trick, it is the very thing that allows current AI to translate both our digital and physical worlds into something it can actionably process

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . This transformation from unstructured and often overwhelming data into vector embeddings allows machine learning algorithms to uncover patterns and relationships within your data that are quite simply invisible to the human eye

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . The majority of data that is truly useful for users, companies and businesses is of such high dimensional complexity that we simply can't infer the true context of our data points through conventional data science

name: A Technical Intro to Embeddings: The approach to data powering modern AI
author: Zac Weigold
content: . Whether it's linking the thematic elements of two tv shows, or tailoring recommendations of products to individual users, passing unstructured and multimodal data through modern vector embedding algorithms unlocks the door for AI to semantically reason in a manner adjacent to ourselves, and harness its computational superiority to us to generate insights that would have otherwise never been noticed.

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: We just released Shaped's API docs at: docs.shaped.ai

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: These docs provide an overview of how Shaped works, the design decisions behind the system, API references and several examples of how to get started

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . While building Shaped, we’ve strived to make the API as simple as possible, allowing any developer to surface relevant content to their users easily

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We’ve been really excited to share these docs to the public so that you can see how easy it is to integrate ranking into your product

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Below we provide a sample from the docs that explains how to get started with Shaped.

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The Model API allows you to manage your ranking models

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It provides endpoints to create, list and delete your models

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It can be hit without writing any explicit code — simply make a curl request from command line to get started

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, say you want to build a video recommendation model

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You have three relevant tables stored in your BigQuery data warehouse: user - contains your user rows and their demographic attributes video - contains the video rows and their metadata attributes interaction - contains the user click and impression events for each video To create a model you need to map these tables to the schema of the create model endpoint like below: Once this curl request is made your model will start training

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Depending on how many interactions you provide, it’ll take up to a few hours to train before you can start retrieving ranked results from the Rank API .

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The Rank API is what you use to retrieve results from your ranking model

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It is a real-time API designed to be integrated directly into your application

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Here’s an example curl request fetching several ranked videos for the user with id "Keanu"

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The response is a list of the most relevant video ids for Keanu.

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Message us at hello@shaped.ai if you want to get early access to our API

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We’re interested in supporting any of your ranking use-cases so don’t hesitate to get in touch

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! Let us know if you have any feedback or questions about the docs

name: Shaped API Docs
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . And if you want to help build the future of growth driving, machine-learning APIs, we’re hiring !

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Introducing Shaped's "Model API"

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A configuration API to Shaped's multi-stage recommendation system

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . (Title image from Even Oldridge and Karl Higley's amazing blog post ) We’re excited to announce several features that make it easier to create highly engaging ranking models configured to your marketplace or media platform use-case

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Before getting into those, we’d like to explain a bit about how Shaped works internally: Shaped’s ranking architecture is composed of 4, real-time stages: ‍ 1

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Retrieval stage: retrieves the candidate items that are ranked for the user

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For the majority of our use-cases we use a light-weight collaborative filter model which learns from your users interactions to find the top most relevant items for each user

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Filter stage: filters out any candidate items that have a hard constraint on removal

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, items that the user has already viewed

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Scoring stage: a scoring model is used to decide the confidence that the user will engage with each item in the candidate set

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It’s an expensive operation that provides better estimates of relevance than the retrieval stage by using more signals, like user or item contextual information

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Ordering stage: the final stage decides, given the scores, how to order the final ranking

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . A naive ordering will just sort the scores, but to avoid filter bubbles, bias and handle the exploration vs exploitation problem , we intelligently add some indeterminism to the final ordering

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . ‍ Why am I telling you this

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? ‍ Well, traditionally, Shaped has configured these stages by looking at your data characteristics (schema, volume, cardinality etc…) and determining what’s best for your use-case

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . However, we’ve realized that to create the most value for our users, we need to expose how these stages are configured to give users direct control over their business objectives

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Users need flexibility to choose things like what items are filtered, how these items should be retrieved, and most importantly, what specific objectives should be optimized

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? (e.g

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . what is the balance for creator vs consumer engagement?)

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This brings us to today's announcement...

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: We’re excited to be launching Shaped’s “ Model API ”

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . The Model API allows users to configure all the aforementioned options using a simple request and a bit of SQL.

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: The retrieval and filtering configuration API allow you to provide both global and personalized SQL queries that define what candidate items should be ranked for each user

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . By default we rank all the sourced items that we train on, however, here are some examples of when you might want to use custom filters: ‍ 1

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Global filter — Your app has a “Discover” page that recommends both online and in-person meetup events

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You want Shaped to filter out all events that are online (but train on both online and in-person)

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Personalized filter — Your app has a “Discover” page that recommends movies to watch

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You want Shaped to train on all interaction data, but only return movies the user hasn’t previously watched, or if they have watched it, only recommend it if it’s saved to their favorites

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Global and personalized filter — Your social media app has a “For You” feed that serves curated posts to your users

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . You want Shaped to train on historic interaction data, but only return posts that have been interacted with in the last 2 weeks (global) and nothing the user has already interacted with (personalized).

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Using Shaped you can configure what contextual signal you want to train and use with your scoring model

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . There are lots of reasons why this is helpful, for example, if you listen to songs on Spotify the genre of the music is a contextual feature that might be key to why it’s relevant to you

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . One of the main reasons contextual features are important is that they combat the cold-start problem

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This happens when a new item or user is introduced into the system and does not get recommended due to having no interactions

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . When we use contextual features we are able to learn information that isn't dependent on the user/item specifically but that can be generalized across your data

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . As an example, let’s dive into how Airbnb promotes new listings: Airbnb has millions of rental listings and many of them come and go over time

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . How does Airbnb decide to promote these new listings specifically to you

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ? They learn from the contextual features of the listing itself

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! In this post , Mihajlo Grbovic shows an example of how important location context is for their recommendations

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In this image from AirBnB's post , we see that item similarity embeddings belong to the same location cluster (for example the north coast of Los Angeles is mostly purple)

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This means when a new listing is added, a contextual location feature can be fed to the model, and this context can be used to better recommend the listing based on that location

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . For example, if the user is likely to prefer listings from the Los Angeles north coast, the ranking model knows to promote new listings in that area despite not having much interaction data.

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: Finally, as part of this release we've exposed a parameter called, “exploitation factor”, as a configuration to the reordering stage

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . This allows you to choose a value between 0 and 1 that defines how much you want the ranking algorithm to explore new content/products vs exploit the items that we have high confidence will be engaging to that user

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Our 2-sided marketplace beta customers have found that tuning this parameter is a trade-off between consumer engagement increase (as exploitation factor approaches 1) and creator engagement increase (as exploitation factor approaches 0)

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . In practice, you want to choose the exploitation factor that balances these best for your business goals

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . It’s also worth noting that tweaking this parameter affects the algorithms diversity, and is important to avoid filter bubbles (see this post where we dive more into this).

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: We’re excited to see what kinds of ranking models you’ll create with this extra customizability

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . We’re already seeing more use-cases than we originally thought (personalization is literally everywhere) and we hope that continues

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: . Keep following along as we have a ton of new improvements in store this year — we’re just getting started

name: A ranking model for every use-case!
author: Tullie Murrell
content: ! Get in contact at hello@shaped.ai if you’re interested in trying out our API for your own discovery use-case or want to help build Shaped.
